1.html:
Why start here

Nobody ever really taught you how to manage your money. At school you learn quadratic equations, but not how to read a payslip, choose a savings account or steer clear of revolving credit. The result: lots of adults improvise, stress at the end of the month and make their financial decisions on gut feeling. This course is here to change that, one lesson a day, with no needless jargon.

The good news: personal finance doesn't require you to be good at maths. All it takes is a few simple rules, applied early and consistently. Time does the rest.

Money is a tool, not a goal

You can see money in two ways. Either as an end in itself ("I want to be rich"), or as a tool that serves your plans: housing yourself, travelling, changing career, helping the people you love, having peace of mind if things go wrong. The second view is far more useful, because it forces you to ask yourself what for.

Personal finance is the art of organising your money so that it serves your priorities, today and tomorrow, without putting you at risk.

In practice, money does three jobs for you:

  • Paying for the present: rent, groceries, transport, leisure.
  • Protecting you: a reserve for the car breaking down, losing your job, the fridge giving up.
  • Building the future: a deposit for a home, training, retirement.

Good money management means finding the balance between these three jobs. Spending everything today leaves you vulnerable. Saving everything stops you living. The aim of this course is to help you find your balance.

The main stages of a financial life

Priorities change with age and life events. Here is a typical path (of course, every life is different):

StageRough ageFinancial priorities
Studying18 to 25Keep a small budget, avoid consumer debt, open a savings account
First job22 to 30Build an emergency fund, understand your payslip and your taxes
Settling down25 to 40Rent or buy, life as a couple, children, first long-term investments
Mid-career40 to 55Pay off the home, fund the children's studies, prepare for retirement
Before and during retirement55 and overSecure your savings, organise your income, think about passing on your wealth

This course roughly follows that order: first taking back control (budget, bank), then saving, understanding taxes, housing, long-term investing, protecting yourself, and finally building an overall strategy.

Your best ally: time

Let's take two fictional characters. Léa starts putting €150 aside every month at 25. Hugo does exactly the same, but from 35. Both stop at 65. Let's assume an average return of 3% a year (an illustrative assumption, not a promise), with interest calculated monthly.

Léa (40 years of saving)Hugo (30 years of saving)
Total paid in€72,000€54,000
Capital at 65 (approx.)€138,900€87,400
Interest earned (approx.)€66,900€33,400

Léa paid in only €18,000 more, but she ends up with about €51,500 more. Why? Because her interest itself earns interest for longer. That's the effect of compound interest, which you'll see in detail in lesson 13 (and, on the business side, in the finance course).

Starting early, even small, is often better than starting late with a lot.

The five pillars of this course

  1. Knowing where you stand: income, spending, net worth (lesson 2).
  2. Mastering your budget without suffocating (lessons 3 to 5).
  3. Using your bank well and avoiding the traps of credit and scams (lessons 6 to 10).
  4. Saving and investing according to your goals and your time horizon (modules 3 and 6).
  5. Protecting yourself: insurance, taxes, retirement, major life events (modules 4, 5 and 7).

An important warning right from the start: this course explains how things work; it doesn't tell you what to buy. It doesn't replace personalised advice. And tax rules, ceilings and rates change often: whenever we quote a figure, we give the reference year, and it's up to you to check the current value on service-public.fr (the French government's official information site) or impots.gouv.fr (the French tax authority's site).

Three habits to adopt from today

  • Look at your accounts once a week, for five minutes. You can only manage well what you know.
  • Pay yourself first: set up an automatic transfer to a savings account on the day your salary arrives, even €20.
  • Wait before buying: for any unplanned purchase above a certain amount, let 48 hours pass. We'll come back to this in lesson 5.

Key takeaways

  • Money is a tool serving your priorities, not a goal in itself.
  • It does three things: paying for the present, protecting you, building the future.
  • Priorities change through the stages of life.
  • Time is your best ally thanks to compound interest: starting early matters more than the amount.
  • Tax rules and rates change: always check the current values.
  • This course explains; it does not give personalised investment advice.

Exercise

  1. Sort these expenses by the job the money is doing (paying for the present, protecting you, building the future): a travel pass, €50 paid into a savings account for unexpected costs, a payment towards the deposit on a future flat, a meal out with friends.
  2. In the Léa and Hugo example, how much more did Léa pay in than Hugo? Roughly how much higher is her final capital?
  3. With no interest at all, how much would Léa have at 65? What does this show?
  4. Thomas, 30, tells himself: "I'll save when I earn more." Give him an argument drawn from this lesson.
  5. Food for thought: write down three plans you'd like your money to work for over the next five years. Which seems most important to you, and why?
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. Travel pass: paying for the present. €50 for unexpected costs: protecting you. Home deposit: building the future. Meal out: paying for the present (and that's absolutely fine, money is also there for living).
  2. Léa paid in €72,000 and Hugo €54,000, so €18,000 more. Her final capital is roughly 138,900 − 87,400 = €51,500 higher. The ten extra years bring in far more than the payments themselves.
  3. Without interest: 150 × 12 × 40 = €72,000. At 3% a year, she has about €138,900, almost double. The interest built up over 40 years weighs almost as much as everything she paid in: that's the power of time.
  4. Starting small now beats waiting: a ten-year head start lets interest earn interest for longer. He can always increase his payments when his salary goes up. And once the saving habit is formed, it sticks.
  5. There's no single right answer. What matters is naming concrete plans (a driving licence, a trip, a deposit, a safety reserve): they'll give meaning to your budget in the next lessons. Often the safety reserve comes first, because it protects all the other plans.

Next lesson: taking stock of your situation, income, spending and net worth.

2.html:
Why it matters

Before setting off somewhere, you need to know where you are. Personal finance is the same: you can't budget, save or borrow sensibly without a clear picture of your situation. And lots of people only have a vague idea. "I earn roughly this much, I spend... not quite sure." This lesson gives you a simple method to take stock in an hour.

Two different pictures: flow and stock

There are two ways of looking at your money, and you mustn't mix them up:

  • The flow: what comes in and goes out each month (salary, rent, groceries). It's the film of your money.
  • The stock: what you own and what you owe at a given moment. It's the snapshot.

You can have a good salary and a negative stock (lots of debt), or a small salary and a comfortable stock (an inheritance, years of saving). Both matter. If you've taken the finance course, you'll recognise the idea: a company's income statement (flow) and balance sheet (stock).

Step 1: your income

List everything that comes into your accounts in a month, net (after contributions, and ideally after tax deducted at source):

  • net salary, regular bonuses (spread over the year: a €600 annual bonus counts as €50 a month);
  • benefits: APL (French housing benefit), prime d'activité (a top-up benefit for low earners), student grant;
  • income from a student job or a freelance activity;
  • regular help from family.

Only count what is regular and reliable. A one-off refund or a birthday present isn't income to build a budget on.

Step 2: your spending

Go through your bank statements for the last three months (a single month can be misleading) and categorise each expense. Distinguish between:

  • Fixed expenses: the same amount every month (rent, subscriptions, insurance, loan repayments).
  • Variable expenses: groceries, going out, fuel, clothes.
  • Annual or irregular expenses: car insurance paid in one go, Christmas presents, car servicing. Divide them by 12 to include them in the month.

It's these irregular expenses that cause "nasty surprises". They aren't unforeseen: they're simply forgotten.

Karim's example (fictional)

Karim, 26, a technician in Lyon, earns €1,950 net a month. Here are his average expenses over three months:

ItemMonthly amountType
Rent and service charges€620Fixed
Groceries€280Variable
Transport€75Fixed
Phone and internet€35Fixed
Insurance (home, car)€40Fixed
Student loan€150Fixed
Car loan€200Fixed
Leisure and going out€250Variable
Subscriptions (streaming, gym)€45Fixed
Miscellaneous (clothes, presents spread out)€120Variable
Total€1,815

He has 1,950 − 1,815 = €135 left each month. That's his current saving capacity.

Savings rate = (income − spending) / income

For Karim: 135 / 1,950 ≈ 6.9%. For comparison, the average savings rate of French households has been around 15 to 18% in recent years according to INSEE (France's national statistics office) (an order of magnitude; it varies over time and includes mortgage capital repayments). Karim isn't in the red, but his margin is thin.

Step 3: your net worth

Now for the snapshot. Your net worth is simple to calculate:

Net worth = what you own (assets) − what you owe (debts)

Assets: money in your current and savings accounts, investments, the resale value of a car or a home. Debts: outstanding capital on your loans, overdraft, money owed to friends or family.

Karim's assetsAmountKarim's debtsAmount
Current account€850Student loan (outstanding)€6,000
Livret A€2,300Car loan (outstanding)€2,400
Car (resale value)€4,500
Total€7,650Total€8,400

Karim's net worth: 7,650 − 8,400 = −€750. Negative! Is that serious? No, it's very common at the start of working life, especially with a student loan. What matters is the direction: if this figure has gone up a year from now, Karim is on the right track.

Watch out for the car: it loses value every year. A debt that finances something that depreciates makes you poorer faster than a debt that finances something that holds its value.

What the review reveals

  • The weight of loans: €350 of repayments out of €1,950, about 18% of his income. Once the car loan is paid off, Karim will gain €200 of margin.
  • The items he can squeeze: leisure and miscellaneous (€370) are the only ones genuinely adjustable in the short term.
  • His reserve: €2,300 on the Livret A is just over one month of spending. We'll see in lesson 11 that the usual target is 3 to 6 months.

Redo this review once or twice a year. It's your dashboard.

Key takeaways

  • Distinguish the flow (the month's income and spending) from the stock (what you own and owe).
  • Analyse at least three months of statements, and spread annual expenses over 12 months.
  • Savings rate = (income − spending) / income.
  • Net worth = assets − debts. It can be negative at first; its progress is what counts.
  • "Unexpected" expenses are often forgotten irregular expenses.
  • Redo your review once or twice a year.

Exercise

  1. Clara pays her car insurance of €420 a year in one go and spends about €360 on Christmas presents. How much should she set aside each month for these two items?
  2. Clara earns €2,200 net and spends on average €1,870 a month (smoothed expenses included). Calculate her monthly savings and her savings rate.
  3. Clara has €1,200 in her current account, €4,500 in an LDDS (a tax-free French savings account) and a car she could sell for €3,000. She still owes €5,200 on a car loan. What is her net worth?
  4. Karim pays off his car loan and changes nothing else. What does his savings rate become?
  5. Food for thought: why is a negative net worth at 25 not necessarily worrying, when it would be more so at 50?
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. (420 + 360) / 12 = €65 a month. By putting this aside every month, these expenses will no longer be "surprises".
  2. Savings: 2,200 − 1,870 = €330. Savings rate: 330 / 2,200 = 15%.
  3. Assets: 1,200 + 4,500 + 3,000 = €8,700. Debts: €5,200. Net worth: 8,700 − 5,200 = €3,500.
  4. His spending drops to 1,815 − 200 = €1,615. Savings: 1,950 − 1,615 = €335. Savings rate: 335 / 1,950 ≈ 17.2%, compared with 6.9% before. Provided he doesn't "absorb" that €200 into new spending: the simplest way is to set up an automatic €200 transfer to a savings account as soon as the loan ends.
  5. At 25, a debt for studies or setting up often finances the future (a degree, moving for work), and there are decades of income left to repay it. At 50, the horizon before retirement is shorter: a negative net worth means less time to build a reserve and prepare for the future. In both cases, what matters is the trend.

Next lesson: building your budget with the 50/30/20 method and its variants.

3.html:
Why it matters

Yesterday you took a snapshot of your situation. Today we move on to the plan: deciding in advance where your money will go, instead of discovering afterwards where it went. A budget isn't a punishment or a list of things you're banned from. It's a way to spend without guilt: if it's planned, you can enjoy it in peace.

The 50/30/20 method

Popularised by US senator Elizabeth Warren, this method has one big advantage: it fits in three numbers. You split your net income into three envelopes:

50% for needs, 30% for wants, 20% for savings and paying off debt.

  • Needs (50%): what you can't avoid. Rent, bills, basic groceries, transport to get to work, compulsory insurance, minimum loan repayments.
  • Wants (30%): what makes life pleasant but remains optional. Restaurants, going out, holidays, streaming, fashionable clothes, a new phone.
  • Savings (20%): emergency fund, projects, paying off expensive debt early, long-term investments.

Example: Inès (fictional)

Inès, 27, earns €2,000 net a month in Nantes. According to the rule:

EnvelopeShareTarget amount
Needs50%€1,000
Wants30%€600
Savings20%€400

Looking at her statements (as in lesson 2), Inès finds that she actually spends €1,150 on needs (her rent is €690), €600 on wants, and has only €250 left to save, i.e. 12.5%. She isn't following the rule. Is that a failure? No: it's information. She now knows where to act.

Why the rule doesn't always fit

50/30/20 is a starting point, not a law. In France, several situations make it hard:

  • Housing in big cities: in Paris or Lyon, rent alone can exceed 40% of a young worker's salary. Needs then easily go above 60%.
  • Low incomes: on €1,400 a month, needs swallow almost everything. Aiming for 20% savings would be unrealistic and discouraging.
  • High incomes: conversely, on €4,000 with moderate rent, you can easily save 30% or more.

Useful variants

VariantWho forIdea
60/30/10High rent, early careerAccept higher needs, save a little but regularly
70/20/10Low incomes, studentsEssentials first, 10% savings as a habit
50/20/30Comfortable incomes, a specific projectSpeed up saving for a deposit or a reserve
Zero-based budgetPeople who like detailEvery euro gets a job, until €0 is left unallocated

The zero-based budget deserves an explanation: at the start of the month, you take your income and allocate it line by line (rent, groceries, going out, savings account, birthday present...) until income − allocations = 0. It doesn't mean "spend everything": savings are one of the allocations. It's more precise but more demanding.

The most powerful principle: pay yourself first

Whatever the method, one trick changes everything: set up an automatic transfer to your savings on the day your salary arrives, not at the end of the month. What's left at the end of the month rarely gets saved: it always finds somewhere to go.

Income − savings = what you can spend, not: income − spending = what's left to save.

Inès decides to do just that: a €300 transfer on the 1st of the month to her savings account. To manage it, she cuts her wants from €600 to €550 (one subscription fewer, a few fewer meal deliveries). Her savings rate rises to 300 / 2,000 = 15%. Not 20% yet, but real progress, without giving up everything.

How to build your budget in practice

  1. Start from your review (lesson 2): net income and actual average spending.
  2. Put each item into need, want or savings. Be honest: a gym membership is a want (unless prescribed by a doctor).
  3. Compare with the target split (50/30/20 or a variant).
  4. Choose one or two actions, not ten. An overly strict budget gets abandoned after three weeks.
  5. Automate your saving at the start of the month.
  6. Review every quarter: a change in salary, rent or circumstances means revisiting the plan.

Key takeaways

  • A budget decides in advance where your money goes; it lets you spend without guilt.
  • The 50/30/20 rule: needs, wants, savings.
  • It's a benchmark: adapt it (60/30/10, 70/20/10...) to your rent and income.
  • Pay yourself first: an automatic transfer to savings on payday.
  • Change one or two things at a time, and review every quarter.

Exercise

  1. Mathis earns €2,400 net. Calculate the three envelopes using the 50/30/20 rule.
  2. Classify as need or want: rent, a streaming subscription, a Navigo pass (Paris public transport pass) to get to work, a weekend in Barcelona, basic food shopping, a new pair of designer trainers.
  3. Chloé earns €1,800 net and pays €850 rent including charges in Paris. Her other needs come to €300. What share of her income goes on needs? Which variant seems most realistic for her, and how much would she save?
  4. Inès gets a €150 net monthly pay rise. If she puts the whole rise into savings on top of her €300, what does her savings rate become?
  5. Food for thought: why does saving scheduled at the start of the month work better than saving "whatever's left"? Think about your own behaviour.
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. Needs: 2,400 × 50% = €1,200. Wants: 2,400 × 30% = €720. Savings: 2,400 × 20% = €480.
  2. Needs: rent, Navigo pass for work, basic groceries. Wants: streaming, weekend in Barcelona, designer trainers (getting dressed is a need, the brand is a want).
  3. Needs: 850 + 300 = €1,150, i.e. 1,150 / 1,800 ≈ 63.9%. 50/30/20 is out of reach. A 60/30/10 variant is already ambitious; more realistic: aim for about 64% needs, 26% wants and 10% savings, i.e. €180 a month. The key thing is to build the habit.
  4. New income: 2,000 + 150 = €2,150. Savings: 300 + 150 = €450. Rate: 450 / 2,150 ≈ 20.9%. She goes above 20% without cutting her current lifestyle: saving your pay rises is a very effective method.
  5. Money sitting in your current account tends to get spent: little temptations, unexpected costs, "I deserve it". By saving first, you naturally adapt your spending to what's left, and you don't have to make the hard decision to put money aside every month. You automate the right decision once and for all. We'll dig into this with the psychology of money in lesson 5.

Next lesson: tracking your spending without the headache, tools, apps and the envelope method.

4.html:
Why it matters

A budget is a plan. But a plan you don't follow stays a good intention. Most budgets fail not because they're badly built, but because people stop looking after three weeks. The secret: tracking that is simple enough to last. This lesson shows you several methods; pick the one that suits you, not the most sophisticated one.

What you really need to track

Good news: you don't need to note down every euro. Remember lesson 2: your fixed expenses (rent, subscriptions, insurance, loans) barely move. Once you know them, they look after themselves. What you need to watch is your variable expenses: groceries, going out, online shopping, fuel. That's where budgets slip.

Spending money left = income − fixed expenses − scheduled savings. That amount, and only that amount, is what you need to steer day to day.

Fictional example: Yanis earns €1,900 net. His fixed expenses come to €1,100 and he schedules €200 of savings at the start of the month. His spending money left for variables is 1,900 − 1,100 − 200 = €600 a month. That's the only figure he needs to track.

Method 1: envelopes

This is the oldest method, and one of the most effective. The idea: you split your spending money into envelopes (originally real envelopes with banknotes). When an envelope is empty, you stop spending in that category until next month, or you take from another envelope, deliberately.

Yanis's envelopePer monthPer week (approx.)
Groceries€280€65
Going out and restaurants€160€37
Fuel€90€21
Miscellaneous (clothes, unexpected costs)€70€16
Total€600€139

(The weekly amounts are rounded: a month has about 4.33 weeks, hence 600 / 4.33 ≈ €139.)

These days, few people pay in cash. The modern version: sub-accounts or "pots" offered by many online banks and neobanks, or a second current account with its own card, topped up every week. You spend with that card, and when the balance hits zero, that's it.

The "weekly spending account" variant

Even simpler: an automatic transfer of €139 every Monday to the account dedicated to variable spending. You only have one question to ask yourself: "how much have I got left this week?". No categories, no spreadsheet.

Method 2: apps

Many banks automatically categorise your spending in their app. There are also aggregator apps that bring several accounts together, which is handy if you bank with more than one bank.

  • Pros: automatic, clear charts, overspending alerts.
  • Limits: the categorisation sometimes gets it wrong (a cash machine withdrawal remains a mystery), and looking at a chart isn't taking action. Some free apps also fund themselves with your data: read the terms.
  • Security: only use authorised services to access your accounts (they go through the permissions provided for by European regulation, without you handing your bank password to just anyone). We'll come back to security in lesson 10.

Method 3: the spreadsheet

For those who like numbers: a table with one row per week and one column per envelope. Ten minutes every Sunday is enough. The advantage: you choose your categories and see how things change over several months. The drawback: it takes discipline.

The ritual that makes it all work

Whatever the method, what counts is regularity:

  • Every week (5 minutes): look at your spending money left. Are you ahead or behind?
  • Every month (20 minutes): compare actual spending with the budget. Which envelope overflowed? Why?
  • Every quarter: adjust the envelopes. If groceries overflow every month, it may not be a lack of discipline but an underestimated budget.

Going over isn't a disaster. If going out overflows by €40 in March, you can take it from the miscellaneous envelope, or accept a slightly quieter April. What matters is that you see it.

Hunting down leaks

Tracking often reveals "leaks": small repeated expenses you no longer notice.

  • Forgotten subscriptions: an app at €4.99, a platform at €13.99, a free trial that turned paid. Make a list once a year.
  • Bank fees: we'll come back to these in lesson 6.
  • Meal delivery: 2 orders at €18 a week is about €156 a month (18 × 2 × 4.33).

Example: having a clear-out, Yanis finds three subscriptions he no longer uses (€4.99, €9.99 and €13.99), i.e. €28.97 a month, or about €348 a year. No effort, just by looking.

Key takeaways

  • Track mainly your variable expenses: fixed ones look after themselves once known.
  • Spending money left = income − fixed expenses − scheduled savings.
  • The envelope method (or sub-accounts, or a weekly account) makes limits visible.
  • Apps help, but looking isn't acting, and be careful with your data.
  • The key is a regular ritual: 5 minutes a week, 20 minutes a month.
  • Hunt down leaks, starting with forgotten subscriptions.

Exercise

  1. Sarah earns €2,300 net, her fixed expenses come to €1,350 and she saves €300 at the start of the month. What is her monthly spending money left? And roughly per week?
  2. Sarah splits her spending money into 4 envelopes: groceries 45%, going out 30%, transport 10%, miscellaneous 15%. Calculate each envelope.
  3. On the 20th of the month, Sarah has spent €230 from the going-out envelope. What does she have left for the rest of the month? What can she do if a €60 night out comes up?
  4. Calculate the annual cost of two subscriptions at €7.99 and €12.99 a month.
  5. Food for thought: which tracking method (envelopes, app, spreadsheet) suits you best, and what made you give up tracking in the past?
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. Spending money left: 2,300 − 1,350 − 300 = €650 a month, i.e. about 650 / 4.33 ≈ €150 a week.
  2. Groceries: 650 × 45% = €292.50. Going out: 650 × 30% = €195. Transport: 650 × 10% = €65. Miscellaneous: 650 × 15% = €97.50. Total: €650.
  3. She has 195 − 230 = −€35 left: she has already gone €35 over the envelope. For the €60 night out, she can dip into the miscellaneous envelope if it's untouched (knowing this reduces her margin for unexpected costs), suggest a cheaper option, or decline. The important thing: decide deliberately, and don't touch the savings already scheduled.
  4. (7.99 + 12.99) × 12 = 20.98 × 12 = €251.76 a year.
  5. No single right answer. The classic reasons for giving up: a method that's too detailed, guilt when seeing the figures, forgetting. Hence the value of a simple, automated system (weekly account, transfer on payday) that requires as little willpower as possible.

Next lesson: the psychology of money, biases, impulse buys and social comparison.

5.html:
Why it matters

If managing money were just a matter of arithmetic, everyone would manage it: you'd just apply the 50/30/20 rule from lesson 3. The problem is that we aren't calculators. We buy on emotional impulse, we compare ourselves with others, we put off boring decisions. Understanding these mechanisms doesn't make them disappear, but it helps enormously to spot them, and to build safeguards.

Our most expensive biases

A cognitive bias is a shortcut in our brain that makes us take decisions that aren't always rational. They have been studied by behavioural economics (the work of Daniel Kahneman and Richard Thaler, both awarded the Nobel Prize in economics). Here are the ones that affect our finances most.

Present bias

We strongly prefer a small reward right now to a big reward later. €100 now for new jeans feels more real than €100 more for our retirement in 40 years. That's why saving is hard, and why automation (paying yourself first) works so well: it takes the decision out of the present moment.

The anchoring effect

The first price we see becomes the reference. A coat "€300 crossed out, €150" seems a bargain. But the real question isn't "how much am I saving?", it's "would I have bought this coat for €150 without the crossed-out label?". During the sales or Black Friday, anchoring works overtime.

Mental accounting

We treat money differently depending on where it comes from. A bonus, a tax refund or a gift is often spent more easily than salary ("it's extra money"). Yet a euro is a euro. On the other hand, this tendency can be used cleverly: decide in advance that half of any bonus goes into savings.

Loss aversion

Losing €100 hurts roughly twice as much as gaining €100 pleases (an order of magnitude from the research of Kahneman and Tversky). The consequence: people hold on to a losing investment hoping to "win it back", or never dare invest out of fear. You'll come across this bias again in the trading course.

Ease of payment

Paying contactless, in one click or in instalments makes spending almost invisible. Studies show that people generally spend more by card than in cash. "Pay in 3 or 4 instalments" is particularly tricky: 4 × €40 feels lighter than €160, but it's the same amount (and sometimes with fees). We'll come back to this in lesson 8.

Social comparison

Social media constantly shows us other people's holidays, cars and clothes, rarely their bank statements. Yet you only ever see people's spending, never their savings or their debts. Your colleague's new car may well be financed by a seven-year loan.

This phenomenon has a name: lifestyle inflation (or lifestyle creep). When income rises, spending rises at the same pace (a bigger flat, smarter restaurants), and the savings rate doesn't budge. You earn more, but you're no freer.

Wealth is often what you can't see: the money you didn't spend.

The "small expenses" effect

A takeaway coffee at €4.50, five days a week, 47 weeks a year (excluding holidays):

4.50 × 5 × 47 = €1,057.50 a year, i.e. €10,575 over 10 years (without even counting interest).

Be careful not to draw a guilt-tripping moral from this! If that coffee is a genuine daily pleasure, it fully belongs in your "wants". The idea is to spend consciously on what matters to you, and cut what brings you nothing. Better to cancel a forgotten subscription than a real pleasure.

Safeguards that work

  • The 48-hour rule: for any unplanned purchase above a threshold (say €50), wait two days. Often the urge passes.
  • The cost in hours of work: if you earn about €12 net an hour, a €960 phone represents 80 hours, about two weeks of full-time work. Is it worth that?
  • Remove the friction-free paths to buying: turn off saved cards on shopping sites, unsubscribe from promotional newsletters, take shopping apps off your home screen.
  • Add friction to your savings... the other way round: keep your savings in an account at another bank, harder to reach in one click.
  • Automate good decisions: scheduled saving, an automatic increase in savings with each pay rise.
  • Define your priorities: knowing what matters to you (travelling, your home, peace of mind) makes it easier to say no to the rest.

Money and emotions

For many people, money is a source of stress, shame or conflict within a couple. Not opening your statements is a very common behaviour: it's the ostrich effect. Unfortunately, not looking doesn't make problems disappear; it lets them grow (we'll see this with over-indebtedness in lesson 9). The 5-minute weekly ritual from lesson 4 is also a remedy for anxiety: a known figure is less frightening than an imagined one.

Key takeaways

  • Our financial decisions are influenced by biases: present bias, anchoring, mental accounting, loss aversion.
  • Easy payments (contactless, instalments) make spending invisible.
  • You only see other people's spending, never their debts or their savings.
  • Beware of lifestyle inflation when your income rises.
  • Safeguards: the 48-hour rule, cost in hours of work, friction when buying, automation.
  • Spend consciously on what matters, rather than depriving yourself of everything.

Exercise

  1. Identify the bias: (a) "I'm keeping this share that's lost 30%, I won't sell at a loss." (b) "I got an €800 bonus, I'll treat myself to a weekend away, it's extra money." (c) "The sofa was €1,200, I got it for €700, what a bargain!"
  2. Nora earns €1,800 net for 151.67 hours a month. What is her net hourly income? How many hours does a €550 games console represent?
  3. Lucas buys a €3.20 drink four times a week, 46 weeks a year. How much does that cost him a year?
  4. Lucas gets a €200 net monthly pay rise. Suggest a simple rule to avoid lifestyle inflation while still enjoying a bit of the rise.
  5. Food for thought: think back to your last regretted purchase. Which mechanism from this lesson was at play? Which safeguard would have prevented it?
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. (a) Loss aversion: refusing to crystallise a loss, even though the rational decision would be to ask whether the share is still worth holding today. (b) Mental accounting: the bonus is a euro like any other. (c) The anchoring effect: the €1,200 price serves as the reference; the real question is whether the sofa was worth €700 to you.
  2. 1,800 / 151.67 ≈ €11.87 an hour. Console: 550 / 11.87 ≈ 46 hours, more than a week of full-time work.
  3. 3.20 × 4 × 46 = €588.80 a year.
  4. A classic rule: 50/50, half the rise (€100) goes by automatic transfer into savings, the other half improves everyday life. Or a more ambitious rule such as 70/30. The key is to decide before the money lands in the account.
  5. A personal answer. Often: an emotional purchase (present bias), a "deal" (anchoring), a split payment (ease of payment) or wanting what others have (social comparison). The 48-hour rule is the most universal safeguard.

Next lesson: we open the module on everyday banking by learning how to choose your bank (traditional, online, neobank) and spot hidden fees.

6.html:
Why it matters

Your bank is the centre of your financial life: your salary arrives there, your spending goes out from there, and one day it will probably sell you a loan or an insurance policy. Yet many people keep the bank their parents chose for them at 18 without ever questioning it. And the difference in fees between banks can reach more than €100 a year, and much more if things go wrong. This lesson teaches you how to compare.

The three main families

The traditional (high-street) bank

These are the banks with physical branches in every town. Their strength: an adviser you can meet, a full range (mortgages, savings, insurance), and the ability to pay in cash or cheques easily. Their weakness: generally higher fees (account maintenance, card, services often bundled into "packages").

The online bank

These are often subsidiaries of large banking groups, with no branches. Everything is done via an app or by phone. Their strength: very low fees, often a free card. The catch: conditions (minimum income, or using the card a minimum amount each month, otherwise fees apply), less flexibility with cash, and no face-to-face appointments.

The neobank

These are newer players, often born in tech, with a very handy app, account opening in a few minutes and free or monthly-subscription offers. Their limits: a sometimes narrower range (mortgages rarely offered), and some don't have a French IBAN (a European IBAN must legally be accepted for transfers and direct debits within the SEPA zone, even if refusals still happen in practice).

TraditionalOnlineNeobank
BranchesYesNoNo
Everyday feesMedium to highLow, with conditionsLow or subscription
AdviserIn branchBy phone or chatMostly chat
Range (mortgages, savings)FullWideOften limited
Cash, chequesEasyMore complicatedOften difficult

This table shows general trends: each bank has its own conditions, which change regularly.

The fees to watch

Every bank publishes a price list (plaquette tarifaire), and all must show a standard summary of fees at the top, which makes comparison easier. Here are the lines to look at:

  • Account maintenance fees: from €0 to a few euros a month.
  • Bank card fee: from €0 to several tens of euros a year (much more for premium cards).
  • Payment instrument insurance: often offered, sometimes of little use because the law already limits your liability in the event of fraud (lesson 10).
  • Fees abroad: payments and withdrawals outside the eurozone, often a percentage of the amount plus a flat fee.
  • Incident fees: intervention charges, rejected direct debits, information letters. We go into these in lesson 7.
  • Withdrawals at another bank: some charge beyond a number of free withdrawals per month.

Incident fees are capped by law. For example, intervention charges (commissions d'intervention) are capped at €8 per transaction and €80 per month (and at lower amounts for customers in financial difficulty). These are the caps that have applied for several years; check the current values on service-public.fr.

Example: Julie compares (fictional)

Julie, 24, is with a traditional bank. She goes through her price list and her statements for the year:

Annual itemHer current bankAn online bank (conditions met)
Account maintenance (€2 a month)€24€0
Bank card€50€0
Payment instrument insurance€25€0 (not taken out)
2 intervention charges at €8€16€0 to €16 depending on the bank
Total€115€0 to €16

Over 10 years, with fees unchanged, the difference can exceed €1,000 (a minimum gap of €99 a year × 10 = €990, and up to €1,150). But be careful: if Julie often pays in cash (she's a waitress and gets tips) or if she values seeing an adviser for her future mortgage, the traditional bank keeps some advantages. She can also negotiate: drop the payment instrument insurance, ask for a cheaper card, or a young person's offer.

Switching banks is easy

Since the Macron law (2015, scheme in force since 2017), bank switching (mobilité bancaire) has been made easier: your new bank takes care, free of charge, of notifying the organisations that pay you money (employer, CAF, the family benefits office) or take payments from you (electricity, phone). You sign a mandate, and it handles the rest. Still, keep the old account open for a month or two, long enough to check everything has been transferred and that no cheques are still outstanding.

Another option: having two banks. For example, an online bank for everyday use and a traditional bank for a future loan or cash. It can also act as a "wall" between everyday money and savings (lesson 5).

The basic account, a right

If a bank refuses to open an account for you, you can ask the Banque de France (France's central bank) to designate a bank that will be obliged to open an account for you, with free basic banking services (a payment card with systematic authorisation, transfers, direct debits). This is the right to an account (droit au compte). Nobody should be left without a bank account in France.

Key takeaways

  • Three families: traditional (branches, adviser, more expensive), online (low fees, with conditions), neobank (app, often a narrower range).
  • Compare using the price list and your real usage (cash, abroad, need for advice).
  • Incident fees are capped by law, but they add up quickly.
  • The differences can exceed €100 a year, i.e. more than €1,000 over 10 years.
  • Bank switching is free and handled by the new bank.
  • The right to an account guarantees everyone access to a bank account.

Exercise

  1. A bank charges €2.50 a month for account maintenance, €45 a year for the card and €24 a year for payment instrument insurance. What is the annual cost?
  2. An online bank is free if you use your card at least once a month; otherwise it charges €5 for each month of inactivity. You don't use your card for 3 months of the year. How much do you pay?
  3. A customer incurs 12 intervention charges in the same month. What is the most they will pay, with the cap of €8 per transaction and €80 per month?
  4. Malik is a tradesman, often takes cheques and cash, and is preparing to buy a property. Which type of bank seems best suited, and why?
  5. Food for thought: why, in your view, do so many people never switch banks when it's free and simple? Link it to lesson 5.
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. 2.50 × 12 + 45 + 24 = 30 + 45 + 24 = €99 a year.
  2. 3 × 5 = €15 over the year. Still far cheaper than the bank in question 1, but only if you know the rule.
  3. 12 × 8 = €96, but the monthly cap is €80: they will pay at most €80. That's already huge, and it shows why you need to keep an eye on your balance (lesson 7).
  4. A traditional bank (or at least an account with a high-street bank): he needs to pay in cheques and cash easily, and an adviser to put together his mortgage application. He can combine it with an online bank for some everyday spending if he wishes.
  5. Several biases are at play: present bias (the effort is immediate, the gain is spread over time), status quo bias (we prefer not to change anything), fear of complexity, and the fact that fees are taken in small, barely visible amounts, like the "small expenses" in lesson 5.

Next lesson: accounts, cards, overdrafts and overdraft charges (agios), how they work and what they cost.

7.html:
Why it matters

The overdraft is one of the most profitable banking products... for the bank. A little dip into the red can seem harmless, but between the interest (the agios, French overdraft charges) and the incident fees, the bill climbs fast. In lesson 6 you saw that incident fees made a big difference between banks. Today we look in detail at how your account, your card and your overdraft work.

The current account and its tools

The current account (compte courant, or deposit account) receives your income and is used to pay your expenses. It generally earns nothing. Its main tools:

  • The transfer: you send money. An instant transfer arrives in a few seconds; within the eurozone, it must not cost more than a standard transfer (a recent European rule).
  • The direct debit: an organisation (energy supplier, phone operator) takes money from your account, with your authorisation (the mandate).
  • The cheque: less and less used, it remains valid for one year and eight days.
  • The bank card: payments and withdrawals.

Types of card

TypeHow it worksWho for
Systematic authorisationThe balance is checked at every payment: impossible to go overStudents, tight budgets
Immediate debitEach expense is debited within one or two daysMost people
Deferred debitAll the month's spending is debited in one go, at the end of the monthPeople who track their budget very closely

Deferred debit can seem comfortable, but it creates an illusion: your displayed balance is higher than what you really have. If you struggle to track your spending (lesson 4), immediate debit or systematic authorisation are safer.

Each card also has limits: a payment limit (often over a rolling 30 days) and a withdrawal limit (often over 7 days). You can usually adjust them temporarily from your app.

Authorised and unauthorised overdrafts

Being overdrawn means having a negative balance: the bank is lending you money, without you having formally asked for it.

  • The authorised overdraft: provided for in your account agreement, with a maximum amount (for example €500) and an interest rate. You can use it without incident fees, but you pay agios.
  • The unauthorised overdraft (or excess): you go beyond the agreed amount, or you have no authorisation. The bank can refuse payments, and it also charges intervention charges for every transaction that causes a problem.

The overdraft rate is generally high, often close to the usury rate (taux d'usure): the maximum legal rate, set each quarter by the Banque de France according to the type and amount of credit. For small loans and overdrafts, it has been around 20 to 24% in recent years (an order of magnitude, check on the Banque de France website).

Calculating agios

Agios = overdraft amount × annual rate × number of days / 365

Agios are calculated day by day on the overdrawn balance, and usually taken every quarter. They often remain modest in euros, which gives a false sense of security.

Example: Théo (fictional)

Théo has an authorised overdraft of €500 at 16% a year. At the end of the month, he stays at −€400 for 10 days before his salary arrives.

Agios: 400 × 16% × 10 / 365 ≈ €1.75. Not much.

But the following month, Théo drops to −€620, beyond his authorisation. Three card payments and one direct debit go through while he is over the limit. His bank charges 4 intervention charges at €8, i.e. €32, plus agios on €620 for about 20 days: 620 × 16% × 20 / 365 ≈ €5.44. Total: about €37.44 for one month. The real cost of an overdraft is mainly the incident fees, not the interest.

(Depending on the bank, the excess may also be charged at a higher rate, and the agreement sets out the details: read yours.)

Other incident fees

  • Rejected direct debit: if your balance is insufficient, the bank can refuse the direct debit and charge fees, capped by law (around €20 maximum per rejection in recent years, and no more than the amount of the direct debit itself). The creditor may also charge you its own fees.
  • Bounced cheque: fees are capped too, and there's a risk of a banking ban (interdiction bancaire: no chequebook for up to 5 years until the situation is put right).
  • Information letter before a rejection: charged for as well.

These caps can change: check the current amounts on service-public.fr.

Avoiding overdrafts: good habits

  • A small buffer in the current account (for example €200) on top of your budget.
  • Text or app alerts when the balance falls below a threshold.
  • Move your direct debits: ask your suppliers to take payment just after your salary arrives.
  • Don't treat the authorised overdraft as available money: it's credit, and expensive credit.
  • If you're often overdrawn, that's a warning sign: your budget needs revisiting (lesson 3), and lesson 9 will show you when to really worry.

Key takeaways

  • Three types of card: systematic authorisation, immediate debit, deferred debit.
  • Deferred debit gives an illusion of a higher balance.
  • Agios = amount × rate × days / 365.
  • The overdraft rate is high, often close to the usury rate.
  • The real cost of an overdraft comes mainly from incident fees (charges, rejections).
  • Habits: a buffer, alerts, well-timed direct debits, and the overdraft is not available money.

Exercise

  1. Calculate the agios on a €600 overdraft for 20 days at 16% a year.
  2. Ambre stays at −€250 for a whole 31-day month, within her authorised limit, at 16%. How much does she pay in agios?
  3. Ambre goes over her limit and has 5 transactions in excess, each charged €8. How much does she pay in charges? Compare with question 2.
  4. Why can a deferred-debit card lead to an overdraft more easily than an immediate-debit card?
  5. Food for thought: some people are overdrawn for a few days every month, just before payday. What concrete solutions, drawn from lessons 3 to 7, would you suggest to break this cycle?
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. 600 × 16% × 20 / 365 ≈ €5.26.
  2. 250 × 16% × 31 / 365 ≈ €3.40.
  3. 5 × 8 = €40 in charges, more than 11 times the agios in question 2. Going over the limit costs far more than the authorised overdraft, because of incident fees.
  4. With deferred debit, the month's spending hasn't yet been taken off the displayed balance. You think you have more money than you really do, and when everything is debited at the end of the month, the balance can plunge below zero all at once.
  5. Examples: gradually build a buffer (even €20 a month until it covers the usual gap); have direct debits moved to just after payday; switch to an immediate-debit or systematic-authorisation card; rework the budget with the envelope method (lesson 4); set up balance alerts. Once out of the cycle, the agios and fees saved can go into savings.

Next lesson: consumer credit and revolving credit, the traps to avoid.

8.html:
Why it matters

"Credit commits you and must be repaid. Check your ability to repay before committing yourself." You've surely seen this compulsory sentence at the bottom of French adverts. It isn't there by chance: consumer credit is useful when well chosen, but it can also be very expensive and drag you into a spiral. Yesterday we looked at the overdraft, the most discreet form of credit. Today we move on to the loans you sign for, and above all the trickiest one: revolving credit.

The main types of consumer credit

  • The personal loan: you borrow a fixed sum, without having to justify what it's for, repaid in fixed monthly instalments over a fixed term.
  • The linked loan (crédit affecté): it finances a specific purchase (a car, a kitchen). Advantage: if the purchase doesn't happen (sale cancelled, car not delivered), the loan is cancelled too.
  • Lease with option to buy (LOA) and long-term lease (LLD): widely used for cars. They aren't loans in the strict sense, but they commit you for several years.
  • Split payment ("pay in 3 or 4 instalments"): often presented as free, it can carry fees, and it encourages impulse buying (lesson 5). European rules are in the process of regulating it more tightly.
  • Revolving credit (crédit renouvelable): a reserve of money available to you, which replenishes as you repay. We'll come to it.

The figure to look at: the APR (TAEG)

TAEG (taux annuel effectif global, the French APR) = the total cost of the loan expressed as an annual rate, including interest AND compulsory fees (arrangement fees, insurance if required...).

The TAEG is compulsory in every credit offer. It's the only rate that lets you compare two offers honestly. Be wary of an advert that highlights an attractive "borrowing rate" but adds fees on the side.

It cannot exceed the usury rate (lesson 7), set by the Banque de France. But even below this ceiling it can be high: revolving credit often has a TAEG of around 15 to 22% (a recent order of magnitude, highly variable), compared with a few per cent for a well-negotiated personal loan.

Also look at the total cost of credit in euros, also compulsory in the offer: it often speaks louder than a percentage.

Revolving credit: how it traps you

The idea seems handy: you have a reserve, say €3,000, often linked to a store card. You use it whenever you like, and repay in small monthly instalments. Every euro repaid becomes available again.

The problem is the combination of three things: a high rate, small monthly payments and a reserve that replenishes itself. You can repay for years without ever seeing the end.

Example: Emma (fictional)

Emma uses €3,000 from her revolving reserve to furnish her flat. The TAEG is 20%. Let's compare with a personal loan at 6% over 24 months.

OptionMonthly paymentTermTotal repaidInterest cost
Revolving 20%, €90 a month€9050 monthsabout €4,415about €1,415
Revolving 20%, €150 a month€15025 monthsabout €3,680about €680
Personal loan 6%, 24 months€132.9624 months€3,191.08€191.08

(Simplified calculation with monthly interest at 20% / 12, without insurance or fees.)

At €90 a month, Emma repays for more than four years and pays about €1,415 in interest, almost half the amount borrowed. In the first month, of her €90, €50 goes on interest (3,000 × 20% / 12) and only €40 pays off capital. Worse: if she uses her reserve again in the meantime, the debt never goes down.

The smaller the monthly payment, the longer the loan lasts, and the more it costs.

Your legal protections

French law tightly regulates consumer credit. The main protections (rules in force in recent years, check on service-public.fr):

  • A 14-day cooling-off period after signing a consumer credit agreement, with no need to give a reason.
  • A standardised information sheet handed over before signing, with the TAEG and the total cost.
  • Creditworthiness check: the lender must check your ability to repay and consult the Banque de France register of repayment incidents (FICP).
  • For a large purchase in a shop, the seller must offer you an alternative to revolving credit (a standard amortising loan).
  • You can repay early; penalties may apply in some cases, but they are limited.
  • A revolving reserve unused for a year must be reviewed for renewal, and it can be cancelled.

When consumer credit can make sense

Credit isn't always bad. It can be justified for a real, lasting need (a car to get to work, with no public transport available), with a monthly payment that sits comfortably in your budget, a low TAEG and a short term. It makes much less sense for holidays, the latest phone or everyday spending: there, you pay more for something that doesn't last.

One simple question before signing: "Could I save up for a few months to buy it outright?" If so, waiting saves you the interest. Your emergency fund (lesson 11) is there precisely to avoid turning to credit when something unexpected happens.

Key takeaways

  • Always compare loans using the TAEG and the total cost in euros.
  • Revolving credit combines a high rate, small payments and a reserve that replenishes itself: a classic trap.
  • The lower the monthly payment, the more the loan costs.
  • Split payment is still credit and encourages impulse buys.
  • You have a 14-day cooling-off period and compulsory information.
  • Consumer credit can be justified for a real, lasting need, rarely for a want.

Exercise

  1. Two offers for an €8,000 car: a loan at 5% TAEG over 48 months (monthly payment €184.23) or over 60 months (monthly payment €150.97). Calculate the total interest cost in each case.
  2. On a €3,000 revolving credit at 20%, what part of the first €90 payment goes on interest? What part repays capital?
  3. An advert announces "borrowing rate 3.9%" and, in small print, "TAEG 7.2%". What's the difference? Which figure should you use to compare?
  4. Hamza signs a personal loan on 3 March and changes his mind. Until roughly what date can he withdraw?
  5. Food for thought: why do shops have an interest in offering a loyalty card linked to revolving credit? Link it to the biases in lesson 5.
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. Over 48 months: 184.23 × 48 − 8,000 ≈ €843 of interest. Over 60 months: 150.97 × 60 − 8,000 ≈ €1,058. The monthly payment falls by €33, but the loan costs about €215 more.
  2. First month's interest: 3,000 × 20% / 12 = €50. Capital repaid: 90 − 50 = €40. More than half the payment goes on interest.
  3. The borrowing rate only counts interest. The TAEG also includes compulsory fees (arrangement, required insurance...). Always compare using the TAEG, here 7.2%.
  4. The period is 14 calendar days from accepting the offer: roughly until 17 March (3 + 14). The exact way of counting is set out in the contract: better to act quickly and in writing.
  5. Revolving credit is very profitable for the lender, and it makes buying easy in the moment: the money seems available, the monthly payment seems painless (present bias, ease of payment). The loyalty card, with its discounts, creates a reason to sign up (anchoring on the promotion). The customer buys more, more often, and pays high interest.

Next lesson: over-indebtedness, how to prevent it, recognise it and get out of it.

9.html:
Why it matters

Every year, more than 100,000 over-indebtedness applications are filed in France with the Banque de France (the order of magnitude of recent years). Behind these figures there are rarely "irresponsible" people: most often, a life accident (job loss, separation, illness) has hit an already tight budget, sometimes loaded with consumer credit. The good news: there is a free procedure to get out of it. And above all, there are warning signs that let you react beforehand.

What is over-indebtedness?

Over-indebtedness (surendettement) is the clear inability to meet all your non-business debts, due now and to come, with your income and assets, while acting in good faith.

The debts concerned: loans, but also unpaid rent, energy bills, taxes, debts to friends or family. It isn't about one difficult month, but a situation that can't sort itself out.

The warning signs

Over-indebtedness rarely happens all at once. It sets in step by step. Here are the signs to take seriously:

  • You're overdrawn every month, earlier and earlier (lesson 7).
  • You use revolving credit to pay everyday expenses (groceries, bills).
  • You take out a loan to repay another one.
  • You put off some bills or choose which ones to pay.
  • You no longer open your post or your statements (the ostrich effect from lesson 5).
  • Your debt ratio is well above a third of your income.

Two simple indicators

Debt ratio = total monthly loan repayments / net monthly income

For a mortgage, banks generally aim for a maximum of 35% (a rule from the High Council for Financial Stability, HCSF, which we'll see in lesson 23). But this ratio doesn't tell the whole story: 35% of €5,000 leaves far more room than 35% of €1,500. Hence the second indicator:

Money left to live on (reste à vivre) = income − loan repayments − rent (or fixed housing costs)

This is what's left for food, getting around, paying for energy, clothes and coping with the unexpected.

Example: Marc (fictional)

Marc, 34, earns €2,100 net. He pays €650 rent and is repaying four loans:

LoanMonthly payment
Car loan€280
Personal loan (home improvements)€180
Revolving no. 1€170
Revolving no. 2 (store card)€120
Total€750

Debt ratio: 750 / 2,100 ≈ 35.7%. Money left to live on: 2,100 − 750 − 650 = €700 for the whole rest of the month. Marc is coping, just. But if his car breaks down or his overtime disappears, he tips over. This is a situation of fragility, even before over-indebtedness.

Reacting early: the first solutions

  • Take full stock (lesson 2): all debts, all income, hiding nothing.
  • Contact your creditors early: a payment holiday or a repayment schedule is easier to obtain before missed payments than after.
  • Close revolving reserves once repaid, so you don't fall back into them.
  • Get free help: the Points conseil budget (state-approved budget advice centres), social workers and some charities offer free support.
  • Be wary of "debt consolidation" (rachat de crédits): bundling your loans into one can lower the monthly payment, but by lengthening the term, which often increases the total cost (remember the calculation in lesson 8). It can help, it can also make things worse: compare the total cost, and beware of unscrupulous intermediaries who ask for fees before any funding (that's illegal).

The over-indebtedness procedure

If the situation is hopeless, you can file an over-indebtedness application (dossier de surendettement) with the Banque de France. The main stages (general rules, check on the Banque de France website or service-public.fr):

  1. Filing: free, online or at a counter. No need for a lawyer or a paid intermediary.
  2. Admissibility: a committee examines the application within a few months (around 3 months). Once the application is declared admissible, seizure proceedings are in principle suspended.
  3. The measures: depending on the situation, the committee can obtain a negotiated repayment plan, impose measures (rescheduling, lower rates, partial write-off), or, in irretrievably compromised situations, refer the case to a personal recovery procedure (rétablissement personnel) that wipes out the debts.
  4. Duration: plans last a few years at most (7 years at most under recent rules).

The flip side: the person is registered on the FICP (the national register of repayment incidents on personal loans) for the duration of the measures, up to a limit of a few years. During that time, getting new credit is very difficult, which is also a protection. The committee always leaves a minimum sum to live on, calculated according to the make-up of the household.

What protects you best

The best prevention is what you've been building since the start of this course: a realistic budget (lesson 3), regular tracking (lesson 4), safeguards against impulse buys (lesson 5), a firm refusal of revolving credit for everyday spending (lesson 8), and, from the next module, an emergency fund that cushions life's accidents.

Key takeaways

  • Over-indebtedness is often caused by a life accident on an already fragile budget.
  • Warning signs: chronic overdraft, credit to pay everyday expenses or another loan, bills put off.
  • Debt ratio = repayments / income; money left to live on = income − repayments − housing.
  • React early: take stock, contact creditors, use the free Points conseil budget.
  • Debt consolidation lowers the monthly payment but often increases the total cost.
  • The Banque de France procedure is free and can go as far as wiping out debts.

Exercise

  1. Sofia earns €1,600 net and repays €520 of loans a month. Her rent is €560. Calculate her debt ratio and her money left to live on.
  2. If Marc pays off his revolving no. 2 (€120), what happens to his debt ratio and his money left to live on?
  3. A company offers to consolidate Marc's €750 of monthly payments into a single €450 payment over 10 years. How much does he save each month? What's the risk?
  4. Which of these situations are warning signs? (a) Using your revolving credit to pay for groceries. (b) Having a mortgage at 30% of your income. (c) Paying the electricity bill with a new loan. (d) Being overdrawn for 3 days once in the year.
  5. Food for thought: why do so many people in difficulty wait too long before asking for help? What would you say to a friend in this situation?
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. Debt ratio: 520 / 1,600 = 32.5%. Money left to live on: 1,600 − 520 − 560 = €520. The ratio looks acceptable, but the money left to live on is very low: the situation is fragile.
  2. Repayments: 750 − 120 = €630. Ratio: 630 / 2,100 = 30%. Money left to live on: 2,100 − 630 − 650 = €820.
  3. He would gain 750 − 450 = €300 a month of breathing room. But he would be repaying for 10 years: 450 × 120 = €54,000. He needs to compare that with what he really owes today (the outstanding capital on his four loans) to measure the total cost. And if he keeps his revolving reserves open, he risks running up new debt on top.
  4. Warning signs: (a) and (c), because credit is financing everyday spending. (b) isn't a sign in itself: it's standard mortgage borrowing, below the usual threshold. (d) is an isolated incident, worth watching but not alarming.
  5. Shame, fear of being judged, the hope that "it'll sort itself out", the ostrich effect. Yet the earlier you act, the more numerous and gentler the solutions. You could tell a friend that it isn't a moral failure, that free help exists (Point conseil budget, Banque de France), and offer to go with them to take stock.

Next lesson: protecting yourself from scams and bank fraud.

10.html:
Why it matters

Payment fraud amounts to several hundred million euros a year in France (the order of magnitude in recent Banque de France reports). And scammers don't only target older people: young adults, who are very connected, are also prime targets, especially for fake investments and fake job offers. The good news: most scams rely on a few tricks that are easy to spot once you know them.

The golden rule

Your bank will never ask you, by phone, text or email, for your login codes or your card PIN, or to approve a transaction you didn't start yourself.

If someone asks you for these, it's a scam, even if the number displayed is your bank's, even if the person knows your name and address.

The most common scams

Phishing

An email or text imitates a well-known organisation (bank, tax office, health insurance, parcel delivery company): "Your parcel is held up, pay €1.99 in fees", "Your Carte Vitale (French health insurance card) is expiring". The link leads to a fake site that captures your card details or login details. Habit: never click on a link you've received; go directly to the official site or app.

The fake bank adviser

This has been the king of scams in recent years. A fake adviser calls you, often with your bank's real number displayed (a technique called spoofing). They talk about suspicious transactions on your account and ask you, "to block them", to approve transactions in your app, to give them a code received by text, or to make a transfer to a "secure account". In reality, you're the one approving the theft. Habit: hang up and call your bank back yourself, on the usual number.

Fake investments

"Guaranteed" crypto-assets, "automatic" trading, savings accounts with exceptional rates, investments in wine or diamonds: websites and social media accounts promise high returns with no risk. Often you even see your "gain" climbing on a dashboard, until the day you want to withdraw your money. These are often Ponzi schemes: the first investors are paid with the new investors' money.

Let's do a calculation: a site promises 10% a month. Over a year, that would be 1.10 multiplied by itself 12 times, i.e. about × 3.14: a gain of more than 200% a year. No legitimate investment promises that without risk. For comparison, the regulated savings accounts you'll see in lesson 12 pay a few per cent a year.

High return + no risk = scam. Return is always the reward for a risk (you'll see this in lesson 26).

Habit: check that the intermediary is authorised on the websites of the AMF (Autorité des marchés financiers, France's financial markets regulator) and the REGAFI register (for banks and payment institutions), and consult the blacklists published by the AMF and the ACPR (the banking and insurance supervisor).

Job scams and "money mules"

A very well-paid job offer asks you to "receive transfers and pass them on" in return for a commission. You then become a money mule: you're laundering stolen money, and you're the one who gets prosecuted. Nobody pays you to lend them your account.

Scams on classified-ad sites

A "buyer" asks you to click on a link to "receive the payment", or sends you a fake payment confirmation email. Rule: you never give your card details in order to receive money.

The signs that should alert you

  • Urgency: "you must act now", "the offer expires tonight".
  • Fear: "your account is about to be blocked", "you're a victim of fraud".
  • Secrecy: "don't mention this to your usual adviser".
  • The too-good-to-be-true promise: high gains, no risk, fast.
  • An unusual channel: an adviser contacting you on WhatsApp, payment requested in prepaid cards or crypto.

Scammers play on our emotions and our biases (lesson 5): fear makes us act fast, the lure of gain makes us lower our guard.

If you're a victim: the right reflexes

  1. Block your card immediately, via your app or the interbank card-blocking line (0 892 705 705, check the number, and write it down in advance).
  2. Notify your bank and dispute the unauthorised transactions in writing.
  3. Change your passwords, starting with your email and your bank.
  4. File a complaint (including online for some card fraud, via the Perceval platform).
  5. Report it: fraudulent texts to 33700, fraudulent websites on the official reporting platform (Pharos) or via cybermalveillance.gouv.fr.

Your right to a refund

The law protects you: for a transaction you did not authorise, the bank must in principle refund you quickly, and you have up to 13 months after the debit to dispute it (within the European Union). A limited excess (around €50) can apply in some cases, for example if the card is lost or stolen together with the PIN.

But be careful: if the bank considers that you were grossly negligent (giving out your PIN, approving the transaction yourself in your app), it can refuse to refund. It's up to the bank to prove this negligence, and disputes are common. If you don't get satisfaction, you can go to your bank's ombudsman (médiateur, free of charge). These rules change: check them on service-public.fr or the Banque de France website.

Key takeaways

  • Your bank will never ask for your codes or ask you to approve a transaction you didn't start.
  • Don't click on links you receive: go through the official site or app.
  • Faced with a suspicious call: hang up and call back your bank yourself.
  • High return with no risk = scam; check authorisations on the AMF and ACPR websites.
  • Warning signs: urgency, fear, secrecy, a promise that's too good.
  • If you're a victim: block the card, bank, passwords, complaint; you have up to 13 months to dispute an unauthorised transaction.

Exercise

  1. You receive a text: "Your parcel could not be delivered, pay €2.49 in fees here: [link]". What do you do?
  2. An "adviser" calls you, and the number displayed really is your bank's. They ask you to approve a €980 "cancellation" transaction in your app. What warning signs do you spot? What do you do?
  3. A site promises a 5% gain a month, "guaranteed". Calculate the equivalent over a year, taking compound interest into account. What do you make of it?
  4. On 2 February, you find on your statement a €320 payment debited on 15 January that you never made. What steps do you take, in what order? Are you still within the time limit to dispute it?
  5. Food for thought: why do fake-adviser scams work even on well-informed people? What personal rule could you adopt to protect yourself?
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. I don't click. If I'm expecting a parcel, I check directly on the delivery company's website or app. I report the text to 33700 and delete it. The small amount is there to capture card details, not to pay fees.
  2. Signs: urgency and fear (a suspicious transaction), a request to approve a transaction I didn't start. The number displayed proves nothing (spoofing). I hang up, approve nothing, and call my bank back on the usual number or use the app's messaging.
  3. 1.05 multiplied by itself 12 times ≈ 1.796, i.e. about +79.6% a year, "guaranteed". That's impossible without huge risk: it's almost certainly a scam. I check the AMF blacklists and pay nothing in.
  4. In order: block the card (app or blocking line), notify the bank and dispute in writing, change my passwords, file a complaint (Perceval for card fraud). Yes, I'm well within the time limit: you have up to 13 months after the debit. But the faster you act, the better.
  5. Because the scammer creates a situation of stress and urgency that short-circuits thinking, with reassuring elements (the real number displayed, accurate personal information, a professional tone). A good personal rule: I never approve anything during a call I didn't make myself. I always hang up and call back.

Next lesson: we open the savings module with the emergency fund, how much, where and why.

11.html:
Why it matters

Welcome to module 3! So far, we've put your budget in order (lesson 3), learnt to choose your bank and avoid the traps of credit (lessons 6 to 9). Now, a simple question: what happens if your washing machine gives up, your car breaks down or you lose your job next month?

Without a reserve, the answer is almost always the same: overdraft, agios, revolving credit… and the vicious circle you saw in lesson 8. An emergency fund (also called a "rainy-day fund" or "safety cushion") is what breaks that circle before it starts. It isn't the most exciting kind of saving, but it's the foundation for everything else: you can't build anything solid on ground that collapses at the first unexpected event.

What an emergency fund is really for

Emergency fund: a sum set aside, available at any time, with no risk of loss, intended solely to cope with the unexpected.

Three words matter in this definition:

  • Available: you must be able to get the money back within a day or two, without penalty.
  • No risk: there's no question of it having lost 20% on the day you need it (it's often when the stock market falls that the economy is doing badly and redundancies arrive).
  • Unexpected: not holidays, not the new phone, not the sales. Those expenses are foreseeable: they belong to savings goals (lesson 14).

In practice, it's there to absorb three kinds of shock:

  1. Small mishaps: car repairs, poorly reimbursed dental bills, a broken computer, an urgent train ticket (a few hundred euros).
  2. Big mishaps: losing your job, end of a contract, long sick leave, separation (several months of spending).
  3. "Forgotten" expenses: property tax (taxe foncière), annual insurance, the year-end adjustment of service charges. Normally your budget anticipates them, but in the first year people are often caught out.

There's also a less visible benefit: peace of mind. Having a few months set aside changes how you make decisions. You can turn down a toxic job, negotiate calmly, not panic. Remember lesson 5 on the psychology of money: financial stress pushes us into bad decisions.

How much to set aside?

The most widespread rule:

Emergency fund ≈ 3 to 6 months of essential spending

Careful: we're talking about essential spending (rent, bills, groceries, transport, insurance, essential subscriptions, loan repayments), not your salary. It's the "needs" part of your 50/30/20 method (lesson 3). If you lose your income, you'll cut restaurants and outings: what needs covering is the bare minimum.

Adjusting to your situation

Your situationRecommended rangeWhy
Student supported by family€500 to €1,000Few fixed costs, family safety net
Civil servant or permanent contract (CDI) in a stable sector3 monthsVery secure income
Permanent contract in the private sector, single3 to 4 monthsUnemployment benefit pays out, but with a delay
Fixed-term contract (CDD), temping, freelance, self-employed6 months or moreIrregular income, little protection
Single parent, or sole household income6 monthsNobody to take over
Homeowner, older car+ 1 or 2 monthsMore risk of big repairs

These ranges are benchmarks, not rules set in stone. What matters is having a clear target figure that suits you.

Example: Inès, 24 (fictional)

Inès is a marketing assistant on a permanent contract in Lyon. She earns €1,750 net a month. Her essential spending:

ItemMonthly amount
Rent + service charges€650
Groceries€280
Transport (TCL pass, Lyon public transport)€35
Electricity, internet, phone€95
Insurance (home, top-up health cover)€60
Student loan repayment€180
Total€1,300

At 3 months, her target is 3 × 1,300 = €3,900. At 6 months, €7,800. As she's on a permanent contract with a solid company, she aims for €3,900 to start with, then will move up towards 4 to 5 months later.

If Inès puts €150 aside a month, she'll need 3,900 / 150 = 26 months. At €200 a month, 19.5 months, so about 20 months. Is that long? Yes, and that's normal. We go step by step.

How to build it, step by step

  1. First milestone: €1,000 (or one month of spending). This is the most important milestone: it covers most small mishaps and keeps you out of overdraft.
  2. Second milestone: 3 months of essential spending. You're protected against most hard knocks.
  3. Third milestone: your full target (up to 6 months depending on your situation).

To make progress without thinking about it:

  • Pay yourself first: set up an automatic transfer to your savings account on the day your salary lands, not at the end of the month (there's never anything left at the end of the month).
  • Use windfalls: a bonus, a tax refund, a 13th-month payment, birthday money. Putting half into your cushion speeds things up a lot.
  • What about debts? If you have revolving credit at 20%, the priority is to pay it off (lesson 8), while keeping a mini-cushion of €500 to €1,000 so you don't sink again at the slightest setback. We'll come back to this order of priorities in lesson 36.

And when you use it?

That's what it's for! Don't feel guilty. Use it, then rebuild it as a priority over the following months, with the same automatic transfer.

Where to keep it?

The criteria are in the definition: available, risk-free. In France, the obvious answer is a regulated savings account (livret réglementé): Livret A (a tax-free, state-regulated French savings account), LDDS (livret de développement durable et solidaire, a similar tax-free account) and, if you're eligible, the LEP (livret d'épargne populaire, a higher-rate account for lower incomes). They are guaranteed, the money can be withdrawn at any time and the interest is exempt from income tax and social contributions. We go into detail in the next lesson.

ProductAvailable?Risk-free?Suitable?
Livret A, LDDS, LEPYesYesYes
Current accountYesYesMeh: 0% and too easy to spend
"Boosted" bank savings accountYesYesYes, but interest is taxed and the promo rate is often temporary
Shares, ETFs, cryptoYesNoNo: you might have to sell in the middle of a fall
Assurance-vie, PEAMore or lessVariableNo: designed for the long term
Plan épargne logement (PEL, a home-savings plan)No (withdrawal = closure)YesNo

A tip: keep your savings account at a separate bank, or at least in an account separate from your current account, so you don't see it "by accident" when you fancy treating yourself. Out of sight, out of temptation.

What about the return? With €3,900 in a Livret A at 1.7% (the rate in force at the end of 2025, check it: it changes regularly), Inès earns about 3,900 × 1.7% ≈ €66 a year. That's not much, and that's normal: the role of this money isn't to earn, it's to protect. It's insurance, and insurance has a cost (here, the income forgone compared with riskier investments). Money beyond your target can, for its part, be invested for the long term (module 6).

Common mistakes

  • Not having one at all, telling yourself "I've got my authorised overdraft". An overdraft is the bank's money, and it's expensive (lesson 7).
  • Having far too much: €50,000 sleeping in a savings account when you need €5,000 is money losing purchasing power to inflation (lesson 15).
  • Mixing it with project savings: if your cushion also pays for holidays, it isn't there when the real mishap arrives. One account for emergencies, another (or a separate line in your tracking) for projects.
  • Investing it on the stock market "because it earns more": it's precisely in a crisis that you risk needing it, at the worst moment to sell.

Key takeaways

  • An emergency fund is for the unexpected, not for projects or wants.
  • It must be available and risk-free.
  • A common target: 3 to 6 months of essential spending, to adapt (more if income is irregular or you're the sole household earner).
  • Progress in milestones: €1,000, then 3 months, then your target.
  • Automate: a transfer on payday, into a separate savings account.
  • Its natural home: regulated savings accounts (Livret A, LDDS, LEP).
  • Its low return is normal: it's insurance, not an investment.

Exercise

  1. Karim has these essential monthly expenses: rent €520, groceries €250, transport €75, energy and telecoms €85, insurance €45, car loan €125. Calculate his emergency fund target at 3 months and at 6 months.
  2. Karim is a temp worker. What range would you advise, and why?
  3. Karim can save €220 a month. How many months will it take him to reach the first milestone of €1,000, then 3 months of spending?
  4. Classify these expenses as "emergency fund" or "other": a) a weekend in Barcelona, b) replacing the water heater, c) a new smartphone because the old one is out of fashion, d) an insurance excess after a car accident.
  5. Food for thought: Chloé has €25,000 in her Livret A and spends €1,200 a month. She considers herself very prudent. What do you think?
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. Total: 520 + 250 + 75 + 85 + 45 + 125 = €1,100 a month. Target at 3 months: 3 × 1,100 = €3,300. At 6 months: €6,600.
  2. His income is irregular (possible periods without assignments): rather the top of the range, 6 months, i.e. €6,600. He can start by aiming for 3 months, then keep going.
  3. 1,000 / 220 ≈ 4.5, so 5 months for the first milestone. For €3,300: 3,300 / 220 = 15 months. And 6,600 / 220 = 30 months for 6 months of spending. Using his end-of-assignment bonuses would speed things up considerably.
  4. a) Other (a project, funded with dedicated savings). b) Emergency fund (an essential unexpected cost). c) Other (a want). d) Emergency fund.
  5. 25,000 / 1,200 ≈ 21 months of spending: well beyond 6 months. Her prudence is commendable, but part of this money (above, say, €6,000 to €7,000) could go towards projects or be invested for the longer term. In a savings account, it's protected but often earns barely more than inflation, or even less.
