It isn't a serious mistake, more a missed opportunity: we'll see in the following modules how to think about the next step, without any ready-made recommendation.

Next lesson: regulated savings accounts (Livret A, LDDS, LEP) and their real return, once inflation is taken off.

12.html:
France's favourite savings product

Yesterday we saw that your emergency fund must be available and risk-free, and that its natural home is a regulated savings account (livret réglementé). Today we open the box. There are more than 55 million Livret A accounts in France, roughly one per inhabitant: it's the country's most popular savings product. But many people don't really know what it earns, or that something better sometimes exists right next to it.

An important warning before we start: the rates and ceilings of these accounts change regularly (the Livret A rate is reviewed twice a year, in February and August). The figures in this lesson are those in force at the end of 2025: always check the current values on service-public.fr before making a decision.

What "regulated" means

Regulated savings account: a savings account whose rules (rate, ceiling, conditions, tax treatment) are set by the State, and are identical at every bank.

Practical consequences:

  • The Livret A at your online bank earns exactly the same as the one at your parents' bank. No point comparing rates between banks.
  • The interest is exempt from income tax and social contributions. What you see is what you get.
  • Your money is available at any time, free of charge.
  • Deposits are guaranteed (the State stands behind them, and the deposit guarantee fund protects up to €100,000 per person per bank).
  • Only one account of each type per person. Opening two is forbidden, and the bank checks.

In return, the money in Livret A and LDDS accounts is largely used to finance social housing and public-interest projects. Your savings are useful, even while they sleep.

The four accounts to know

AccountWho for?Deposit ceilingRate (end-2025 benchmark)
Livret AEveryone, from birth€22,9501.7%
LDDS (sustainable development and solidarity account)Adults resident in France€12,0001.7% (always equal to the Livret A)
LEP (popular savings account)Modest incomes, below a taxable-income ceiling€10,0002.7%
Livret jeune (youth savings account)12 to 25-year-olds€1,600At least the Livret A rate, set by each bank

A few details:

  • The ceiling applies to deposits. Interest can take you above it: if your Livret A is full at €22,950, interest is still added.
  • The LEP is the best regulated account, but it's reserved for households whose reference taxable income (revenu fiscal de référence) is below a ceiling (around €22,000 to €23,000 for a single person in 2025, more for a couple or with children). Many students and young workers are eligible without knowing it. Your reference taxable income appears on your tax notice (we'll come back to this in module 4).
  • With a Livret A + LDDS, one person can save up to 22,950 + 12,000 = €34,950 tax-free, which comfortably covers most people's emergency fund.

How the rate is set

The Livret A rate comes from a formula that blends inflation and short-term market rates, and the government can depart from it. The result: when inflation rises, the rate follows (with a lag), and when it comes down, the rate falls. It thus went from 0.5% in 2021 to 3% from 2023 to early 2025, then 2.4% in February 2025 and 1.7% in August 2025.

How interest is calculated: the fortnight rule

Interest isn't calculated to the day, but by fortnight (quinzaine: from the 1st to the 15th and from the 16th to the end of the month):

  • A deposit starts earning from the 1st or 16th that follows.
  • A withdrawal stops earning from the start of the current fortnight.

So: deposit just before the 15th or the end of the month, and withdraw just after the 1st or the 16th. Honestly, on a few thousand euros, it's a matter of a few cents: don't stress about it, but know that it exists.

Interest is paid once a year, on 31 December, and itself starts earning the following year: that's compound interest, on an annual basis (we'll go into it in detail tomorrow).

Annual interest ≈ average balance × rate

Example: €5,000 held all year in a Livret A at 1.7% earns 5,000 × 1.7% = €85, tax-free.

The real return: nominal rate versus real rate

Here's the heart of the lesson. The rate displayed (1.7%) is the nominal rate: it tells you how many extra euros you'll have. But what really matters is what those euros will let you buy. If prices rise faster than your savings account, you're getting poorer, even with more euros in your account.

Real rate ≈ nominal rate − inflation

Exact formula: (1 + taux nominal) / (1 + inflation) − 1

Period (benchmarks)Livret A rateInflation over one year (approx.)Real rate (approx.)
20233%4.9%− 1.8%
2025 (second half)1.7%1%+ 0.7%

In 2023, with a "record" rate of 3%, savers were actually losing about 1.8% of purchasing power: (1.03 / 1.049) − 1 ≈ − 1.8%. Conversely, in 2025, a lower rate of 1.7% with inflation of about 1% gave a slightly positive real return: (1.017 / 1.01) − 1 ≈ + 0.7%.

The moral: a high rate isn't necessarily a good rate. Historically, the Livret A earns roughly inflation, sometimes a bit more, sometimes a bit less. It preserves your purchasing power; it doesn't grow it. That's perfect for an emergency fund, but not enough to grow long-term savings. We'll dig into inflation in lesson 15.

Regulated accounts versus bank savings accounts

Banks also offer their own savings accounts ("super livrets", "boosted" accounts), sometimes with tempting promotional rates. Two traps:

  • The boosted rate often lasts only a few months, then drops.
  • The interest is taxed: by default at the flat tax (PFU, prélèvement forfaitaire unique), around 30% (income tax + social contributions; this rate was changed in 2026 for some income, check on impots.gouv.fr). We'll look at this in detail in lesson 19.

Example (fictional): a bank savings account at 2.5% gross on €6,000 earns €150 gross. After a deduction of about 30%, €105 is left, i.e. about 1.75% net: barely better than the Livret A at 1.7%, and only while the promotion lasts.

In what order should you fill them?

A simple, commonly used logic (this isn't personalised advice, just reasoning):

  1. The LEP first, if you're eligible: it's the best risk-free rate available.
  2. The Livret jeune if you're between 12 and 25 (a small ceiling, but a rate at least as high).
  3. The Livret A, then the LDDS: same rate, same tax treatment.
  4. Beyond your emergency fund and your short-term projects, think about longer-term investments (module 6).

Example: Malik, 23, first job, taxable income below the LEP ceiling, has €8,000 of savings. In a Livret A at 1.7%, he'd earn €136 a year. In an LEP at 2.7%, 8,000 × 2.7% = €216. That's €80 more a year, just by checking his eligibility.

Key takeaways

  • Livret A, LDDS, LEP and Livret jeune have rules set by the State: the same rates everywhere, untaxed interest, money available at any time.
  • End-2025 benchmarks: Livret A and LDDS at 1.7%, LEP at 2.7%. Ceilings of €22,950, €12,000 and €10,000. Check them: they change often.
  • The LEP is the most attractive, subject to income: many young people are eligible.
  • Interest is calculated by fortnight and paid on 31 December.
  • Real rate ≈ nominal rate − inflation: this is what measures your true gain.
  • Regulated accounts roughly protect your purchasing power, without growing it.

Exercise

  1. Sofia has €12,000 in her Livret A all year, at 1.7%. How much interest does she earn? How much tax will she pay on it?
  2. She is eligible for the LEP (2.7%). If she transfers €10,000 to it and keeps €2,000 in her Livret A, how much more does she earn over the year?
  3. A savings account pays 2% and inflation is 3%. Calculate the real rate, approximately then exactly.
  4. A bank savings account offers 3% gross for 3 months, then 1% gross. The interest is taxed at about 30%. On €10,000 for one year, how much do you get net? Compare with a Livret A at 1.7%.
  5. Food for thought: your uncle tells you "the Livret A is for losers, it earns nothing". What's true and what's false in that statement?
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. 12,000 × 1.7% = €204. Tax: €0; Livret A interest is exempt from income tax and social contributions.
  2. LEP: 10,000 × 2.7% = €270. Livret A: 2,000 × 1.7% = €34. Total: €304, i.e. €100 more than before.
  3. Approximate: 2% − 3% = − 1%. Exact: 1.02 / 1.03 − 1 ≈ − 0.97%. She loses about 1% of purchasing power a year.
  4. First 3 months: 10,000 × 3% × 3/12 = €75. Next 9 months: 10,000 × 1% × 9/12 = €75. Gross total: €150. Net after 30%: 150 × 0.7 = €105. Livret A: 10,000 × 1.7% = €170, untaxed. The Livret A wins comfortably, despite the "3%" promotion on display. (Simplified calculation, ignoring compounding during the year.)
  5. True: the Livret A won't make you rich; its real return hovers around zero over time. False: that's not what it's for! It's perfect for money you might need quickly and absolutely don't want to risk losing: the emergency fund and short-term projects. The real "loser" is rather the person with no cushion who ends up overdrawn at 16%, or the one who puts their emergency fund on the stock market. Each pot of money has its role, and therefore its product.

Next lesson: compound interest and the effect of time, or why saving early changes everything.

13.html:
The most underestimated force in your financial life

Yesterday we saw that the interest on your Livret A was paid on 31 December and itself started earning the following year. That small detail hides a powerful mechanism: compound interest. Properly understood, it changes how you see saving, and above all the importance of starting early. Misunderstood, it works against you (remember the revolving credit in lesson 8: compound interest works on debts too).

Don't panic, there's only one formula to remember, and we'll mostly reason with examples.

Simple or compound interest: the difference

  • With simple interest, interest is calculated each year on your starting capital only. €1,000 at 4%: €40 a year, always €40.
  • With compound interest, the interest is added to the capital and earns in its turn. It's "interest on interest".

Final value = Capital × (1 + rate) to the power of the number of years

VF = C × (1 + i)^n

Example: €10,000 invested at 4% a year.

PeriodSimple interestCompound interest
5 years€12,000€12,167
10 years€14,000€14,802
20 years€18,000€21,911
30 years€22,000€32,434
40 years€26,000€48,010

In the first years, the difference is almost invisible. Then it takes off: after 40 years, compound interest has almost multiplied the capital by five (1.04 to the power of 40 ≈ 4.8), compared with 2.6 with simple interest. Compound growth isn't a straight line, it's a curve that accelerates. You'll see these calculations in more depth in the finance course, in the lesson on the time value of money.

Important: 4% a year is a hypothetical rate chosen here for illustration. No risk-free investment today guarantees 4% a year for 40 years, and higher-yielding investments carry a risk of loss (module 6).

The rule of 72: mental arithmetic

To find out how long it takes your money to double:

Number of years to double ≈ 72 / rate (in %)

  • At 1.7% (Livret A at end-2025): 72 / 1.7 ≈ 42 years.
  • At 4%: 72 / 4 = 18 years (check: 1.04 to the power of 18 ≈ 2.03).
  • At 7%: 72 / 7 ≈ 10 years.

It works for debts too: a revolving card debt at 20% that isn't repaid doubles in 72 / 20 ≈ 3.6 years. A thousand euros left unpaid becomes about €6,200 in ten years. That's why you pay off expensive debts first.

The real magic ingredient: time

In the formula C × (1 + i)^n, the n is an exponent. It does all the work. Let's look at three fictional characters, all investing at a hypothetical 4% a year.

  • Emma starts at 25: she invests €100 a month (€1,200 a year) for only 10 years, then stops and lets the money work until 65.
  • Lucas starts at 35: he invests €100 a month for 30 years, until 65.
  • Nora starts at 25 and never stops: €100 a month for 40 years.
CharacterTotal paid inCapital at 65Of which interest
Emma (25 to 35)€12,000€46,729€34,729
Lucas (35 to 65)€36,000€67,302€31,302
Nora (25 to 65)€48,000€114,031€66,031

Simplified calculation: payments of €1,200 at the end of each year.

Look closely. Lucas paid in three times as much as Emma (€36,000 against €12,000), and yet Emma earned more interest than him. Her first 10 years had 30 more years to grow. As for Nora, who simply started early and kept going, she has more than €114,000, over half of which didn't come out of her pocket.

The lesson isn't "it's too late after 30" (Lucas does very well!). It's: every year counts, and the euros you save at 20 or 25 are the most "powerful" of your life.

The three levers, and the one people forget

Your final capital depends on three things:

  1. The amount you save.
  2. The rate you get (which depends on the risk you accept; we'll come back to this in module 6).
  3. The time, by far the most powerful lever and the only one you can never catch up on.

And there's a fourth lever people forget: fees. They compound too, but against you. €10,000 at 5% for 30 years gives €43,219. If 1% of annual fees brings the return down to 4%, you're left with only €32,434. A little "1%" has cost you about a quarter of the final capital. Remember this reflex for lessons 27 to 29: one percentage point of fees is never a detail over the long term.

What this means for you in practice

  • Start small, but start: €30 or €50 a month at 20 is better than €0 while waiting "to earn more". €50 a month for 40 years at 4% gives about €57,000.
  • Automate: a monthly standing transfer, as for your emergency fund (lesson 11).
  • Don't touch the interest: withdrawing it breaks the mechanism.
  • Pay off your expensive debts first: there's no point earning 4% on one side while paying 20% on the other.
  • Be patient: the curve is flat at the start. That's normal, and it's where most people give up.

Key takeaways

  • With compound interest, interest itself earns interest: VF = C × (1 + i)^n.
  • Growth is slow at first, then accelerates strongly over the years.
  • Rule of 72: your money doubles in about 72 / rate years.
  • Time is the most powerful lever: starting early often counts for more than paying in a lot.
  • Compound interest also works against you: expensive debts and fees.
  • Rates of 4% or more are never guaranteed without risk: they are assumptions.

Exercise

  1. You invest €3,000 at 4% a year. How much will you have after 20 years? And after 30?
  2. Using the rule of 72, how long does a sum invested at 3% take to double? And at 6%?
  3. Option A: €100 a month (€1,200 a year) for 20 years. Option B: €200 a month (€2,400 a year) for 10 years. Same total paid in (€24,000), same 4% rate, payments at the end of the year. Which gives more at the end of the payment period?
  4. A €1,000 revolving credit at 20% a year isn't repaid. How much is owed after 5 years (annual compound interest)?
  5. Food for thought: Yanis, 22, says: "I'll start saving at 30, when I'm really earning a living." What do you tell him, while staying realistic about his situation?
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. 20 years: 3,000 × 1.04 to the power of 20 ≈ €6,573. 30 years: 3,000 × 1.04 to the power of 30 ≈ €9,730. The last 10 years earned more (€3,157) than the previous 10.
  2. At 3%: 72 / 3 = 24 years. At 6%: 72 / 6 = 12 years. Doubling the rate roughly halves the doubling time.
  3. A: about €35,734 after 20 years. B: about €28,815 after 10 years. A wins: the money had more time to work. (Careful, the comparison is made at different dates. If B's capital is left to grow for 10 more years at 4%, it reaches 28,815 × 1.04 to the power of 10 ≈ €42,650, and overtakes A, because the money was paid in earlier. Time, always time.)
  4. 1,000 × 1.2 to the power of 5 ≈ €2,488. The debt has more than doubled, as the rule of 72 predicted (doubling in 3.6 years).
  5. He's right on one point: on a small salary, the priority remains the budget, having no expensive debts and an emergency fund. But waiting 8 years means giving up the most powerful ingredient: time. Even €30 a month builds a habit, and those first euros will have the most years to grow. He can increase his payments when his salary goes up. Don't let the perfect be the enemy of the good.

Next lesson: setting short, medium and long-term savings goals, and knowing how much to put aside each month.

14.html:
Saving "for nothing" doesn't last

You have your emergency fund (lesson 11), you know where to keep it (lesson 12) and you've understood that time works for you (lesson 13). One question remains, and it makes all the difference between those who really save and those who "try": what are you saving for?

"Putting money aside" in general is vague, and vagueness doesn't stand up to a deal on trainers. "Having €1,500 in July to go to Portugal with my friends" is concrete, motivating and, above all, calculable. Today we learn to turn wishes into figures-based goals, and to choose the right product according to the time horizon.

A good goal is a SMART goal

The method comes from the business world, but it works very well for your money:

  • Specific: "a deposit to buy a studio flat", not "savings".
  • Measurable: a precise amount (€20,000).
  • Achievable: compatible with your real budget.
  • Realistic: consistent with your other priorities.
  • Time-bound: a deadline (in 6 years).

Savings goal = a project + an amount + a date

Once those three elements are set, the rest is just arithmetic.

Three horizons, three logics

HorizonExamplesPriorityTypical products
Short term (under 2 years)Holidays, a computer, driving licence, end-of-year presentsAvailability, no riskRegulated savings accounts
Medium term (2 to 8 years)Car, home deposit, wedding, gap yearSecurity, a little returnSavings accounts, assurance-vie euro funds, plan d'épargne logement (home-savings plan)
Long term (over 8 years)Retirement, children's education, financial independenceReturn, accepting fluctuationsAssurance-vie, PEA, PER (modules 6 and 7)

The golden rule: the closer the deadline, the less risk you can take. If you need the money in 8 months, a 20% market fall just beforehand would be a disaster, because you wouldn't have time to wait for a recovery. With a 25-year horizon, on the other hand, you have time to ride out crises. We'll develop this idea in lesson 26 on the risk/return trade-off. This table gives general benchmarks, not recommendations for your situation.

How much to put aside each month?

For the short and medium term, the simple formula is more than enough:

Monthly effort = (target amount − already saved) / number of months left

Interest from a savings account reduces the effort a little, but not by much over a few years: better to treat it as a small bonus. Over the long term, on the other hand, compound interest makes a real difference and online simulators are useful.

Example: Camille, 26 (fictional)

Camille is a nurse in Nantes, €2,000 net a month. Her emergency fund is already built. She sets herself three goals:

GoalAmountDeadlineMonthly effort (without interest)
Trip to Portugal€1,50010 months€150
Second-hand car€6,0003 years (36 months)€167
Deposit for a flat€20,0006 years (72 months)€278
Total€595

With a savings account at 1.7% (end-2025 rate, check it), the effort for the car drops to about €163 a month, and for the deposit to about €264. Interest helps, but most of it comes from her payments.

The problem: with the 50/30/20 method (lesson 3), Camille can put about 20% of her income towards savings, i.e. €400 a month. She's almost €200 short. That's the situation almost everyone is in: you can't do everything at once.

Prioritising when you can't do everything

Camille has several levers, which she can combine:

  1. Push back a deadline: the deposit in 8 years instead of 6? That would need 20,000 / 96 ≈ €208 a month.
  2. Reduce an amount: a €4,500 car instead of €6,000?
  3. Stagger: finish the trip first (10 months), then switch that €150 to the other goals.
  4. Increase the inflow: a bonus, overtime, selling things, cutting some "wants" spending.

A classic order of priority (we'll come back to it in lesson 36):

  • First, no expensive debts and an emergency fund.
  • Next, essential or fixed-date goals (the deposit on a future rental, the car to get to work).
  • Then important but flexible goals (a home deposit).
  • Finally, pleasure goals (the trip), which matter too: a budget with no pleasure at all always ends up cracking (lesson 5).

Organising your goals in practice

  • One pot per goal: "sub-accounts" in your banking app, a Livret A for emergencies and the LDDS for projects, or simply a tracking table. What matters is knowing at all times how much is earmarked for what.
  • Automatic transfers on payday, one per goal if your bank allows it.
  • A regular check-in: every quarter, see where you stand. Goal reached? Redirect the transfer to the next one.
  • Visualise: giving your pot a name ("Lisbon 2026") really does boost motivation; it's a well-documented effect in psychology.
  • Adjust without guilt: life changes, and so do goals. A modified goal isn't a failure.

And watch out for a common mistake: don't dip into your emergency fund for a project. If the trip costs more than planned, you scale back the trip, not the safety cushion.

Key takeaways

  • A savings goal = a project + an amount + a date (the SMART method).
  • Monthly effort = amount remaining / number of months: simple and sufficient for the short and medium term.
  • Three horizons: short (under 2 years), medium (2 to 8 years), long (over 8 years).
  • The closer the deadline, the less risk you take.
  • You can't fund everything at once: prioritise, stagger, postpone.
  • One pot and one automatic transfer per goal, a check-in every quarter.

Exercise

  1. Théo wants to buy a €1,200 computer in 8 months. He has €0 so far. How much must he save each month?
  2. Léna wants €9,000 in 30 months to fund her master's degree. She already has €2,400. How much must she save each month (ignoring interest)?
  3. Sort these goals by horizon (short, medium, long): a) preparing for retirement, b) buying an e-bike in a year, c) a home deposit in 5 years, d) Christmas presents, e) funding the education of a 2-year-old child.
  4. Paul earns €1,800 net and can save €250 a month. He wants €3,000 for a trip in 12 months and €4,000 for a car in 24 months. Is it possible? If not, suggest a solution.
  5. Food for thought: why is it risky to put money for a home deposit planned in 18 months into shares, even though shares earn more on average than savings accounts over the long term?
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. 1,200 / 8 = €150 a month.
  2. She's short by 9,000 − 2,400 = €6,600. 6,600 / 30 = €220 a month.
  3. a) Long. b) Short. c) Medium. d) Short. e) Long (about 16 years).
  4. Trip: 3,000 / 12 = €250 a month. Car: 4,000 / 24 ≈ €167 a month. Total ≈ €417, far more than his €250. Not possible as it stands. Possible solutions: postpone the trip, cut its budget (for example €1,500, i.e. €125 a month); or stagger: €250 a month for 16 months for the car (€4,000), then the trip afterwards. Or increase his income. There's no single right answer: what counts is that the plan is costed and sustainable.
  5. Because shares can fall sharply over a short period (falls of 20 to 30% in a few months have already happened, in 2008, 2020 and 2022). The long-term average is no use if you have to sell at the worst moment: with an 18-month horizon, you don't have time to wait for the recovery, and your project could be delayed by several years. The average return is only reliable when the horizon is long.

Next lesson: inflation and purchasing power, or how to protect your savings against rising prices.

15.html:
The invisible enemy of your savings

Remember 2022 and 2023? Groceries, electricity, a tank of petrol: everything went up at once. This phenomenon has a name, inflation, and it doesn't just affect your shopping trolley. It also silently nibbles away at the money sleeping in your accounts. In lesson 12, we saw that the real return on a savings account is its rate minus inflation. Today we get to the bottom of it: what inflation is, how it's measured, and how not to let it eat your savings. This is the last lesson of module 3.

What is inflation?

Inflation: a general, lasting rise in prices. When prices go up, each euro buys fewer things: the purchasing power of money falls.

In France, it's INSEE (the national statistics office) that measures it, using the consumer price index (IPC, the French CPI). Every month it tracks the price of a "basket" of goods and services representative of what households buy: food, energy, rent, transport, leisure, health… When we say "inflation is 2%", we mean that this basket costs 2% more than a year earlier.

A few benchmarks (annual averages, approximate values):

YearInflation in France (approx.)
2015 to 2019between 0% and 2% a year
20211.6%
20225.2%
20234.9%
20242.0%
2025around 1%

Across 2022 and 2023 combined, prices rose by about 1.052 × 1.049 ≈ 10.4%. In other words, €100 from 2021 bought only the equivalent of about €91 in 2021 money by the end of 2023.

The European Central Bank (ECB) aims for inflation of around 2% a year over the medium term: a little inflation is considered healthy for the economy. You'll see how central banks act through interest rates in the finance course.

Your inflation isn't INSEE's

The CPI is an average. If your budget is heavily concentrated on food and energy (often the case for students and small budgets), you may have felt stronger inflation than the official figure in 2022. Conversely, a household without a car and with stable rent may have felt it less. INSEE even offers a personalised inflation simulator.

The effect of inflation on your money

Inflation works like compound interest, but in reverse:

Future purchasing power = sum / (1 + inflation) to the power of the number of years

  • €1,000 kept for 10 years with 2% inflation a year buys only the equivalent of 1,000 / 1.02 to the power of 10 ≈ €820 today.
  • At 3% a year, €10,000 under the mattress for 10 years loses about a quarter of its value: 10,000 / 1.03 to the power of 10 ≈ €7,441.
  • Rule of 72 (lesson 13): at 2% inflation, prices double in about 36 years. What costs €100 when you're 25 will cost about €200 when you're 61.

That's why keeping a lot of money in a current account at 0% is a guaranteed loss, even if the balance doesn't move.

Nominal versus real: the key to reading figures

Remember this distinction well; it's useful everywhere:

  • Nominal: in current euros, the figure displayed.
  • Real: adjusted for inflation, what it represents in purchasing power.

Real change ≈ nominal change − inflation

For your salary

Example (fictional): in 2023, Jules gets a 3.5% pay rise. He's pleased… but inflation is 5% that year (a figure rounded for the example). His real salary has fallen: 1.035 / 1.05 − 1 ≈ − 1.4%. On €2,000 a month before, he gets €2,070, which buys as much as €1,971 did the previous year. Keep this reflex for lesson 37 on salary negotiation: a pay rise below inflation is a cut in purchasing power.

For your savings

Example: €10,000 in a savings account at 1.7% for 10 years becomes about €11,836. If average inflation is 2% a year, that €11,836 buys only the equivalent of 11,836 / 1.02 to the power of 10 ≈ €9,710 today. The account has grown, but purchasing power has melted slightly. (Fictional assumptions: in reality, the savings account rate moves with inflation.)

How to protect your savings?

There's no miracle solution, but there are principles. What follows is a general overview, not a recommendation tailored to your situation.

1. For short-term money: accept it, and limit the damage

Your emergency fund and your near-term projects must stay risk-free (lessons 11 and 14). So you accept that they earn roughly inflation. Regulated savings accounts are designed for this: their rate is partly indexed to inflation, with a lag. The LEP, if you're eligible, is often the one that protects best. And above all: don't leave more sleeping in your current account than you need for the month.

2. For long-term money: "real" assets

Over long periods, some assets have historically done better than inflation, at the cost of sometimes sharp fluctuations:

  • Shares: a company can raise its prices when inflation rises, so its profits follow in the long run. But they can fall sharply in some years (2022 was an example).
  • Property: rents and prices often follow inflation over time, with cycles and plenty of costs (module 5).
  • Inflation-linked bonds (in France, OATi): their value is adjusted for inflation. More technical; we cover them in the finance course.

We'll study these investments in module 6, with their risks. The key idea: over a long horizon, taking no risk at all is also a risk, that of slowly losing purchasing power.

3. The best shield: your income

Often forgotten: your main protection against inflation is the ability of your income to rise. Training, negotiating your salary, developing your skills (lesson 37) protects you far better at 25 than any investment.

And debts?

Inflation has the opposite effect on fixed-rate debts: your mortgage payment doesn't move, while your salary (in principle) rises with prices. The debt "weighs" less and less. Conversely, a variable-rate loan can become more expensive when inflation pushes rates up. We'll come back to this in lesson 23.

Key takeaways

  • Inflation is the general rise in prices; it reduces the purchasing power of each euro.
  • It's measured by INSEE (CPI). Benchmarks: about 5% in 2022 and 2023, around 1 to 2% afterwards. The ECB aims for 2%.
  • Real ≈ nominal − inflation, for salaries as for savings.
  • At 2% inflation, prices double in about 36 years.
  • Short-term money: savings accounts, accepting a real return close to zero. No large sums in the current account.
  • Long-term money: real assets have historically beaten inflation, with risks.
  • The best protection is often the growth of your income.

Exercise

  1. A big grocery shop costs €60 today. With 5% food inflation, how much will it cost in a year?
  2. You keep €2,000 in cash for 10 years, with inflation of 2% a year. In 10 years, what will something that costs €2,000 today cost? What do you conclude?
  3. Your salary rises by 4% while inflation is 2%. Calculate the change in your real salary (approximate then exact).
  4. A savings account earns 2.5% while inflation is 3%. Have you gained or lost purchasing power? By roughly how much?
  5. Food for thought: your grandmother keeps €15,000 in her current account "because at least there I'm not risking anything". Is that true? How would you explain it to her, without telling her what to buy?
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. 60 × 1.05 = €63.
  2. 2,000 × 1.02 to the power of 10 ≈ €2,438. Your €2,000 in cash will no longer be enough: you've lost about 18% of purchasing power (2,000 / 2,438 ≈ 0.82). Money that earns nothing loses value.
  3. Approximate: 4% − 2% = + 2%. Exact: 1.04 / 1.02 − 1 ≈ + 1.96%. Your purchasing power really is growing.
  4. You've lost purchasing power: 1.025 / 1.03 − 1 ≈ − 0.49%, about half a point. Your balance has risen in euros, but you can buy slightly less.
  5. It's true that she isn't at risk of seeing her balance go down: the risk of nominal loss is zero. But she faces a certain risk of real loss: with 2% inflation a year, her €15,000 will have the purchasing power of only about €12,300 in today's money in 10 years (15,000 / 1.02 to the power of 10). You could explain that there are equally safe and accessible options, such as the Livret A or the LDDS, which at least partly offset inflation, and suggest she talks to her adviser. Without recommending any risky investment: at her age and depending on her needs, security may well remain the priority.

Next lesson: we open module 4 with income tax, its scale, its brackets, and the difference between the marginal rate and the average rate.

16.html:
Why it matters

"If I accept this pay rise, I'll move into a higher bracket and earn less." You've surely heard this before. It's false, and yet many people believe it, to the point of turning down bonuses or overtime. Welcome to module 4, devoted to tax. Don't panic: income tax in France follows a fairly simple logic, and once you've understood the difference between the marginal rate and the average rate, you'll never be caught out by this kind of misconception again.

As always in this module: tax rules change every year (the scale is re-indexed, the rules evolve). The figures below are orders of magnitude with their reference year. For your own situation, always check on impots.gouv.fr, which offers an official simulator.

What is income tax?

Income tax (impôt sur le revenu, IR): a tax paid each year by tax households on all their income (salaries, self-employed income, pensions, rents…). It is progressive: the more you earn, the higher the share taken.

A few basic ideas:

  • The tax household (foyer fiscal): a single person, or a married or PACS-partnered couple (PACS being France's civil partnership), with any dependent children. A student can be attached to their parents' household or file their own return (we'll see the consequences in lesson 18).
  • It's calculated on the previous year's income: in 2025, you declare your 2024 income.
  • About 45% of households pay income tax in France, depending on the year: many young workers pay none, or very little.
  • Don't confuse income tax with the social contributions deducted on your payslip (CSG, pension, unemployment insurance): they're not the same thing; we cover them in lesson 20.

From salary to taxable income

You're not taxed on your gross salary, nor exactly on your net salary. For an employee, the calculation starts from taxable net pay (net imposable, shown on your payslip and pre-filled in your return), to which a flat 10% allowance for work expenses is applied (with a minimum and a maximum). If your actual expenses (transport, meals…) are higher, you can deduct those instead.

Taxable income ≈ annual taxable net salary − 10%

Example: with €50,000 of taxable net pay over the year, your taxable income is 50,000 × 0.9 = €45,000.

The progressive bracket scale

Here is the 2025 scale, which applies to 2024 income, for one part (one "share" of the family quotient: a single person with no children). The thresholds are revised every year, generally roughly in line with inflation.

Taxable income bracket (per part)Rate
Up to €11,4970%
From €11,497 to €29,31511%
From €29,315 to €83,82330%
From €83,823 to €180,29441%
Above €180,29445%

The key point: each rate only applies to the part of income that falls within its bracket. You fill the brackets like buckets, one after the other.

Example: Hugo, 31 (fictional)

Hugo is a developer in Toulouse, single, with taxable income of €45,000.

BracketPart of income in the bracketRateTax
€0 to €11,497€11,4970%€0
€11,497 to €29,315€17,81811%€1,959.98
€29,315 to €45,000€15,68530%€4,705.50
Total€45,000€6,665.48

Hugo pays about €6,665 in income tax, or about €555 a month.

Marginal rate and average rate: THE distinction

Marginal tax rate (taux marginal d'imposition, TMI): the rate of the highest bracket reached. It's the rate applied to the next euro you earn.

Average rate = total tax / taxable income. It's the actual share of your income taken by tax.

For Hugo:

  • Marginal rate: 30%.
  • Average rate: 6,665.48 / 45,000 ≈ 14.8%.

Hugo is "in the 30% bracket", but he certainly doesn't pay 30% of his income in tax: he pays less than 15%. The average rate is always lower than the marginal rate.

What is each one for?

  • The average rate tells you how much tax weighs in your budget.
  • The marginal rate tells you how much one extra euro really brings you (or how much a deducted euro saves you). If Hugo receives a taxable €1,000 bonus, it will cost him 1,000 × 30% = €300 in extra tax: he keeps €700 (before social contributions). It's also the rate that matters when judging the value of a tax deduction, for example payments into a PER (lesson 33).

The bracket-jump myth

Let's go back to the sentence at the start. Imagine Sarah, with taxable income of €29,300, just below the 30% bracket. She gets a rise that takes her to €29,400.

  • At €29,300: tax of €1,958.33.
  • At €29,400: tax of €1,985.48.

Her tax goes up by €27.15. Why? The €15 that stayed in the 11% bracket costs €1.65, and the €85 that enters the 30% bracket costs €25.50. Total: €27.15. Of her €100 rise, she keeps about €73. Earning more always means earning more after tax: only the part above the threshold is taxed at the higher rate.

A few mechanisms worth knowing (without going into detail)

  • The décote: for small amounts of tax, a mechanism reduces the tax due, or even cancels it. That's why many young workers pay less than the scale would suggest.
  • The collection threshold: if the final tax is below €61, it isn't collected.
  • The family quotient, tax reductions and tax credits: they can lower tax considerably. That's the subject of lesson 18.
  • Student jobs: the wages of students under 26 are exempt up to a certain limit (around three times the monthly SMIC, the French minimum wage, per year). Check the year's ceiling on impots.gouv.fr.

Key takeaways

  • Income tax is progressive: it's calculated by brackets, on the previous year's income.
  • For an employee: taxable income ≈ taxable net pay − a 10% allowance.
  • 2025 scale (2024 income): 0%, 11%, 30%, 41%, 45%. The thresholds change every year.
  • Each rate only applies to the part of income in its bracket.
  • Marginal rate = the rate on the next euro; average rate = tax / income, always lower.
  • Moving up a bracket never makes you lose money.

Exercise

Use the 2025 scale above, for a single person (one part), ignoring the décote.

  1. Léo has taxable net pay of €32,000 over the year. Calculate his taxable income after the 10% allowance.
  2. Calculate Léo's tax, his marginal rate and his average rate.
  3. Nadia has taxable income of €90,000. Calculate her tax and her average rate.
  4. Nadia receives a bonus that increases her taxable income by €1,000. How much extra tax will she pay?
  5. Food for thought: a colleague turns down overtime "so as not to move into the 30% bracket". Explain their mistake with a worked example.
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. 32,000 × 0.9 = €28,800.
  2. 0% bracket: €0. 11% bracket: (28,800 − 11,497) × 11% = 17,303 × 0.11 = €1,903.33. He doesn't go over €29,315, so nothing at 30%. Tax: €1,903.33. Marginal rate: 11%. Average rate: 1,903.33 / 28,800 ≈ 6.6% (and only 5.9% of his €32,000 taxable net pay).
  3. €0 + €1,959.98 (11% bracket) + (83,823 − 29,315) × 30% = 54,508 × 0.3 = €16,352.40 + (90,000 − 83,823) × 41% = 6,177 × 0.41 = €2,532.57. Total: €20,844.95. Average rate: 20,844.95 / 90,000 ≈ 23.2%, whereas her marginal rate is 41%.
  4. Her marginal rate is 41%: 1,000 × 41% = €410. She keeps €590 of this bonus (before social levies).
  5. Only the part of income above the threshold (€29,315 of taxable income for one part in 2025) is taxed at 30%. Example: if he goes from €29,000 to €30,000 of taxable income, the first €315 are taxed at 11% (€34.65) and the next €685 at 30% (€205.50). He pays €240.15 more tax but earns €1,000 more: he keeps about €760. Turning it down means losing that €760. (Note: overtime is even partly exempt from income tax, up to a certain limit.)

Next lesson: tax at source and the annual tax return, or how tax is actually paid every month.

17.titre: Tax at source and the tax return
17.html:
Why it matters

Yesterday we learnt to calculate income tax using the scale. But in practice, how do you pay it? Since 2019, the answer fits in three words: tax at source (prélèvement à la source). The tax is taken straight from your salary every month, before it even reaches your account. Handy, but it causes a common confusion: "if it's taken automatically, I don't need to file a return any more, right?" Wrong. Today we take the mechanism apart: the rate, the annual return and the adjustment that can bring a pleasant or unpleasant surprise in September.

As throughout the tax section: dates and rules can change. Check the current year's calendar on impots.gouv.fr.

The principle: paying tax as you go

Tax at source (PAS): income tax is deducted every month directly from income (salary, pension, unemployment benefit) by the employer or body paying it, then passed on to the tax authority.

Before 2019, tax was paid a year in arrears: in 2018, you paid tax on your 2017 income. The problem: the young graduate starting work paid their first taxes a year later, and the retiree whose income had fallen was still paying tax calculated on their working income. Tax at source brings the payment of tax closer to the moment you receive the income.

For income with no "payer" (self-employed income, rent received), the principle is the same but takes the form of instalments (acomptes) taken directly from your bank account every month or every quarter. You'll see this for the micro-entreprise in lesson 38.

Your deduction rate

Your employer knows nothing about your tax situation (and that's deliberate). It simply receives a rate from the tax authority, which it applies to your taxable net pay.

Deduction rate ≈ previous year's tax / previous year's taxable net income

Monthly deduction = month's taxable net pay × rate

Example: let's take Hugo from lesson 16 again (fictional). €50,000 of taxable net pay, €6,665 of tax. His rate: 6,665 / 50,000 ≈ 13.3%. On monthly taxable net pay of €4,167, about €554 is deducted every month. You'll notice this rate is even lower than his average rate of 14.8%: it's calculated on income before the 10% allowance.

The three types of rate

RateWho for?How it's set
PersonalisedBy default, for any household that filed the previous yearCalculated by the tax authority from your last return
IndividualisedMarried or PACS couples, on requestSplits the household's tax according to each partner's income, instead of a single rate for both
Non-personalised ("neutral")First job, or on request if you don't want your employer to know your rateAn official grid that depends only on the salary amount, as for a single person with no children

For your first job, the tax authority doesn't yet have a return: your employer applies the neutral rate. It may be too high or too low for your real situation; it'll be corrected the following year.

Adjusting your rate during the year

In your personal space on impots.gouv.fr (the "Gérer mon prélèvement à la source" section, "Manage my tax at source"), you can adjust your rate if your income changes a lot: losing your job, a big pay rise, going part-time. You must also report a marriage, PACS, birth or divorce there within 60 days. Adjusting downwards is regulated: if you underestimate your income too much, penalties can apply.

The annual return: still compulsory

The rate applied throughout the year is only an estimate. Only the return allows the exact tax to be calculated, taking account of all your income and your situation (children, donations, childcare costs…). So it remains compulsory, even if your final tax is €0.

A typical year's calendar (example for 2025):

WhenWhat
JanuaryPayment of a 60% advance on certain tax credits and reductions (home help, childcare, donations…)
April to early JuneOnline declaration of the previous year's income. Deadlines depend on your département
July to AugustReceipt of the tax notice: final tax and new rate
Late July - AugustRefund if you've overpaid
SeptemberThe new rate applies to your salary. The balance is taken if you've underpaid

The return is filed online, and it's largely pre-filled (salaries, unemployment benefit…). Your job: check everything is correct, and add what's missing. For many employees whose situation hasn't changed, the return is even automatic: the tax authority validates it itself if you change nothing. Be careful: it's up to you to check that it's accurate.

The reference taxable income

Your tax notice also shows your reference taxable income (revenu fiscal de référence, RFR). This figure is used for much more than tax: eligibility for the LEP (lesson 12), student grants, social housing, certain benefits. All the more reason always to file a return, even on a small income: no tax notice means no RFR, and rights you won't be able to access.

The adjustment: the moment of truth

Once the exact tax is known, the tax authority compares it with what has been deducted:

  • You've overpaid: a refund by transfer, usually at the end of the summer.
  • You've underpaid: the balance is taken from your account, in one go in September if it doesn't exceed €300, otherwise in four instalments, from September to December.

Example (fictional): Lina got a pay rise in 2024, but her rate, calculated on her 2023 income, had stayed low. She paid €1,200 through tax at source. Her return in spring 2025 calculates a real tax of €1,600. That leaves €400 to pay: as that's more than €300, it's taken in four instalments of €100, from September to December 2025. And from September, her new, higher rate applies to her salary.

Practical tip: if your salary has risen significantly, or if you've had income not subject to tax at source (a large year-end bonus, freelance income), plan ahead for an adjustment in September. Put the money aside in your savings account or adjust your rate upwards. Remember lesson 11: "forgotten" expenses are one of the classic traps.

Key takeaways

  • Since 2019, income tax has been deducted at source, every month, from your salary or via instalments.
  • Deduction = taxable net pay × rate. The rate is calculated from your last return.
  • Three rates: personalised, individualised (couples), non-personalised (neutral).
  • The annual return remains compulsory: only it calculates the exact tax.
  • Calendar: return in spring, notice in summer, adjustment from September.
  • You can adjust your rate, and must report changes in your situation on impots.gouv.fr.
  • The reference taxable income is used for many benefits: file a return even on a small income.

Exercise

  1. Your taxable net pay is €2,500 a month and your deduction rate is 4%. How much is deducted each month? Over the year?
  2. The following year, your return shows that your real tax was €1,600. What happens, and when?
  3. Your rate is 7.5% and your taxable net pay is €3,000 this month, because you received a bonus. How much is deducted that month?
  4. Inès starts her first permanent contract in September after her studies. What rate will her employer apply, and why?
  5. Food for thought: your friend Bastien, a student with a small job, says: "I don't declare my income, I don't pay any tax anyway." Why is this a bad idea?
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. 2,500 × 4% = €100 a month, i.e. 100 × 12 = €1,200 over the year.
  2. You're short by 1,600 − 1,200 = €400. As that's more than €300, the balance is taken from your bank account in four instalments, from September to December, i.e. €100 a month. Your rate will also be raised from September.
  3. 3,000 × 7.5% = €225. The deduction follows the month's pay: a bonus increases the deduction in the month it's paid.
  4. The non-personalised (neutral) rate: it's her first job, and the tax authority has no return of earned income from which to calculate a personalised rate. It will be adjusted after her first return. If the rate doesn't suit her, she can also request one on impots.gouv.fr as soon as she has declared income.
  5. First, filing a return is a legal obligation, even with no tax to pay. Next, without a return he has no tax notice and no reference taxable income, which are required for many procedures: grants, housing, the LEP, various benefits. Finally, if tax has been deducted by mistake (the neutral rate applied to his wages), he can only get it back by filing a return. And if he forgets, late-payment penalties can apply if tax is due.

Next lesson: the family quotient, tax reductions and tax credits, or how your personal situation changes your tax.

18.html:
Two people, same salary, very different tax bills

In lesson 16 we calculated the tax for a single person. But two people earning exactly the same can pay very different amounts of tax: one lives alone, the other has two children; one gives to charities, the other employs someone at home. French income tax takes account of your family situation and certain expenses. Today we look at the three main tools: the family quotient, tax reductions and tax credits.

An essential reminder: all the amounts and ceilings quoted are benchmarks for 2025 (2024 income), rounded, and they change every year. For your situation, check on impots.gouv.fr or service-public.fr, and use the official simulator.

The family quotient: divide to calculate better

Family quotient (quotient familial): the household's taxable income is divided by a number of "parts" (shares), the scale is applied to this income per part, then the result is multiplied by the number of parts.

Impôt = barème(revenu / parts) × parts (tax = scale(income / parts) × parts)

The idea: the same income doesn't represent the same standard of living depending on how many people it supports. As tax is progressive, dividing the income "drops" it down the brackets, which reduces the total tax.

How many parts?

SituationNumber of parts
Single person1
Married or PACS couple2
Each of the first two children+ 0.5
From the third child+ 1 per child
Parent bringing up children alone+ 0.5 extra

Example: a married couple with two children has 2 + 0.5 + 0.5 = 3 parts. With three children, 4 parts. Careful: an unmarried cohabiting couple (neither married nor in a PACS) files two separate returns, one part each.

Example: Marc and Julie (fictional)

Marc and Julie are married, with household taxable income of €60,000. Let's calculate with the 2025 scale from lesson 16.

  • Without children (2 parts): income per part = €30,000. Tax for one part: (29,315 − 11,497) × 11% + (30,000 − 29,315) × 30% = 1,959.98 + 205.50 = €2,165.48. For the household: × 2 = €4,330.96.
  • With two children (3 parts): income per part = €20,000. Tax for one part: (20,000 − 11,497) × 11% = €935.33. For the household: × 3 = €2,805.99.

The two children reduce their tax by about €1,525 a year.

The cap: a limited benefit

Without a limit, the family quotient would mainly benefit very high incomes (the higher the marginal rate, the bigger the reduction). So the benefit is capped: each extra half-part cannot reduce tax by more than about €1,800 a year (€1,791 for 2024 income, with specific caps for certain situations).

For Marc and Julie, the €1,525 benefit for two half-parts is well below the cap (2 × 1,791 = €3,582): no problem. But if their income were €120,000, the raw calculation would give a reduction of more than €6,800. It would be brought down to €3,582, and their tax would be about €18,749 instead of €15,496.

What about students?

Up to 25 (21 if not studying), a young adult can choose to be attached to their parents' household (they bring them a half-part, and their income is added to the parents') or to file on their own (the parents can then, under certain conditions, deduct maintenance payments they make to them). The best option depends on everyone's income: run both simulations on impots.gouv.fr before choosing.

Tax reduction or tax credit: the nuance that matters

Once tax has been calculated using the scale and the family quotient, certain expenses reduce it, in euros. Two mechanisms, which look alike but aren't identical:

Tax reduction: lowers the tax due, but can't take it below zero. If it exceeds the tax, the excess is lost.

Tax credit: lowers the tax due, and if it exceeds the tax, the difference is refunded to you.

For someone who pays little or no tax, the difference is huge: a tax credit can bring them money, a reduction nothing at all.

The most common ones (2025 benchmarks)

ExpenseTypeBenefit (order of magnitude)
Donations to public-interest charitiesReduction66% of the donation (75% for help to people in difficulty, up to a limit), up to 20% of taxable income
Employing someone at home (cleaning, tutoring, gardening…)Credit50% of spending, within an annual ceiling (around €12,000 of spending, increased depending on the situation)
Childcare costs for a child under 6 (nursery, registered childminder)Credit50% of spending, capped at about €3,500 per child
Rental property or SME investments (schemes vary)ReductionHighly variable, often complex and risky

Part of these benefits is paid as an advance in January (60%), thanks to tax at source (lesson 17).

The example continued

Marc and Julie (with their two children) gave €200 to a charity and paid €3,000 in childminder fees for their 2-year-old.

  • Reduction for donations: 200 × 66% = €132.
  • Credit for childcare: 3,000 × 50% = €1,500.
  • Final tax: 2,805.99 − 132 − 1,500 ≈ €1,174.

Their €200 donation actually cost them only €68: the State funded the rest.

Traps to avoid

  • Spending money purely for the tax benefit: saving €66 on a €100 donation still means spending €34. Tax breaks are never free.
  • Products sold "to pay less tax" (tax-break property, some funds): they often carry high fees and significant risks. We'll come back to this in lesson 39.
  • Forgetting to declare your donations or childcare costs: the benefit isn't automatic; you have to fill in the right boxes. Keep your receipts (tax receipts, certificates).
  • Confusing a deduction with a reduction: a deduction (for example maintenance payments, or a payment into a PER as seen in lesson 33) lowers your taxable income. It saves "marginal rate × amount", whereas a reduction lowers the tax directly.

Key takeaways

  • The family quotient divides income into parts: impôt = barème(revenu / parts) × parts.
  • Single person: 1 part; married or PACS couple: 2; + 0.5 per child for the first two, + 1 after that.
  • The benefit per half-part is capped (about €1,800 in 2025).
  • A tax reduction stops at zero; a tax credit can be refunded.
  • Donations: a 66% reduction. Home help and childcare: a 50% credit, with ceilings.
  • Never spend money just for the tax benefit, and check the year's rules on impots.gouv.fr.

Exercise

2025 scale from lesson 16, ignoring the décote and the cap unless stated otherwise.

  1. How many parts for: a) a PACS couple with no children, b) a married couple with three children, c) an unmarried cohabiting couple with one child (for each return)?
  2. A married couple with one child has taxable income of €45,000. How many parts? Calculate their tax.
  3. Without the child, this couple's tax would be €2,420.66. How much does the child save them? Does the cap apply?
  4. Rose owes €300 in tax. She's entitled to a €400 tax benefit. What happens if it's a reduction? And if it's a credit?
  5. Food for thought: an adviser offers you an investment "that will save you €3,000 in tax". What questions should you ask yourself before accepting?
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. a) 2 parts (like a married couple). b) 2 + 0.5 + 0.5 + 1 = 4 parts. c) Cohabiting partners file separately: 1 part for one, and 1.5 parts for the one who declares the dependent child.
  2. 2 + 0.5 = 2.5 parts. Income per part: 45,000 / 2.5 = €18,000. Tax per part: (18,000 − 11,497) × 11% = €715.33. For the household: 715.33 × 2.5 ≈ €1,788.33.
  3. 2,420.66 − 1,788.33 = €632.33. That's well below the cap of about €1,791 per half-part: no cap applies.
  4. Reduction: the tax falls to €0, and the remaining €100 is lost. Credit: the tax falls to €0 and Rose is refunded €100.
  5. How much does this investment cost me (amount invested, entry and management fees)? What's the risk of losing capital? How long is my money locked up? What's my marginal bracket, and do I really pay enough tax to benefit? What is the investment worth without the tax benefit? Is the adviser paid on commission? A tax benefit doesn't turn a bad investment into a good one. We'll come back to this in lesson 39.

Next lesson: how savings and investments are taxed, with the flat tax (PFU) and allowances.

19.html:
What you earn, and what you keep

In module 3 you saw that Livret A interest wasn't taxed, whereas interest on a bank savings account was (lesson 12). That's not a detail: on long-term investments, tax can make a difference of several thousand euros. The good news is that the rules rest on a few simple principles. Today we set them out, so that you'll later understand why the assurance-vie, the PEA or the PER (modules 6 and 7) each have their appeal.

Careful: the taxation of savings is one of the areas that changes most. The rates quoted are benchmarks, with their year. Always check the rules in force on impots.gouv.fr before making a decision. And nothing here constitutes personalised investment advice.

Two levies, not one

Income from your savings (interest, dividends, capital gains) is generally subject to two separate levies:

  • Income tax, which you've known about since lesson 16.
  • Social levies (prélèvements sociaux: CSG, CRDS, solidarity levy), which fund the Sécurité sociale (France's social security system). Their rate was 17.2% for a long time. The 2026 social security financing act raised it for part of capital income (to around 18.6%), with exceptions: exactly the kind of change to check every year.

The single flat-rate levy (PFU)

PFU (prélèvement forfaitaire unique), or "flat tax": since 2018, most investment income has been taxed by default at an overall rate of 30%, i.e. 12.8% income tax + 17.2% social levies.

(With the 2026 rise in social levies mentioned above, this overall rate goes up to about 31.4% for the income concerned. In this lesson's examples, we keep the historical benchmark of 30% to keep the calculations simple.)

It applies in particular to:

  • interest on (non-regulated) bank savings accounts, term deposits, recent PELs;
  • dividends and capital gains in an ordinary securities account (compte-titres ordinaire, CTO);
  • capital gains on crypto-assets (with their own rules);
  • assurance-vie gains, with a special regime (see below).

Example (fictional): Thomas receives €1,000 of dividends in his securities account. Under the PFU, he pays 1,000 × 30% = €300 and keeps €700. Part of it (12.8%) is even deducted at source by the bank, as an instalment, then adjusted when he files his return.

Opting for the scale

You can choose to subject all of your investment income for the year to the progressive income-tax scale, instead of the 12.8% (social levies are still due). The option is ticked on your return and applies to all such income for the year. In exchange, some advantages come back, such as a 40% allowance on dividends.

€1,000 of dividendsPFUScale, TMI 11%Scale, TMI 30%
Income tax€1281,000 × 60% × 11% = €661,000 × 60% × 30% = €180
Social levies (17.2%)€172€172€172
Total€300€238€352

Rule of thumb: with a marginal rate of 0% or 11%, opting for the scale is often more advantageous; from 30% upwards, the PFU generally is. (Simplified calculation: we ignore the small deductible portion of CSG here.) The impots.gouv.fr simulator does the comparison for you.

The wrappers that change the picture

The legislator encourages certain investments by giving them gentler tax treatment. They're often called tax wrappers (enveloppes fiscales): they aren't investments in themselves, but "containers" with their own rules.

WrapperTaxation of gains (2025 benchmarks)Lesson
Livret A, LDDS, LEP, Livret jeuneCompletely exempt (neither income tax nor social levies)12
PEA (plan d'épargne en actions, a share savings plan for European shares)After 5 years: exempt from income tax, only social levies remain due. Before 5 years: PFU and, in general, closure of the plan28
Assurance-vie (a French tax-advantaged savings/investment contract)After 8 years: an annual allowance on gains withdrawn of €4,600 (€9,200 for a couple), then a reduced rate of 7.5% (subject to conditions) + social levies. Before 8 years: PFU27
PER (plan d'épargne retraite, a retirement savings plan)Payments deductible from taxable income, but withdrawals taxed33
Ordinary securities accountPFU (or the scale by option), no advantage28

The key point: you're only taxed on gains, when you withdraw

In an assurance-vie or a PEA, as long as you withdraw nothing, income tax doesn't apply (with a few nuances, such as social levies taken every year on an assurance-vie euro fund). And when you withdraw, only the portion of gains contained in the withdrawal is taxed, not the capital you paid in. Combined with compound interest (lesson 13), this deferral of tax is a real advantage over time.

Comparative examples (fictional, with 17.2% social levies)

  • €2,000 capital gain in a securities account: 2,000 × 30% = €600 of PFU.
  • The same €2,000 in a PEA more than 5 years old: only the social levies, 2,000 × 17.2% = €344.
  • €3,000 of gains withdrawn from an assurance-vie more than 8 years old, single person: below the €4,600 allowance, so €0 income tax; social levies: 3,000 × 17.2% = €516.

What about other savings income?

  • Property capital gains: the sale of your main residence is exempt. For other property, a specific regime applies, with allowances depending on how long you've owned it (module 5).
  • Rent received: taxed under the scale + social levies, with simplified regimes (micro-foncier, furnished letting). Outside the scope of this introductory course.
  • Employee savings (profit-sharing schemes, participation and intéressement, placed in a PEE company savings plan): exempt from income tax subject to conditions, social levies due.

Good reflexes

  • Always think in terms of net return: 4% gross taxed at 30% makes 2.8% net, to compare with a tax-free savings account.
  • Think about the wrapper before the investment: the same fund can be taxed far less in a PEA or an assurance-vie than in a securities account.
  • Open early a PEA or an assurance-vie, even with a small amount: the 5- and 8-year periods run from opening (or the first payment), not from each payment.
  • But tax must never be the only criterion: fees, risk, lock-in period and fit with your goals (lesson 14) come first.

Key takeaways

  • Savings income bears income tax and social levies (historically 17.2%, raised for some income in 2026).
  • By default: the 30% PFU (12.8% + 17.2%), or the scale by option, attractive for lower brackets.
  • Regulated savings accounts: completely exempt.
  • PEA after 5 years and assurance-vie after 8 years: lighter taxation, and you're only taxed on gains, when you withdraw.
  • Always compare after-tax returns.
  • The rules change often: check the current year on impots.gouv.fr.

Exercise

Use a 30% PFU and social levies of 17.2%.

  1. You receive €500 of interest on a bank savings account. How much do you pay under the PFU? How much do you keep?
  2. You make a €1,500 capital gain. How much do you pay in a securities account? And in a PEA opened 6 years ago?
  3. Léonie has a marginal rate of 41%. She receives €1,200 of dividends. Compare the PFU and opting for the scale (40% allowance). Which does she choose?
  4. One investment earns 3% gross a year, taxed under the PFU. Another earns 2.2% net of tax. Which earns more after tax?
  5. Food for thought: why does the State give gentler tax treatment to the PEA after 5 years and the assurance-vie after 8 years? What behaviour is it trying to encourage?
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. 500 × 30% = €150 in tax. You keep €350.
  2. Securities account: 1,500 × 30% = €450. PEA over 5 years old: only the social levies, 1,500 × 17.2% = €258. Saving: €192.
  3. PFU: 1,200 × 30% = €360. Scale: 1,200 × 60% × 41% = €295.20 of income tax + 1,200 × 17.2% = €206.40 of social levies, i.e. €501.60. She chooses the PFU, without hesitation.
  4. 3% × (1 − 30%) = 2.1% net, against 2.2% net for the second. The second earns slightly more, even though its displayed rate seemed lower. Always compare net!
  5. To encourage long-term saving. It finances the economy (companies, the State) in a stable way, and helps households prepare for their projects and their retirement. By reserving the advantage for those who keep their money invested for a long time, the State discourages quick in-and-out moves and rewards patience, which is also, as we saw with compound interest, the saver's best ally.

Next lesson: social contributions and your payslip, to finally understand how you get from gross to net salary.

20.titre: From gross to net: your payslip
20.html:
Why your salary "shrinks" before it arrives

First job interview, you're offered "€30,000 gross a year". Great! Then your first payslip arrives: about €1,900 a month lands in your account, not €2,500. Where did the rest go? Don't panic, nothing has vanished: it has funded your pension, your health cover, your unemployment insurance and part of your income tax. To finish this module on tax, we learn to read a payslip and get from gross to net. It's essential for comparing two job offers, negotiating your salary (lesson 37) and building your budget (lesson 3).

As always: contribution rates change regularly and depend on your collective agreement, your status and your company. The figures below are orders of magnitude for 2025. The official details are on service-public.fr and on the Urssaf website (the body that collects social contributions).

The four levels of salary

Gross salary − employee social contributions = net salary (before tax)

Net salary before tax − tax at source = net pay (what reaches your account)

  • Gross salary: the figure in the employment contract and in job ads. The basis for every calculation.
  • Net before tax: gross minus the social contributions paid by the employee.
  • Taxable net: a slightly higher amount than net, used to calculate income tax (more on this below).
  • Net pay (net à payer): what you really receive, after tax at source (lesson 17).

And on the other side of the table, there's a fifth amount: the total cost to the employer, i.e. gross plus employer contributions.

The rule of thumb

Status (private sector)Net before tax ≈
Non-managerial (non-cadre)about 77 to 78% of gross
Managerial (cadre)about 75% of gross
Civil serviceabout 80 to 85% of gross (depending on bonuses)

Example: the SMIC (French minimum wage) is about €1,800 gross a month in 2025 for full-time work, i.e. about €1,400 to €1,430 net. And the €30,000 gross a year from the introduction comes to €2,500 gross a month, i.e. about 2,500 × 0.77 ≈ €1,925 net for a non-managerial employee.

Where do the contributions go?

Social contributions aren't a "lost" tax: they're contributions that open up rights for you.

ContributionWhat it fundsEmployee share (2025 benchmark)
Old-age insurance (Sécurité sociale)Your basic state pensionabout 7.3%
Supplementary pension (Agirc-Arrco)Your supplementary pensionabout 4% (more above a ceiling)
CSG and CRDSSocial security, social debt, family benefitsabout 9.7% (on 98.25% of gross)
Top-up health cover (mutuelle) and income protectionSupplementary health cover, incapacity, deathvariable (often a few tens of euros)
Health insurance, unemploymentHealth, unemployment benefit0% for the employee (paid by the employer)

Your pension, which you'll see in detail in lesson 32, is therefore largely funded by these lines. They're also what entitle you to unemployment benefit, sick pay, and maternity and paternity leave.

Detailed example: Inès's payslip (fictional, simplified)

Inès, non-managerial, earns €2,300 gross a month. Here's a very simplified version of her payslip (rounded 2025 rates, a standard company).

LineBaseRateAmount
Gross salary€2,300.00
Old-age insurance (capped)€2,3006.90%− €158.70
Old-age insurance (uncapped)€2,3000.40%− €9.20
Supplementary pension€2,3003.15%− €72.45
General balancing contribution (pension)€2,3000.86%− €19.78
Deductible CSG€2,259.756.80%− €153.66
Non-deductible CSG€2,259.752.40%− €54.23
CRDS€2,259.750.50%− €11.30
Mutuelle (employee share)− €30.00
Net before tax€1,790.68
Tax at source€1,886.213.50%− €66.02
Net pay€1,724.66

Employee contributions come to €509.32, about 22% of gross: the rule of thumb holds. CSG and CRDS are calculated on 98.25% of gross (2,300 × 0.9825 = €2,259.75), as a flat-rate allowance for work expenses.

Why is taxable net higher than net?

Tax at source isn't calculated on €1,790.68, but on a taxable net of €1,886.21. The reason: part of what was taken off your gross is still subject to income tax. That's the case for the non-deductible CSG and the CRDS (€54.23 + €11.30), and for the employer's share of the mutuelle (here €30), treated as a benefit. 1,790.68 + 54.23 + 11.30 + 30 = €1,886.21. It's this taxable net, totalled over the year, that you find pre-filled in your tax return (lesson 17).

The cost to the employer

The employer also pays contributions, on top of gross pay: health insurance, family benefits, unemployment, pensions, workplace accidents… For an average salary, they amount to around 40% of gross. But for low salaries, significant reductions cut them sharply: at SMIC level, they're close to zero for some contributions.

In practice, for every €100 paid into Inès's account, the company often pays out well over €130. That's useful to know when negotiating, and essential if you one day become self-employed or an employer (lesson 38).

Other lines worth knowing

  • Overtime: paid at a higher rate (usually 25% or 50%) and partly exempt from contributions and income tax, up to a limit.
  • Meal vouchers (titres-restaurant): the part paid by the employer isn't taxed; yours is deducted from your salary.
  • Transport: the employer reimburses at least 50% of your public transport pass.
  • Paid holiday: a counter shows the days you've earned and taken. Check it!
  • The annual total: at the bottom of the December payslip, the taxable net for the year. Handy for checking your return.

Keep your payslips, ideally indefinitely (or until you draw your pension): they prove your rights. Many companies put them in a digital safe.

Key takeaways

  • Gross − employee contributions = net before tax; net − tax at source = net pay.
  • Rule of thumb: net ≈ 78% of gross for a non-managerial employee, 75% for a manager.
  • Contributions fund your pension, your health, your family and your unemployment cover: they're rights, not lost money.
  • Taxable net is higher than net (non-deductible CSG, CRDS, employer's share of the mutuelle).
  • The employer also pays its own contributions: the total cost is well above gross, except for reductions on low salaries.
  • Always compare job offers on equal status and benefits, and keep your payslips.

Exercise

  1. Estimate the net salary before tax of a non-managerial employee paid €2,800 gross a month (78% rule of thumb).
  2. You're offered €42,000 gross a year, over 12 months, as a manager (cadre). Estimate your monthly net before tax.
  3. Your net before tax is €1,900, your taxable net €2,000 and your deduction rate 5%. How much reaches your account?
  4. Offer A: €36,000 gross a year, non-managerial. Offer B: €38,000 gross a year, managerial. Compare the estimated monthly nets. What other factors would you look at?
  5. Food for thought: your friend says "contributions are stolen money, I'd rather get everything as net pay". What do you reply?
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. 2,800 × 0.78 ≈ €2,184 net a month.
  2. 42,000 / 12 = €3,500 gross a month. 3,500 × 0.75 ≈ €2,625 net a month before tax.
  3. Deduction: 2,000 × 5% = €100 (calculated on the taxable net). In the account: 1,900 − 100 = €1,800.
  4. A: 36,000 / 12 × 0.78 = €2,340. B: 38,000 / 12 × 0.75 = €2,375. The net gap (about €35 a month) is much smaller than the gross gap (about €167 a month). Also look at: the number of monthly salaries (a 13th month?), bonuses, the mutuelle, meal vouchers, remote working, days of holiday and RTT (extra days off for working over 35 hours), commuting time, career prospects. A manager also contributes a bit more to their supplementary pension, which earns them more rights.
  5. Contributions fund very concrete rights: pensions, health reimbursements, sick pay, unemployment benefit, maternity and paternity leave. Without them, you'd have to take out equivalent private insurance yourself, often more expensive, especially if you have health problems. You can debate their level or their efficiency, and that's a genuine political debate, but it isn't money that disappears: it's a form of collective insurance and compulsory retirement saving.

Next lesson: we open module 5 on housing with renting: budget, application file, lease, deposit, rights and duties.

21.html:
Why it matters

For most young workers, rent is the biggest expense of the month, often between a quarter and a third of their salary. Remember lesson 3: in the 50/30/20 method, housing alone eats a large part of the 50% for "needs". Choosing your home well means giving yourself breathing room for everything else: emergency fund, goals, pleasures.

And renting isn't just paying rent. There's an application file to put together, a lease to sign, a deposit to pay, rights to know and duties to respect. Today we open module 5, on housing, with the most common situation: renting.

What rent can you afford?

The most widespread rule, among landlords and letting agencies alike:

Net monthly income ≥ 3 × rent including charges, i.e. rent of at most roughly a third of your income.

It isn't a law, but it's the filter most landlords apply to your application. And it's also a good safeguard for you: beyond that, your budget becomes very tight.

Example (fictional): Léa, 23, has just landed her first permanent job in Lyon. She earns €1,900 net a month. Her rent ceiling: 1,900 / 3 ≈ €633 including charges. She finds a 28 m² studio at €580 excluding charges + €40 of charges, i.e. €620. Ratio: 1,900 / 620 ≈ 3.06. It passes, just.

The real costs of housing

The advertised rent is only part of the bill. Also think about:

  • service charges (upkeep of shared areas, sometimes cold water, household waste): check whether they're included in the amount advertised;
  • electricity and gas, often paid by you, varying greatly with insulation (look at the DPE, the energy performance certificate);
  • home insurance, compulsory for an unfurnished home (you'll see this in detail in lesson 31);
  • internet, and transport if you move away from the centre to pay less.

A cheaper but poorly insulated home 45 minutes from work isn't necessarily a good deal.

The move-in budget: what you need before you even move in

This is the classic trap: you work out the monthly rent but forget the sum you need to pay upfront. Back to Léa (fictional figures, 2025 orders of magnitude).

ItemAmount
Deposit (1 month excluding charges, unfurnished)€580
Agency fees (28 m² × €10 + 28 m² × €3 for the inventory)€364
First month's rent including charges€620
Home insurance (first year)€120
Removal (van hire, boxes)€250
Basic equipment (curtains, bulbs, small furniture)€300
Total€2,234

More than a month's salary! That's exactly what an emergency fund and "goals" savings are for (lessons 11 and 14). If you're planning a move, set this amount aside several months in advance.

Good news: agency fees charged to tenants are capped by law (the ALUR law). The cap depends on the area (higher in Paris and other high-pressure cities), is expressed in euros per m² and is revised regularly: check the current amount on service-public.fr. If you rent directly from a private landlord, there are no agency fees at all.

The rental application file

In big cities, good homes go within days. Having a complete file ready (ideally as a PDF) often makes the difference. The law sets a restricted list of documents a landlord may ask you for:

  • an identity document;
  • proof of current address (rent receipts, a certificate of accommodation);
  • proof of your professional situation (employment contract, student card);
  • proof of income (last 3 payslips, last tax notice, grant certificate).

A landlord is not allowed to ask you for, for example, a bank statement, a certificate of good account management, your medical records, an ID photo or a reservation cheque. If you're asked for these, it's a warning sign (and sometimes a scam; remember lesson 10: never pay any money before you've visited and signed).

The guarantor

If your income is borderline, the landlord will often ask for a guarantor (garant, or caution): someone who commits to paying if you don't. Often a parent. If you don't have one, the Visale guarantee from Action Logement is a free guarantee, available in particular to under-30s and certain employees: check the current conditions on the official Visale website.

The lease: what you're signing

The lease (bail, or tenancy agreement) sets the rules of the game. The key points:

Type of letMinimum lease termMaximum depositTenant's notice
Unfurnished3 years (private landlord)1 month's rent excluding charges3 months, reduced to 1 month in high-pressure areas and in some cases
Furnished1 year (9 months for a student)2 months' rent excluding charges1 month

The lease is automatically renewed at the end of its term. You, the tenant, can leave whenever you like as long as you give notice. The landlord can only give you notice at the end of the lease and only for specific reasons (selling, taking the home back to live in, a serious reason such as unpaid rent).

The rent can only be increased once a year, and only if the lease provides for it, within the limit of the rent reference index (IRL) published by INSEE. In some cities (notably Paris, Lyon, Lille, Bordeaux, Montpellier), there's also rent control (encadrement des loyers): the rent cannot exceed an increased reference rent. The cities concerned change: check.

The inventory (état des lieux)

On moving in and moving out, an inventory (état des lieux) is drawn up: a room-by-room description of the home. It's THE document that will protect your deposit. Be meticulous: note every scratch, every stain, take dated photos. You have 10 days after moving in to report a forgotten defect in writing (and the first month of the heating season for the heating).

The deposit and its rules

The deposit must be returned within 1 month of handing back the keys if the move-out inventory matches the move-in one, 2 months otherwise. If it's late, the landlord owes a penalty of 10% of the monthly rent excluding charges for each month of delay begun.

The landlord may only withhold sums for justified damage (quotes, invoices) or unpaid rent and charges. They can't withhold for normal wear and tear: paint that has yellowed after six years, carpet worn where people walk, that isn't damage.

Rights and duties

Your duties as a tenant: pay the rent and charges on time, use the home "peacefully" (no nuisance), insure the home, carry out routine upkeep and minor repairs (seals, bulbs, boiler servicing), and not carry out major works without written consent.

Your rights: a decent home (minimum floor area, no health risk, minimum energy performance, with the most energy-hungry homes being progressively banned from letting), peaceful enjoyment of the premises (the landlord can't enter your home without your consent), free rent receipts on request, and major repairs paid for by the landlord (roof, a boiler at the end of its life...).

Help with housing costs
