Depending on your income, you may be entitled to APL (aide personnalisée au logement, French housing benefit) paid by the CAF, including if you're a student or in your first job. The amount depends on income, rent, the city and the make-up of the household. Run a simulation on the CAF website: many young people don't claim benefits they're entitled to.

Key takeaways

  • Rent including charges of at most about a third of net income: it's the landlords' filter and a good safeguard for your budget.
  • Plan a move-in budget often greater than a month's salary (deposit, agency fees, first rent, removal).
  • The list of documents for the file is limited by law; without a guarantor, look at the Visale guarantee.
  • Unfurnished lease: 3 years, deposit of 1 month excluding charges. Furnished: 1 year, deposit of 2 months at most.
  • A precise, photographed move-in inventory protects your deposit.
  • Deposit returned within 1 month (matching inventory) or 2 months, otherwise a penalty of 10% of the rent per month of delay.
  • The rules (fee caps, rent control, notice) change: check on service-public.fr.

Exercise

  1. You earn €2,100 net a month. Under the one-third rule, what's the maximum rent including charges you can aim for?
  2. You rent a furnished flat at €650 excluding charges. What's the maximum deposit the landlord can ask for?
  3. Your move-out inventory matches, your rent excluding charges was €580, and the landlord returns your deposit 2 months late (months begun). How much does he owe you as a penalty?
  4. For a 35 m² flat, an agency charges you €10/m² for the viewing, file and lease, plus €3/m² for the inventory. How much do you pay?
  5. Food for thought: Malik earns €1,500 net and is looking at a €600 studio including charges in a big city. What options does he have to find a home without endangering his budget?
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. 2,100 / 3 = €700 including charges. It's a ceiling, not a target: the less you spend on rent, the more you have left to save.
  2. For a furnished let, the maximum is 2 months' rent excluding charges: 2 × 650 = €1,300.
  3. The penalty is 10% of the monthly rent excluding charges per month of delay begun: 2 × 10% × 580 = 2 × 58 = €116, on top of returning the deposit.
  4. 35 × 10 = €350 and 35 × 3 = €105, i.e. €455. Always check that these amounts respect the legal cap for the area currently in force.
  5. €600 is 40% of his income (most landlords require 1,500 × 3 = €4,500, he's a long way off). Options: check his entitlement to APL, which would lower his share of the cost; look for a flatshare (sharing rent and charges); look a little further from the centre if transport stays reasonable; ask for a guarantor or the Visale guarantee to reassure the landlord; find out about social housing or residences for young workers. What to avoid: signing up to rent that leaves nothing for the emergency fund.

Next lesson: renting or buying? We'll do the real maths, far from slogans like "renting is throwing money down the drain".

22.html:
"Renting is throwing money down the drain": really?

You've surely heard this, often at a family dinner. The idea: rent goes to the landlord, whereas a mortgage payment "stays yours". It's appealing, but it's false in its simplistic form. An owner also pays sums they'll never see again: interest, notary fees, property tax, works... So the right question isn't "rent versus mortgage payment", but the tenant's unrecoverable costs versus the owner's unrecoverable costs.

Today we learn to do this real calculation. It doesn't give a universal answer: it depends on the city, rates, your situation and above all how long you plan to stay.

What you get back and what you don't

When you repay a mortgage, your monthly payment contains two things (we'll go into detail in lesson 23):

  • the capital repaid: a form of forced saving, which you find again as wealth (if the property's price doesn't fall);
  • the interest: the rent on the money, paid to the bank, lost to you.

Tenant's unrecoverable costs = rent (+ home insurance)

Owner's unrecoverable costs = interest + borrower insurance + property tax + non-recoverable service charges + upkeep and works + opportunity cost of the deposit + purchase costs (notary, guarantee) spread over the ownership period, minus any capital gain

You came across opportunity cost as early as lesson 1: the deposit you put into the flat can no longer be invested elsewhere. If you could have earned 3% a year on it, that's income forgone.

The calculation on an example (fictional)

Inès and Thomas, 30, rent a 3-room flat in Nantes for €900 a month excluding recoverable charges, i.e. €10,800 a year. An equivalent flat is for sale at €250,000.

If they buy: notary fees of about 7.5% for an existing property (lesson 24), i.e. €18,750. They put in €38,750 (the notary fees + €20,000) and borrow €230,000 over 25 years at 3.5%, giving a monthly payment of about €1,151 excluding insurance. In the first year, of the roughly €13,800 repaid, about €7,957 is interest and only €5,861 is capital.

Owner's unrecoverable cost (year 1)Annual amount
Loan interest€7,957
Borrower insurance (0.30% of €230,000)€690
Property tax€1,200
Non-recoverable service charges€600
Upkeep and works (≈ 1% of the price a year)€2,500
Opportunity cost of the deposit (€38,750 × 3%)€1,162.50
Total€14,109.50

Compared with €10,800 of rent, the owner "loses" €3,309.50 more a year, without even counting the €18,750 of notary fees. At this stage, renting clearly wins.

And if the price goes up?

The last ingredient is the change in the property's price. If the flat gains 2% a year, that's about €5,000 of capital gain in the first year. The owner's net cost falls to 14,109.50 − 5,000 = €9,109.50, i.e. €1,690.50 less than the rent. It then takes about 18,750 / 1,690.50 ≈ 11 years to "pay back" the notary fees through this advantage (a bit less in reality, since the interest share falls every year).

If the price stagnates, on the other hand, buying stays more expensive than renting for a very long time. And if the price falls (which happened in several French cities between 2022 and 2024), buying can be costly, especially if you have to sell quickly.

What to take from this example: the result depends enormously on uncertain assumptions (price changes, rates, works). Change them a little and the conclusion flips. That's why serious online simulators ask you for all these parameters.

Two quick benchmarks

The price-to-rent ratio

Price-to-rent ratio = purchase price / annual rent of an equivalent property

For Inès and Thomas: 250,000 / 10,800 ≈ 23. It would take 23 years of rent to pay for the property. The higher this ratio, the more renting is relatively advantageous. As an order of magnitude, below 15 to 20, buying often becomes attractive; above 25 to 30 (common in the very big cities), renting often has the edge. It's only a benchmark, not a rule.

How long you'll own it

The most important factor of all. Purchase costs (notary, guarantee, arrangement fees) are paid only once, at the start. The longer you stay, the more they're spread out. If you sell after 2 or 3 years (job transfer, separation, a baby on the way), you're very likely to lose money compared with renting. An idea often quoted: below 5 to 7 years of ownership, buying rarely pays off; but the threshold depends on the city and the market.

What the figures don't say

The financial calculation is only part of the decision. Other factors matter, in both directions:

Arguments for buyingArguments for renting
Forced saving: without a loan, many people wouldn't save as muchMobility: change city or job without constraints
A fixed monthly payment (fixed rate) while rents rise with the IRLNo big unexpected works (roof, façade renovation)
Freedom to do the place up, the security of not being given noticeDeposit invested elsewhere, diversified savings
A home paid off by retirementNo risk of falling prices

The key point: the tenant only comes out ahead if they really save the difference. If Inès and Thomas stay tenants, they must invest every month the equivalent of what they'd have put into repaying capital, and invest their deposit (we'll see how in module 6). A tenant who spends everything they "save" will end up less wealthy than an owner, even if the theoretical calculation proved them right.

Beware of the opposite too: buying a property that blows your budget (and your debt ratio, lesson 23) can leave you without an emergency fund. An owner with no safety cushion is very vulnerable to the unexpected.

Key takeaways

  • "Renting is throwing money away" is false: owners also have unrecoverable costs (interest, property tax, works, purchase costs).
  • The real calculation compares the tenant's and the owner's unrecoverable costs, including the opportunity cost of the deposit.
  • The price-to-rent ratio gives a first benchmark: the higher it is, the more attractive renting is.
  • How long you'll own is decisive: purchase costs are spread out over time.
  • The result depends on uncertain assumptions, especially price changes: test several scenarios.
  • Staying a tenant only pays off if you save and invest the difference.

Exercise

  1. A flat sells for €180,000. An equivalent property rents for €650 a month. Calculate the price-to-rent ratio.
  2. For this same existing property, estimate the notary fees at a rate of 7.5%.
  3. In the first year, the owner would pay €5,000 of interest, €900 of property tax, €1,800 of upkeep, €400 of non-recoverable charges and €1,000 of opportunity cost. Compare with the annual rent.
  4. Same situation, but the property gains 2% in value a year. Roughly how many years does it take for this advantage to offset the notary fees?
  5. Food for thought: Sofia, 26, has just arrived in Bordeaux for her first job and doesn't know whether she'll stay. Her parents are pushing her to buy "so as not to throw money away". What would you advise her to look at before deciding?
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. Annual rent: 650 × 12 = €7,800. Ratio: 180,000 / 7,800 ≈ 23. As for Inès and Thomas, we're in a zone where renting remains competitive.
  2. 180,000 × 7.5% = €13,500.
  3. Owner's unrecoverable costs: 5,000 + 900 + 1,800 + 400 + 1,000 = €9,100, against €7,800 of rent. Without a capital gain, renting costs €1,300 less a year (and the owner has also paid €13,500 of notary fees).
  4. First-year capital gain: 180,000 × 2% = €3,600. Owner's net cost: 9,100 − 3,600 = €5,500, i.e. 7,800 − 5,500 = €2,300 less than the rent. Notary fees "paid back" in 13,500 / 2,300 ≈ 5.9 years, so about 6 years. But if prices stagnate, buying never pays off in this simplified scenario: everything rests on the assumption of rising prices.
  5. First, how long she'll own it: if she might leave in 2 or 3 years, the purchase costs will be hard to spread out, and selling quickly can lose money. Next, the price-to-rent ratio in her area, her emergency fund (would a cushion remain after the deposit?), her borrowing capacity and her debt ratio. Finally, if she stays a tenant, she must commit to saving regularly. Renting for a few years to get to know the city and build up a deposit is a perfectly rational decision.

Next lesson: mortgages, with how to calculate the monthly payment, the role of term and rate, your borrowing capacity and the famous 35% debt ratio.

23.html:
Why it matters

A mortgage is probably the biggest financial contract of your life: hundreds of thousands of euros, over 20 or 25 years. A tenth of a point on the rate or five extra years on the term, and the final bill changes by several thousand, sometimes tens of thousands of euros. Yesterday we saw that interest is an unrecoverable cost for the owner: today we learn how to calculate it and how much a bank will agree to lend you.

The monthly payment: how it's calculated

A standard mortgage is repaid in equal monthly instalments: you pay the same amount every month, from the first to the last. This amount is calculated with a formula that comes straight from compound interest (lesson 13):

Monthly payment = Capital × t / (1 − (1 + t)^(−n))

M = C × t / (1 − (1 + t)^−n), where t = annual rate / 12 and n = number of months

No need to learn it by heart: every bank simulator and spreadsheet (the PMT function) does it for you. But understanding what it says is valuable. If you want to see how it's derived, you'll find it in the site's finance course.

Example: €200,000 borrowed over 25 years (300 months) at 3.5% a year. t = 0.035 / 12 ≈ 0.0029. The formula gives a monthly payment of €1,001.25 (excluding insurance).

Interest first, capital later

Each payment contains a share of interest and a share of capital. Interest is calculated on the outstanding capital. In the first month, it's 200,000 × 0.035 / 12 = €583.33: of your €1,001.25 payment, only €417.91 repays capital! Over the whole first year, you repay about €5,096 of capital and pay about €6,919 of interest.

Over time, the outstanding capital falls, so the interest falls, and the capital share rises. The document that sets all this out month by month is called the amortisation schedule (tableau d'amortissement): the bank must give it to you with the loan offer.

Term and rate: the two levers

The effect of the term

Still €200,000 at 3.5%:

TermMonthly paymentTotal interest cost
15 years€1,429.77€57,358
20 years€1,159.92€78,381
25 years€1,001.25€100,374

Lengthening the term lowers the monthly payment, but makes the total cost soar: going from 15 to 25 years cuts the payment by about 30%, but almost doubles the interest. That's the big trade-off: a manageable payment today against a higher total cost.

The effect of the rate

€200,000 over 25 years:

RateMonthly paymentTotal interest cost
3%€948.42€84,527
3.5%€1,001.25€100,374
4%€1,055.67€116,702

Half a point on the rate means about €16,000 more or less interest over 25 years. Hence the value of shopping around (several banks, possibly a broker). Mortgage rates have moved a lot in recent years: about 1% in 2021, over 4% at the end of 2023, around 3 to 3.5% in 2025. Check current rates before any simulation.

Fixed or variable rate

In France, the vast majority of mortgages are fixed-rate: your payment doesn't change for the whole term, whatever happens to market rates. A variable rate sometimes starts lower but can rise; if you choose one, it's better if it's "capped". For a first purchase, the security of a fixed rate is often appreciated.

Debt ratio and borrowing capacity

The bank won't lend you just any amount. Since 2022, a standard from the High Council for Financial Stability (HCSF) has been binding on banks:

Debt ratio = total monthly loan payments (including insurance) / net monthly income before tax. Ceiling: 35%, with a maximum term of 25 years (27 years in some cases of new builds or construction).

Banks may depart from these rules for a small share of their applications (about 20%), reserved mainly for main residences and first-time buyers. These rules may change: check they still apply.

Example (fictional): Amandine and Karim earn €4,000 net a month together, with no other loans.

  • Maximum monthly payment: 4,000 × 35% = €1,400, insurance included.
  • If borrower insurance costs about €50 a month, €1,350 is left for the loan itself.
  • At 3.5% over 25 years, a €1,350 payment lets them borrow about €269,700 (it's the monthly payment formula, run backwards).

Careful: other existing loans (car, consumer, revolving: remember lesson 8) count in the calculation. With a €250-a-month car loan, only €1,150 would be left for the mortgage, and a borrowing capacity of about €229,700, i.e. €40,000 less. Paying off small loans before applying for a mortgage is often a very good idea.

Money left to live on

The debt ratio doesn't tell the whole story. Banks also look at money left to live on (reste à vivre): what's left once the payment is made. A couple earning €10,000 a month and paying €3,500 a month keeps €6,500; a single person earning €2,000 and paying €700 keeps €1,300. Same debt ratio, very different situations. They also look at how you run your accounts (no repeated overdrafts, regular saving) and your deposit.

The other elements of the offer

  • The TAEG (the French APR): it includes the nominal rate, insurance, arrangement and guarantee fees. It's what you should compare from one bank to another, as for consumer credit (lesson 8).
  • Arrangement fees: often a few hundred euros up to 1% of the amount, negotiable.
  • Early repayment penalties (IRA): if you repay early (when selling, for example), the bank can charge penalties, capped by law at 6 months' interest on the amount repaid, without exceeding 3% of the outstanding capital. They're negotiable at signing.
  • Protective time limits: after receiving the offer, you must wait at least 10 days before accepting it. That's the time to reread it calmly.

We'll talk about borrower insurance, guarantees and notary fees in the next lesson, because they weigh heavily on the bill.

Key takeaways

  • A standard mortgage is repaid in equal monthly instalments; at first, they're mostly interest.
  • Lengthening the term lowers the payment but sharply increases the total cost.
  • A few tenths of a point on the rate mean thousands of euros: compare offers, and compare the TAEG.
  • Maximum debt ratio: 35% including insurance, maximum term 25 years (HCSF rules, check them).
  • Other loans reduce your borrowing capacity: pay them off before you start.
  • The bank also looks at your money left to live on, your deposit and how you run your accounts.

Exercise

  1. You earn €3,800 net a month. What maximum monthly payment (including insurance) will a bank accept, with a 35% debt ratio?
  2. You already have a €200-a-month car loan. What monthly payment is left for your mortgage?
  3. You borrow €150,000 at 3.2%. Over 20 years, the payment is €846.99 and the interest cost €53,279. Over 15 years, it's €1,050.36 for €39,065 of interest. How much interest do you save with 15 years, and how much more does it cost you each month?
  4. In the first month of a €150,000 loan at 3.2%, what is the interest share of the payment?
  5. Food for thought: your bank tells you "we can lend you €270,000". Does that mean you should borrow €270,000?
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. 3,800 × 35% = €1,330 a month, insurance included.
  2. 1,330 − 200 = €1,130. The car loan "eats" €200 of mortgage payment, which corresponds to tens of thousands of euros less borrowing capacity.
  3. Interest saving: 53,279 − 39,065 = €14,214 (€14,213.50 with the cents). Extra monthly effort: 1,050.36 − 846.99 = €203.37. If your budget allows it without sacrificing your emergency fund, the shorter term is much cheaper.
  4. 150,000 × 0.032 / 12 = €400 of interest. Of an €846.99 payment (20 years), only €446.99 repays capital in the first month.
  5. No! It's a maximum, calculated by the bank according to its rules. You need to look at your real budget (lesson 3): money left to live on, the emergency fund you want to keep, your plans (children, travel, career change), costs to come (works, property tax, service charges). Borrowing a bit less than the maximum leaves you a precious safety margin over 20 or 25 years.

Next lesson: borrower insurance, loan guarantees and notary fees, those extra costs that weigh heavily on the bill.

24.html:
The costs people forget in the simulation

Yesterday we calculated a mortgage's monthly payment and your borrowing capacity. But when you buy, the bill doesn't stop at interest. Three items are added, and together they can amount to several tens of thousands of euros:

  • borrower insurance, which protects the bank (and your family) if you can no longer repay;
  • the loan guarantee, which protects the bank if you stop paying;
  • notary fees (frais de notaire), paid on the day of signing.

Good news: on some of them, you have real room for manoeuvre.

Borrower insurance

Legally, it isn't compulsory. In practice, no bank will lend without it for a property purchase. It repays all or part of the loan in your place if you die or can no longer work.

The cover

CoverWhat it covers
DC (death)The outstanding capital is repaid in the event of death.
PTIA (total and irreversible loss of autonomy)You can no longer work and need help with everyday activities.
ITT (temporary incapacity for work)Monthly payments are covered during sick leave, after a waiting period (often 90 days).
IPT / IPP (total / partial permanent disability)Lasting disability, according to a disability rate defined in the contract.

Read the exclusions carefully (certain sports, back problems or mental health conditions sometimes poorly covered): that's often where contracts differ.

The cover split (quotité)

When two people borrow together, each is insured for a quotité, i.e. a percentage of the capital. The total must be at least 100%.

  • 50 / 50: if one dies, the insurance repays half the outstanding capital; the survivor pays the other half.
  • 100 / 100: if one dies, everything is repaid. Maximum protection, but double the premium.
  • A split in proportion to income (70 / 30 for example) is a common compromise.

How much does it cost?

The premium is expressed as a percentage per year, either of the initial capital (a fixed amount each month) or of the outstanding capital (an amount that falls over time). It depends mainly on your age, your health and whether you smoke.

Example (fictional): Amandine and Karim, 31 and 33, borrow €200,000 over 25 years. Their bank offers them its group policy at 0.30% of the initial capital a year.

Bank's policy (0.30%)Insurance delegation (0.12%)
Annual cost€600€240
Monthly cost€50€20
Cost over 25 years€15,000€6,000

By going to an outside insurer with equivalent cover, they save €9,000. This is insurance delegation (délégation d'assurance): the bank must accept it if the cover is at least equivalent to what it requires, and can't change its loan rate in return.

The Lemoine law

Since 2022, the Lemoine law has changed the picture:

  • you can switch borrower insurance at any time, free of charge, even after signing (with equivalent cover);
  • the health questionnaire is abolished for loans where the insured share is below €200,000 per person and which end before you turn 60;
  • the right to be forgotten for former cancer and hepatitis C patients has been reduced to 5 years after the end of treatment; the AERAS agreement also helps people with an aggravated health risk.

In practice: even if you accepted your bank's insurance in a rush, you can shop around a few months later. Check the exact conditions in force on service-public.fr.

Loan guarantees

On top of insurance, the bank wants a guarantee in case you simply stop paying. Two main families:

  • The mortgage charge (hypothèque, or the lender's lien now called the special legal mortgage): in case of serious arrears, the bank can force the sale of the property. It goes through the notary, which costs fees on registration, and above all on release (mainlevée) if you sell before the end of the loan.
  • The bank guarantee (caution, from a specialist body such as Crédit Logement, or a mutual for some civil servants): the body repays the bank, then turns to you. Cost often around 1 to 1.5% of the amount borrowed, part of which may be returned to you at the end of the loan.

On €200,000 borrowed, a guarantee at 1.2% costs about €2,400. The caution is the most common solution today, but ask for both quotes each time.

Notary fees

The name is misleading: most of these fees do not go to the notary, but to the State and local authorities.

Notary fees ≈ 7 to 8% of the price for an existing property, ≈ 2 to 3% for a new build.

They're made up of three parts:

  • transfer duties (droits de mutation, taxes), by far the biggest share for existing property: about 5.8% of the price, and up to about 6.3% in the départements that used the option to raise them opened in 2025 (first-time buyers are exempt from the rise, subject to conditions);
  • the notary's fees (émoluments), their actual pay, set by a regulated scale (around 1% of the price);
  • disbursements and miscellaneous costs (planning documents, land registry...).

For an existing flat at €250,000, allow about 250,000 × 7.5% = €18,750. For a new build at the same price, about 250,000 × 2.5% = €6,250. New builds are however often more expensive per m², so it isn't an automatic advantage.

These rates change (départements have some leeway on transfer duties): make an estimate with the notaires de France simulator before building your financing plan.

Who pays for what?

Banks generally prefer the deposit to cover at least the notary and guarantee fees, because these sums create no value in the property: if you sold the next day, they'd be lost. A deposit of about 10% of the price is a frequently quoted benchmark. That's why the patient saving of lessons 11 to 15 matters so much for a property project.

The total cost, in one sentence

When comparing offers, add up: interest + insurance + guarantee + arrangement fees. That's what the TAEG seen yesterday summarises. And alongside that, don't forget the notary fees, which don't depend on the bank but weigh on your deposit.

Key takeaways

  • Borrower insurance is required by banks: death, PTIA, ITT and disability cover, split according to a quotité when two people borrow.
  • Insurance delegation can save several thousand euros; the Lemoine law lets you switch insurance at any time.
  • The bank requires a guarantee: a mortgage charge or a caution (often 1 to 1.5% of the amount borrowed).
  • Notary fees are about 7 to 8% of the price for existing property, 2 to 3% for new builds, and are mostly taxes.
  • A deposit covering at least the notary and guarantee fees reassures banks.
  • Rates and rules change: simulate and check on service-public.fr and official sites.

Exercise

  1. You borrow €180,000 over 20 years with insurance at 0.25% of the initial capital a year. What is its annual, monthly and total cost?
  2. Estimate the notary fees for a €200,000 property, existing (7.5%) and new (2.5%).
  3. A couple borrows with a quotité of 60% on Zoé and 40% on Hugo. Hugo dies when €150,000 remains to be repaid. How much does the insurance repay?
  4. On a €220,000 loan over 25 years, the bank offers insurance at 0.34% of the initial capital, an outside insurer 0.10% with equivalent cover. What's the total saving?
  5. Food for thought: why might a couple who earn roughly the same and have a child prefer a 100 / 100 quotité despite the cost?
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. Annual cost: 180,000 × 0.25% = €450. Monthly: 450 / 12 = €37.50. Total over 20 years: 450 × 20 = €9,000.
  2. Existing: 200,000 × 7.5% = €15,000. New: 200,000 × 2.5% = €5,000.
  3. The insurance covers Hugo's quotité: 150,000 × 40% = €60,000. Zoé will have to repay the remaining €90,000 alone.
  4. Bank: 220,000 × 0.34% = €748 a year. Outside: 220,000 × 0.10% = €220 a year. Saving: (748 − 220) × 25 = 528 × 25 = €13,200. That's exactly what insurance delegation makes possible.
  5. With 50 / 50, if one dies, the survivor must pay half the loan alone on a single salary, while bringing up a child: the payment could then be a huge share of their income. With 100 / 100, the home is fully paid off. It's a trade-off between a certain cost (higher premium) and protection against a rare but dramatic event. There's no single right answer: it depends on income, savings and other protection (income protection, lesson 31).

Next lesson: case study, we follow a couple through their first home purchase from A to Z, from budget to signing.

25.html:
Putting it all together

Since the start of the module, we've looked at renting (lesson 21), the rent-or-buy calculation (lesson 22), mortgages (lesson 23), then insurance, guarantees and notary fees (lesson 24). Today we put the pieces of the puzzle together by following a couple, step by step, from the idea of buying to their first month in their new flat.

All the figures are fictional but realistic for 2025. Rates, ceilings and fees change: in real life, redo the calculations with the conditions of the moment.

Step 1: take stock

Camille, 29, a nurse, and Yanis, 31, a technician, live in Toulouse. They rent a 3-room flat for €950 a month including charges and want to buy their main residence. Their situation:

ItemAmount
Net monthly income (€2,300 + €2,200)€4,500
Available savings (Livret A, LDDS)€45,000
Existing loansnone
Current monthly savingsabout €900

First reflex, from lesson 2: a clear review. Second reflex, from lesson 11: don't put all your savings into the purchase. They decide to keep €10,000 as an emergency fund (about three months of spending). Their deposit will therefore be €35,000.

Step 2: estimate the budget

With €4,500 of income, the 35% rule (lesson 23) allows them a monthly payment of 4,500 × 35% = €1,575, insurance included. But Camille and Yanis want to keep some margin: they'd like a child in the next few years, and Camille is considering part-time work. They set themselves a more prudent personal ceiling of about €1,250 a month.

They get an agreement in principle from their bank, and a simulation from a broker, which puts them at around 3.4% over 20 or 25 years. This document will reassure sellers during viewings.

Step 3: find the property and build the financing plan

After several months of viewings, they fall for an existing 62 m² 3-room flat at €220,000, well insulated (DPE rating C), in a well-connected area. They check the minutes of the co-ownership's general meetings (no major works voted or in the pipeline) and the amount of the service charges.

Financing plan: price + notary fees + guarantee fees + arrangement fees = deposit + amount borrowed

NeedsAmount
Property price€220,000
Notary fees (≈ 7.5%)€16,500
Bank guarantee (estimate)€2,400
Arrangement fees€800
Total to finance€239,700
Deposit− €35,000
Amount to borrow€204,700

The deposit covers the fees (16,500 + 2,400 + 800 = €19,700) and about €15,300 of the price: banks like that.

The preliminary sale agreement

They sign a compromis de vente (preliminary sale agreement) at the notary's, with a condition precedent of obtaining a loan: if no bank will lend to them on the stated terms, the sale is cancelled and they get their deposit back (often 5 to 10% of the price, paid into a notary's account, never directly to the seller). They also have a 10-day cooling-off period after signing.

Step 4: choose the term

The bank offers them 3.4% over 20 or 25 years. They compare:

20 years25 years
Monthly payment excluding insurance€1,176.69€1,013.83
Insurance (delegation, 0.15% of initial capital)€25.59€25.59
Total monthly payment€1,202.28€1,039.42
Debt ratio (on €4,500)26.7%23.1%
Total interest cost€77,705€99,449

Choosing 20 years costs about €163 more a month, but saves about €21,745 in interest. Both options respect their personal ceiling of €1,250. They go for 20 years, negotiating the option to adjust repayments (temporarily lower the payment if hard times come) and reduced early repayment penalties.

For insurance, they used delegation (lesson 24): their outside policy at 0.15% costs them €307 a year instead of the roughly €600 of the bank's policy, with equivalent cover and a 50 / 50 quotité.

Step 5: signing and the new budget

After receiving the loan offer, they wait the legal 10 days before accepting it, then sign the final deed (acte authentique) at the notary's about three months after the compromis. They get the keys.

Their new monthly housing budget:

ItemPer month
Loan payment + insurance€1,202.28
Property tax (€1,100 a year)€91.67
Service charges€120.00
Total€1,413.95

That's about €464 more than their €950 rent. Their monthly savings therefore drop from €900 to about €436. But be careful how you read that figure: of the €1,202 payment, about €600 a month is already repaying capital at the start (it's savings "in bricks and mortar"), and that share grows every month. In the first month, interest comes to 204,700 × 3.4% / 12 ≈ €580.

They also add an "upkeep" line to their budget: a water heater to replace or water damage happens, and there's no longer a landlord to pay instead of them.

The mistakes they avoided

  • Emptying all their savings into the deposit: with no cushion, the first unexpected event becomes a crisis.
  • Borrowing the maximum the bank offered: they set their own ceiling according to their plans.
  • Signing up to the bank's insurance without comparing: several thousand euros saved.
  • Forgetting the service charges and property tax in the calculation: here they amount to over €200 a month.
  • Neglecting the co-ownership: a façade renovation voted just after the purchase can cost thousands of euros.

Key takeaways

  • Keep your emergency fund out of the deposit.
  • Set your own monthly payment ceiling, often lower than the bank's maximum.
  • The financing plan adds up price, notary fees, guarantee and arrangement fees, minus the deposit.
  • The compromis must include a loan condition precedent; you have a 10-day cooling-off period.
  • Compare several terms: a shorter term costs more per month but much less in total.
  • Your new housing budget includes property tax, service charges and upkeep, not just the loan payment.

Exercise

  1. Estimate the notary fees for an existing flat at €260,000 (7.5% rate).
  2. Price €180,000, notary fees €13,500, guarantee €2,000, arrangement fees €500, deposit €25,000. How much must be borrowed?
  3. Income €3,600 net, monthly payment €1,050 plus €30 of insurance. What is the debt ratio? Can the bank lend under the 35% standard?
  4. Back to Camille and Yanis: how much interest do they save by choosing 20 years rather than 25?
  5. Food for thought: a year after the purchase, Yanis loses his job. What did the couple put in place that helps them get through this period?
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. 260,000 × 7.5% = €19,500.
  2. 180,000 + 13,500 + 2,000 + 500 = €196,000 to finance. Minus the deposit: 196,000 − 25,000 = €171,000.
  3. (1,050 + 30) / 3,600 = 1,080 / 3,600 = 30%. That's below the 35% ceiling: the application passes this criterion (the bank will also look at money left to live on and the deposit).
  4. 99,449.28 − 77,704.60 = €21,744.68, i.e. about €21,745. For €163 more a month over 20 years, that's a nice saving.
  5. First, the €10,000 emergency fund they kept out of the deposit. Next, their €1,202 payment can still be met with Camille's salary (€2,300) plus Yanis's unemployment benefit, even if the budget gets tighter. The adjustable repayments they negotiated let them temporarily lower the payment. Finally, depending on their contract, job-loss cover (if they took it out, which is rare) might kick in. Conversely, had they borrowed the maximum at 35% and emptied their savings, the situation would quickly have become critical.

Next lesson: we open the module on long-term investing with the risk/return trade-off, applied to your savings.

26.html:
The golden rule of investing

Welcome to module 6, on long-term investing. Until now, your savings have mostly lived in savings accounts: simple, available, risk-free (lessons 11 and 12). But you also saw, in lesson 15, that inflation nibbles away at their return. To grow savings over 10, 20 or 30 years, you often have to accept something else. Before talking about assurance-vie, the PEA or ETFs, you need to understand the rule that governs all investments:

There's no such thing as a high return without risk. The more an investment promises to earn, the more it can lose.

Remember this sentence well. It'll also protect you from scams (lesson 10): an "investment guaranteed at 12% a year" doesn't exist.

The three dimensions of an investment

Every investment is judged on three criteria, sometimes shown as a triangle:

  • return: what the investment earns (interest, dividends, capital gains);
  • risk: the possibility of losing part of your capital, or of its value fluctuating a lot;
  • liquidity: how easily and quickly you can get your money back.

No investment is excellent on all three at once. The Livret A is perfectly liquid and risk-free, but its return is modest. Shares have a higher expected return, but their value can fall sharply. Property can be profitable, but it's not very liquid: selling takes months.

What is risk, in practice?

For a saver, risk takes two forms:

  • volatility: the value goes up and down, sometimes violently, from one month or year to the next;
  • capital loss: when you need your money, it's worth less than what you paid in.

Volatility is only a real problem if you're forced to sell at the wrong moment. That's where your investment horizon comes in.

The main families of investments

Here are orders of magnitude (approximate, not to be taken as promises: past returns are no guide to future returns).

InvestmentAnnual return, order of magnitudeRiskLiquidity
Regulated savings accounts1.5 to 3% in recent years, close to inflationNoneImmediate
Assurance-vie euro fundsabout 2 to 3% (2023-2024)Very low, capital guaranteed by the insurerA few days
Bondsvariable depending on rates and the issuerLow to mediumGood
Propertyrents + price changes, highly variableMediumLow
Shares (global market, over the long run)about 6 to 8% a year as a historical averageHigh in the short termGood

For shares, the average hides very different years: rises of over 20%, but also brutal falls, such as about − 40% to − 50% during the 2008 crisis, or a plunge of about a third in a few weeks at the start of the Covid crisis in 2020. Markets recovered, but it took several years after 2008.

The effect of return over time

Why accept this risk? Remember compound interest (lesson 13). Over 20 years, €10,000 invested at different rates becomes:

Annual returnCapital after 20 years
2%€14,859
4%€21,911
6%€32,071

A few extra points of return almost double the final result. That's the reward, the risk premium, that markets offer on average to those who accept fluctuations. But this reward is never guaranteed.

Time, your best ally

Over one year, shares can lose 30% or more. Over 15 or 20 years, historically, diversified stock markets have most often ended up higher, even after going through crises. The risk of loss falls with the horizon, without ever disappearing completely.

Money you'll need in less than 2 to 3 years shouldn't be exposed to high risk. Money you won't need for 8 to 10 years or more can bear more volatility.

That's the direct link with lesson 14: each goal has its horizon, each horizon its investment. The fund for next year's driving licence goes in a savings account; savings for retirement in 35 years can lean more towards shares.

Watch out for one trap: losses are harder to recover than people think. After a 30% fall, you need a rise of about 43% to get back to where you started; after a 50% fall, you need + 100%.

Diversify: don't put all your eggs in one basket

Diversification means spreading your money across several investments that don't react in the same way. If one company goes bust, it has little impact on a portfolio of hundreds of companies. If shares fall, the euro fund doesn't move.

Example (fictional): Mehdi, 35, has €10,000 invested for the long term: €6,000 in diversified shares and €4,000 in a euro fund. In a bad year, shares lose 30% and the euro fund earns 2.5%. His portfolio is worth 6,000 × 0.70 + 4,000 × 1.025 = 4,200 + 4,100 = €8,300, i.e. − 17%. Had he put everything in shares, he'd have lost 30%. Diversification doesn't remove risk; it softens it.

That's the logic of asset allocation: deciding what share of your savings goes into each type of investment. You'll see in lesson 29 that a "world" ETF lets you diversify your shares across hundreds of companies in one go. The site's finance course goes into the theory behind it (expected return, standard deviation, portfolio).

Your risk profile

Your capacity to take risks depends on three things:

  • your horizon: when will you need this money?
  • your situation: do you have an emergency fund, a stable income, debts?
  • your emotional tolerance: could you watch your savings fall by 30% without panicking and selling everything at the worst moment? (Remember the biases from lesson 5.)

When you open an investment, the bank or insurer must have you fill in a questionnaire to assess this profile. Answer honestly: it isn't an exam. And remember: this course gives you no personalised advice; it gives you the tools to understand and ask the right questions.

Key takeaways

  • No return without risk: an investment that promises a lot with no risk is suspect.
  • An investment is judged on three criteria: return, risk, liquidity.
  • Shares have historically had the best return over the long run, but with sharp temporary falls.
  • The investment horizon is key: short-term money risk-free, long-term money more exposed.
  • Diversification reduces risk without removing it.
  • Your risk profile depends on your horizon, your situation and your tolerance for losses.

Exercise

  1. You invest €5,000 at 3% a year for 10 years (compound interest). How much do you get?
  2. A €10,000 portfolio holds 60% shares and 40% euro fund. Shares lose 30%, the euro fund earns 2.5%. What's the new value?
  3. After a 30% fall, by how much must your investment rise to get back to its starting value?
  4. Rank these needs from shortest to longest horizon, and say which type of investment seems suitable: a trip in 8 months, a deposit for a property purchase in 4 years, a retirement top-up in 30 years.
  5. Food for thought: a friend tells you about an investment "guaranteed at 12% a year, no risk, but you need to decide quickly". What do you think of this offer in the light of this lesson?
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. 5,000 × 1.03¹⁰ = €6,719.58.
  2. 6,000 × 0.70 + 4,000 × 1.025 = 4,200 + 4,100 = €8,300, a fall of 17%.
  3. You need 0.70 × (1 + h) = 1, so h = 1 / 0.70 − 1 ≈ 42.9%. A 30% fall is recovered by a rise of almost 43%.
  4. Trip in 8 months: regulated savings account, no risk. Deposit in 4 years: short-to-medium horizon, the capital must be secure (savings accounts, euro funds), since a market fall just before the purchase would be very awkward. Retirement in 30 years: a long horizon; a large share in riskier, diversified investments such as shares can be justified, depending on your profile.
  5. It's a warning sign: a return that's high and risk-free doesn't exist. Pressure ("decide quickly") is a scam classic (lesson 10). You need to check that the intermediary is authorised (AMF and ACPR lists) and, if in doubt, pay nothing in.

Next lesson: the assurance-vie, France's favourite investment: euro funds, unit-linked funds, fees and tax.

27.html:
France's favourite investment

With total holdings of around €2,000 billion, assurance-vie (literally "life insurance") is the most widely used investment in France after savings accounts. Yet many people have one without really knowing how it works. Its name is misleading: it isn't really insurance in the usual sense (like car insurance); it's above all a savings wrapper, with advantageous tax and inheritance rules.

Yesterday you saw the risk/return trade-off. Assurance-vie is interesting precisely because it lets you set the slider between security and return yourself, within a single wrapper.

One wrapper, several funds

An assurance-vie is a contract (the wrapper) into which you pay money, invested in one or more funds: the euro fund and unit-linked funds.

You can make payments whenever you like (or scheduled monthly payments), and withdraw your money at any time: this is called a rachat (partial or total surrender). Contrary to popular belief, the money is not locked up for 8 years. The 8-year period only matters for tax.

The euro fund

This is the secure fund (fonds euros). The insurer guarantees your capital (with a small nuance: the guarantee may be net of management fees). It invests mainly in bonds. The interest is permanently locked in each year: this is the ratchet effect (effet cliquet): what's been earned can't be lost again.

Return: around 1% in 2021 (very low rates), about 2.5% on average in 2023 and 2024, with big differences between contracts. That's a bit above savings accounts in some years, below in others. Some contracts require a minimum percentage of unit-linked funds to access their euro fund.

Unit-linked funds (UC)

These are all the other funds (unités de compte, UC): share funds, bond funds, ETFs (lesson 29), property (SCPI, SCI)... Their value fluctuates: the capital isn't guaranteed. In return, the expected return over the long run is higher, especially for shares. You choose the split yourself (self-directed management), or you leave the choice to the insurer according to your profile (managed portfolio).

If you put 70% in the euro fund and 30% in share UCs, you already have a diversified allocation, like Mehdi's in the previous lesson.

Fees: keep a close eye on them

Type of feeOrder of magnitude
Fees on payments (entry fees)0% on most online contracts, up to 3 to 5% in some bank networks (negotiable)
Annual management fees on the wrapperabout 0.5% to 1% a year
Fees on UC fundsfrom 0.1% to 0.3% for an ETF, often 1.5% to 2% for an active fund
Switching fees (changing funds)often free online, sometimes charged

These fees look small, but they apply every year and compound. Example (fictional): €20,000 invested for 20 years in funds earning 5% gross a year. With 0.6% management fees, 4.4% net remains: you get about €47,319. With 1% fees, 4% remains: about €43,822. Gap: almost €3,500, for 0.4 points of fees.

Before signing up, read the key information document and compare. Contracts offered over the counter at traditional banks are often more expensive than online contracts: remember lesson 6 on hidden fees.

Tax: what counts is the age of the contract

As long as you don't withdraw anything, your gains are not subject to income tax. The only exception: on the euro fund, social levies are taken every year on the interest. When you withdraw, only the share of gains contained in the withdrawal is taxed, not your capital.

Share of gains in a withdrawal = withdrawal amount × (total gains / contract value)

Then everything depends on the age of the contract (2025 rules, for total payments below €150,000, check on impots.gouv.fr):

Age of the contractIncome tax on gainsSocial levies
Less than 8 years12.8% (flat-rate levy, the PFU from lesson 19), or the scale by option17.2%
8 years or moreannual allowance of €4,600 of gains (€9,200 for a married or PACS couple), then 7.5%17.2%

The social levy rate was changed for some capital income from 2026: check the rate applicable to assurance-vie when you withdraw.

Example (fictional): Nadia paid €20,000 into a contract opened 10 years ago, entirely in unit-linked funds. It's now worth €26,000, i.e. €6,000 of gains. She withdraws €6,500 to change her car.

  • Share of gains: 6,500 × 6,000 / 26,000 = €1,500. The remaining €5,000 is capital, not taxed.
  • Income tax: the contract is more than 8 years old and €1,500 is below the €4,600 allowance: €0.
  • Social levies: 1,500 × 17.2% = €258.

Had her contract been less than 8 years old, she'd have paid 1,500 × 30% = €450 (12.8% + 17.2%).

The most frequently given tip

Since it's the contract's opening date that starts the 8-year clock, not the date of each payment, many people open a cheap contract early with a small payment, to "start the clock". The day they need it, the contract will already have its age.

Passing on wealth, in a nutshell

Assurance-vie is also a tool for passing on wealth. On death, the capital is paid to the beneficiaries you've named in the beneficiary clause, outside the normal estate. For payments made before age 70, each beneficiary benefits from an allowance of €152,500 (rules in force in 2025). We'll come back to this in lesson 34. Take care drafting this clause and update it when your life changes.

Key takeaways

  • Assurance-vie is a wrapper, not a single investment; the money remains available at any time.
  • The euro fund guarantees the capital; unit-linked funds offer a higher expected return, with no guarantee.
  • Fees (entry, management, funds) weigh heavily over time: compare contracts.
  • On a withdrawal, only the share of gains is taxed.
  • After 8 years, an annual allowance of €4,600 (€9,200 for a couple) applies to gains: opening early is useful.
  • The beneficiary clause organises passing on wealth, with favourable tax treatment.
  • Rates and ceilings change: check on impots.gouv.fr or service-public.fr.

Exercise

  1. You pay €5,000 into a contract that charges 3% entry fees. How much is actually invested?
  2. You've paid €10,000 into a contract worth €12,500. You withdraw €5,000. What's the share of gains in this withdrawal?
  3. Same withdrawal. Calculate the tax (including social levies at 17.2%) if the contract is more than 8 years old (single person), then if it's less than 8 years old (30% PFU).
  4. €10,000 invested for 15 years in funds earning 4.5% gross a year: compare the result with 1% annual fees and with 2% annual fees.
  5. Food for thought: Lucas, 22, has €300 of savings on top of his emergency fund. Why might it be worth his while to open a low-fee assurance-vie contract right now?
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. Fees: 5,000 × 3% = €150. Amount invested: €4,850. You'll already need to earn 3% just to get your stake back.
  2. Total gains: €2,500. Share of gains: 5,000 × 2,500 / 12,500 = €1,000 (and €4,000 of capital).
  3. Over 8 years: €1,000 is below the €4,600 allowance, so €0 income tax; social levies 1,000 × 17.2% = €172. Under 8 years: 1,000 × 30% = €300.
  4. With 1% fees, the net return is 3.5%: 10,000 × 1.035¹⁵ ≈ €16,753. With 2%, it's 2.5%: 10,000 × 1.025¹⁵ ≈ €14,483. Gap: about €2,270, just because of fees.
  5. Because the 8-year clock starts when the contract is opened. If he opens it now with a small payment, his contract will be 8 years old when he's 30, just when he might have plans (buying a home, children). Future payments will benefit from this tax age. He just needs to choose a contract with no entry fees and reasonable management fees, and bear in mind that the euro fund / UC split depends on his horizon and profile.

Next lesson: the PEA and the ordinary securities account, the two wrappers for investing directly in shares.

28.html:
Becoming a (tiny) part-owner of companies

In lesson 26 you saw that shares have historically offered the best return over the long run, at the price of big swings. Yesterday you discovered that you can access them through the unit-linked funds of an assurance-vie. But there are two wrappers designed specifically for investing on the stock market: the PEA (plan d'épargne en actions, a French share savings plan) and the ordinary securities account (compte-titres ordinaire, CTO). Today we look at how they work and how they differ.

Reminder: what a share earns

A share is a slice of a company's capital. It can earn money in two ways: dividends (part of the profits paid out to shareholders) and capital gains (the difference between the selling price and the purchase price).

If you buy a share at €50 and sell it at €65 after receiving €3 of dividends, your total gain is 15 + 3 = €18. But if it falls to €35, you lose €15 (minus the dividends received). A share's price depends on the company's results and on what investors expect: the site's finance course explains how a company is valued, and the trading course how stock market orders work.

An important reminder: buying a few shares in companies picked on gut feeling concentrates your risk. Many individuals who buy and sell often lose money. For most savers, diversification (lesson 29) is the most reasonable route.

The ordinary securities account (CTO)

This is the simplest and freest wrapper:

  • no ceiling on payments;
  • every security in the world: French, American, Japanese shares, bonds, funds, ETFs...;
  • you can open as many as you like, and withdraw whenever you like;
  • but no tax advantage.

Dividends and realised capital gains (at the time of sale) are taxed in the year you receive them, under the single flat-rate levy (PFU) seen in lesson 19: 12.8% income tax + 17.2% social levies, i.e. 30% (2025 rates; you can opt for the progressive scale if that's better for you). Capital losses can be offset against capital gains in the same year and the following 10 years.

The PEA: the tax wrapper for European shares

The rules of the game

  • One PEA per person (so two for a couple), reserved for French tax residents.
  • Payment ceiling: €150,000. It's the payments that count: if your PEA climbs to €300,000 thanks to capital gains, no problem. There's also a PEA-PME (with a combined ceiling of €225,000 with the PEA) and a "young person's" PEA for 18 to 25-year-olds attached to their parents' tax household, limited to €20,000.
  • Eligible securities: mainly shares in companies headquartered in the European Union (or the European Economic Area), and funds or ETFs that respect this rule. No direct US shares, no bonds.
  • Fees are capped by law (brokerage, custody fees), which protects against abusive pricing.

How the tax works

Inside the PEA, you can sell, buy and receive dividends: no tax as long as the money stays in the wrapper. Everything happens when you withdraw, depending on the age of the plan:

Age of the PEA at withdrawalConsequenceTaxation of gains
Less than 5 yearsA withdrawal in principle means closing the plan (except in certain cases: redundancy, disability, starting a business...)30% PFU (12.8% + 17.2%)
5 years or morePartial withdrawals possible, the plan stays open and you can keep paying inExempt from income tax, only social levies (17.2%) remain due

As with assurance-vie, it's the opening date that starts the clock. Opening a PEA early, even with a small payment, lets you "start the clock".

Comparison on an example (fictional)

Julien, 27, invests €10,000 in European shares. Six years later, his investment is worth €14,000. He sells everything. Gain: €4,000.

Securities accountPEA (over 5 years)
Income tax4,000 × 12.8% = €512€0
Social levies4,000 × 17.2% = €6884,000 × 17.2% = €688
Total€1,200€688
Net gain€2,800€3,312

The PEA saves him €512. And in the securities account, he'd also have paid 30% every year on his dividends, which slows compound growth; in the PEA, dividends are reinvested tax-free. Over 20 or 30 years, the gap becomes very large.

PEA, CTO or assurance-vie: what does what?

WrapperStrengthsLimits
PEAVery gentle tax after 5 years, capped feesEuropean shares (and eligible ETFs) only, €150,000 ceiling, withdrawal before 5 years penalised
Securities accountTotal freedom of securities and amountsTaxed at 30% every year on realised gains and dividends
Assurance-vieSecure euro fund, tax benefits after 8 years, passing on wealthChoice of funds limited to the contract, annual management fees

There's no single "right" wrapper: many savers combine several according to their goals and horizons (lesson 14). This course doesn't tell you which to choose: it's up to you to match these rules with your situation.

Opening and using a wrapper

PEAs and securities accounts can be opened at a traditional bank, an online bank or an online broker. Compare brokerage fees (per order placed) and any custody fees: on small amounts, fixed fees of €5 to €10 per order can eat a good chunk of the gain. Also check that the firm is properly authorised in France (AMF and ACPR registers), especially for platforms that advertise heavily.

Key takeaways

  • A share earns through dividends and capital gains, but can also lose money.
  • The securities account: all securities, no ceiling, gains taxed at 30% (PFU, 2025 rate).
  • The PEA: European shares and eligible ETFs, a €150,000 payment ceiling, one per person.
  • After 5 years, PEA gains are exempt from income tax (social levies only).
  • Before 5 years, a withdrawal in principle closes the PEA: only put long-term money in it.
  • Opening early lets you start the clock; compare brokerage fees.

Exercise

  1. In your securities account, you make a €2,500 capital gain. How much tax do you pay with the 30% PFU?
  2. Same capital gain, realised by withdrawing from your PEA opened 7 years ago. How much do you pay?
  3. Your PEA is 3 years old and you want to withdraw €2,000 for a trip. What happens?
  4. You receive €300 of dividends in your securities account. How much do you get net, with the PFU? And if these shares were in a PEA?
  5. Food for thought: Inès wants to invest in shares of a big American tech company and in an ETF that tracks shares across the whole world. Which wrapper for each?
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. 2,500 × 30% = €750 (€320 income tax + €430 social levies).
  2. After 5 years, only social levies apply: 2,500 × 17.2% = €430. Saving: €320.
  3. Before 5 years, a withdrawal in principle means closing the PEA: you lose its age, and the gains are taxed under the PFU. That's why you only put money in a PEA that you won't need for a long time. For a trip, the savings should be in a savings account.
  4. Securities account: 300 × 30% = €90 of tax, leaving you €210. In a PEA, dividends stay in the wrapper with no immediate tax: you can reinvest the full €300.
  5. The American share is not eligible for the PEA: it can only go in a securities account (or sometimes as a unit-linked fund in an assurance-vie). For the world ETF, there are PEA-eligible ETFs that replicate a global index using a technical mechanism (synthetic replication, lesson 29): so it can go in a PEA, with the advantageous tax treatment after 5 years.

Next lesson: ETFs and passive investing, or how to invest simply, in a diversified way and for very low fees.

29.html:
What if you stopped trying to beat the market?

Yesterday you saw the wrappers for investing in shares (PEA, securities account). One question remains: which shares should you buy? Picking companies yourself takes time and knowledge, and exposes you to concentration risk. Handing your money to a professional fund manager is expensive, and guarantees nothing. There's a third way, which has become very popular over twenty years: buying the whole market in one go, for next to nothing. That's the promise of ETFs and passive investing.

What is an ETF?

An ETF (exchange-traded fund, also called a tracker or listed index fund) is a fund that aims to reproduce the performance of a stock market index as faithfully as possible, and that is bought and sold on the stock exchange like a share.

An index is a basket of shares that represents a market. A few examples (approximate compositions):

  • the CAC 40: 40 large companies listed in Paris;
  • the S&P 500: about 500 large American companies;
  • the MSCI World: about 1,400 to 1,500 large and mid-sized companies from 23 developed countries, about 70% of them American in recent years;
  • "All World" or ACWI indices, which add emerging countries.

By buying a single unit of an MSCI World ETF, you indirectly become a shareholder in more than a thousand companies. That's the diversification of lesson 26, in a single click.

Active versus passive management

Active management (traditional fund)Passive management (ETF)
AimDo better than the marketDo as well as the market
MethodA manager selects the securitiesThe fund replicates the index
Ongoing annual feesoften 1.5 to 2%often 0.05 to 0.4%

Why passive often wins

Fees

A fund's fees are taken every year, whatever the performance. They compound, like interest (lesson 13), but to your detriment.

Example (fictional): Clara invests €10,000 for 25 years. The market returns 6% a year gross (an assumption, not a promise). She compares two options:

OptionAnnual feesNet returnCapital after 25 years
World ETF0.2%5.8%€40,939
Active fund that just matches the market1.8%4.2%€27,970

Gap: about €12,969, more than the initial stake! Just to match the ETF, the active manager must beat the market by 1.6 points a year, every year, for 25 years.

The statistics

Long-term studies (notably the SPIVA reports, published regularly by S&P) show that, over 10 to 15 years, a large majority of active funds, often around 80 to 90% depending on markets and periods, do worse than their benchmark index once fees are deducted. And those that win over one period aren't necessarily the same ones over the next: it's impossible to know in advance which to choose.

That doesn't mean no manager ever beats the market. It means that, for an individual, identifying in advance the good managers is extremely difficult.

What an ETF doesn't do

An ETF isn't a risk-free investment. It replicates the market, including its falls. If the index loses 20%, your ETF loses about 20% too. In 2008 or 2020, share ETFs plunged like the rest of the market. Everything we said in lesson 26 applies: a long horizon, an emergency fund on the side, and the ability not to panic.

Other points to watch:

  • a "world" ETF is still concentrated: a lot of United States, and a few very large tech companies weigh heavily;
  • some ETFs are highly specialised (one sector, a trendy theme, leveraged...): they are much riskier and no longer fit the idea of simple diversification;
  • currency risk: an ETF holding American shares is sensitive to the dollar exchange rate.

Reading an ETF's factsheet properly

When you look at an ETF, several pieces of information appear on its factsheet (the key information document):

  • the index replicated: the most important, it determines what you own;
  • the ongoing charges (often shown as the TER): the lower the better, for the same index;
  • assets under management: a very small ETF risks being closed;
  • the replication method: physical (the fund really holds the index's shares) or synthetic (the fund holds another basket and swaps its performance for the index's via a contract called a swap). Synthetic replication lets world ETFs, for example, be eligible for the PEA;
  • accumulating or distributing: an accumulating ETF automatically reinvests dividends; a distributing ETF pays them out to you. In a securities account, the accumulating version avoids being taxed every year on dividends;
  • its ISIN code, which identifies the product precisely (two ETFs with similar names can be very different).

A simple strategy

Many long-term savers settle for a very simple set-up: an emergency fund in a savings account, a secure pot (a euro fund, for example) for medium-term projects, and one or two broadly diversified ETFs for the long term. This is sometimes called a "lazy portfolio". It's cheap, easy to follow, and saves you spending your evenings scrutinising the markets. It isn't personalised advice: it's a logic worth knowing, which you adapt to your horizon and profile.

If you want to understand the mechanics of markets and stock orders, the site's trading course goes further. But bear in mind that long-term investing and trading are two very different activities: most retail traders lose money.

Key takeaways

  • An ETF replicates an index and trades on the stock exchange like a share.
  • It offers instant diversification (hundreds or even thousands of companies).
  • Its fees are very low, and over 20 or 30 years, fees make a huge difference.
  • Over the long run, a large majority of active funds do worse than their index after fees.
  • A share ETF is not risk-free: it follows the market down too.
  • Check the index, fees, size, replication, accumulating or distributing, and PEA eligibility.

Exercise

  1. You have €15,000 in an ETF with 0.25% annual fees. How much do you pay in fees a year? And in an active fund at 1.9%?
  2. €5,000 invested for 25 years in a market returning 7% gross a year: compare the final capital with 0.2% fees (net return 6.8%) and with 2% fees (5%).
  3. You hold 50 units of an ETF bought at €100 each. The index falls 20%. What's your investment worth?
  4. In a securities account, why can an accumulating ETF be more tax-efficient than a distributing ETF?
  5. Food for thought: an adviser shows you an active fund that has beaten the market over the last three years, with 2% annual fees. What questions do you ask yourself?
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. ETF: 15,000 × 0.25% = €37.50 a year. Active fund: 15,000 × 1.9% = €285 a year, more than seven times as much.
  2. With 0.2% fees: 5,000 × 1.068²⁵ ≈ €25,897. With 2%: 5,000 × 1.05²⁵ ≈ €16,932. A gap of about €8,965.
  3. Initial value: 50 × 100 = €5,000. After the fall: 5,000 × 0.80 = €4,000. It's only a realised loss if you sell; with a long horizon, you can wait for a possible recovery, with no guarantee.
  4. With a distributing ETF, dividends are paid to you and taxed every year (30% with the PFU, 2025 rate). With an accumulating ETF, they're reinvested in the fund: tax only applies when you sell, on the capital gain. So all your money keeps working, which strengthens the compound-interest effect. In a PEA, the question matters less since dividends aren't taxed as long as they stay in the wrapper.
  5. Three years is very short: is it skill or luck? The good funds of one period aren't necessarily those of the next. Next, the 2% fees are certain, every year, whereas future outperformance isn't. Finally, is the adviser paid on this product (retrocessions)? We'll come back to this in lesson 39 on self-interested advice.

Next lesson: investing regularly, with scheduled investing (DCA), which smooths out entry points and turns saving into a habit.

30.html:
The paralysing question: "Is now the right time?"

You now have the building blocks: risk and return (lesson 26), wrappers (lessons 27 and 28), diversified ETFs (lesson 29). And yet many people freeze when it's time to act, with the same question: "What if the market falls right after I invest?" Nobody can predict markets in the short term, not you, not the experts on TV. So instead of looking for the perfect moment, you can decide to stop looking for it altogether. That's the idea behind scheduled investing.

The principle of DCA

DCA (dollar cost averaging, also called scheduled investing or purchase-price averaging) means investing the same amount at regular intervals (for example every month), whatever the level of the market.

In practice, you set up an automatic payment of €100 or €200 every month into your assurance-vie or your PEA, invested in one or more funds. And you don't think about it any more.

The mechanism is simple: with a fixed amount, you buy more units when the price is low and fewer units when it's high. Your average purchase price smooths itself out automatically.

An example in a choppy market (fictional)

Yasmine invests €200 a month in an ETF for 6 months. The unit price yo-yos:

MonthUnit priceAmount investedUnits bought
1€100€2002.00
2€80€2002.50
3€60€2003.33
4€80€2002.50
5€100€2002.00
6€120€2001.67
Total€1,20014.00

Her average cost price is 1,200 / 14 ≈ €85.71 per unit, whereas the average price over the period is €90. At the end of month 6, her 14 units are worth 14 × 120 = €1,680, for €1,200 invested.

Had she invested everything at once in month 1, at €100, she'd have had 12 units, worth 12 × 120 = €1,440. Here, the dip in the middle worked in DCA's favour: she bought lots of cheap units in month 3.

Average cost price with DCA = total invested / total number of units bought. It's always less than or equal to the simple average of the prices.

But DCA doesn't always win

Let's try again with a market that rises steadily: €100, 105, 110, 115, 120, then 125. With €200 a month, Yasmine would buy about 10.73 units, at an average price of about €111.85. In month 6, they'd be worth about €1,341. Had she invested everything in month 1, her 12 units would be worth €1,500.

This is an important and honest result: since stock markets have historically gone up more often than down over the long run, investing a large sum in one go has, on average, given a better result than spreading it out, in about two cases out of three according to several studies. DCA isn't a magic formula for earning more.

So why talk about it? Because its real advantages lie elsewhere.

The real advantages of DCA

1. It fits your reality: you save every month

Most people don't have a large sum to invest: they have a salary, every month. DCA is simply the natural translation of the monthly saving in your budget (lesson 3). It's the "pay yourself first" principle: the payment goes out just after your salary, before spending, as we saw in lesson 4.

2. It defuses emotions

Remember the psychology of money (lesson 5): when markets crash, fear pushes you to sell; when they soar, euphoria pushes you to buy too high. With an automatic payment, there's no decision to make. Better still: falls become "sales", since your €200 buys more units.

3. It reduces regret

Investing €20,000 the day before a crash is a painful experience that can put you off investing for years. By spreading it out, that scenario becomes impossible. For someone with a large sum who's afraid, spreading the investment over a few months is a reasonable psychological compromise, even if it isn't optimal on average.

4. It puts time on your side

This is the winning combination of the whole module: compound interest + regularity + time. With €150 a month and a hypothetical return of 5% a year (monthly payments compounded monthly):

PeriodTotal paid inFinal capital (5% assumption)
20 years€36,000about €61,655
30 years€54,000about €124,839

Ten more years, and the final capital doubles. Once again: starting early counts more than anything (lesson 13). These figures are simulations, not promises: the real return may be lower, and there will be years of decline.

Setting up DCA

  • Choose the wrapper (assurance-vie, PEA) according to your horizon and tax (lessons 27 and 28).
  • Choose the fund: for DCA, a diversified fund such as a broad ETF is the most common; DCA into a single share concentrates the risk.
  • Check the fees: in an assurance-vie, scheduled payments are often free; in a PEA, fixed brokerage fees per order can weigh on small amounts (some brokers offer scheduled investment plans with reduced fees).
  • Set a sustainable amount: better €50 for 20 years than €300 for 6 months before stopping.
  • Keep your emergency fund intact: DCA is long-term money. If something unexpected happens, it's not what you should sell in a panic.
  • Don't check every day: once a quarter or once a year is plenty.

Key takeaways

  • DCA means investing the same amount at regular intervals, whatever the market.
  • It smooths the purchase price: more units when prices are low, fewer when they're high.
  • On historical average, investing in one go has often done slightly better, but DCA matches the reality of a monthly salary.
  • Its main strength is psychological: no decisions, no timing, fewer regrets.
  • Combined with time and compound interest, it can grow modest savings significantly.
  • Choose a sustainable amount, a diversified fund and low fees, and keep your emergency fund separate.

Exercise

  1. You invest €100 a month for 3 months. The unit price is €50, then €25, then €50. How many units do you have, and what's your average cost price?
  2. In question 1, what's the simple average of the prices? Why is your cost price lower?
  3. What are your units worth at the end of month 3, and what's your gain or loss?
  4. With €100 a month for 20 years and a hypothetical return of 5% a year, you get about €41,103. How much did you pay in, and what share of the final capital comes from gains?
  5. Food for thought: Arthur, 30, receives a €20,000 inheritance. He already has an emergency fund and wants to invest for the long term, but he's very afraid of a crash right afterwards. What options does he have, and what are their pros and cons?
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. Month 1: 100 / 50 = 2 units. Month 2: 100 / 25 = 4 units. Month 3: 100 / 50 = 2 units. Total: 8 units for €300. Average cost price: 300 / 8 = €37.50.
  2. Simple average: (50 + 25 + 50) / 3 ≈ €41.67. Your cost price is lower because, in month 2, your €100 bought twice as many units: the low-price period weighs more in your average.
  3. 8 × 50 = €400, for €300 invested: a gain of €100, even though the unit price has returned exactly to its starting level. That's the smoothing effect.
  4. Paid in: 100 × 12 × 20 = €24,000. Gains: 41,103 − 24,000 = €17,103, about 42% of the final capital.
  5. Option 1: invest everything at once. On historical average, this has often worked best, but if there's a crash right afterwards, he risks panicking and selling at the worst moment. Option 2: spread it (for example €2,000 a month over 10 months). Less optimal on average, but more comfortable, and it limits regret. Option 3: a mix (part now, the rest spread out). The most important thing isn't to choose the theoretically perfect solution, but the one he can stick with without panicking for 15 or 20 years, with diversified, low-cost funds. This isn't personalised advice: it's up to him to choose according to his profile.

Next lesson: we open the module "Protecting yourself and preparing for the future" with the essential insurance policies: home, civil liability, health and income protection.

31.html:
Why it matters

So far, we've mainly talked about growing your money: savings, savings accounts, PEA, ETFs, scheduled investing. This module changes angle: we're going to protect what you're building. Because a single uncovered accident (water damage to the downstairs neighbour's flat, six months off work, a hospital stay) can wipe out years of savings in a few weeks.

Insurance is a simple exchange: you pay a small, certain sum (the premium) to get rid of an uncertain but potentially enormous risk. Remember lesson 26 on the risk/return trade-off: here, you accept "losing" a little every year to remove the disaster scenario.

Golden rule: insure what you couldn't pay for yourself. The rest, your emergency fund (lesson 11) can absorb.

Home insurance and civil liability

What's compulsory

If you're a tenant, you must insure your home at least against tenant's risks (fire, water damage, explosion): the landlord can ask you for a certificate every year. If you're a co-owner in a block, civil liability cover is compulsory. An owner-occupier of a detached house isn't legally obliged, but going without would be very unwise (and the bank often requires it with a loan, lesson 24).

What a "multirisque habitation" (comprehensive home policy) includes

  • Damage to the home: fire, water damage, natural disasters, broken glass.
  • Your belongings (furniture, appliances, computer): against theft, fire, etc. Check the ceiling and how you're compensated (new-for-old or with a deduction for wear).
  • Private civil liability (responsabilité civile): it pays for damage that you (or your children, your dog) cause to other people. Your bike hits a pedestrian, your washing machine floods the flat below: that's what kicks in.

Civil liability is often the most valuable cover: bodily injury caused to someone can cost hundreds of thousands of euros. It's almost always included in a comprehensive home policy. If you live with your parents, you're usually covered by their policy: check.

Excess (franchise): the part of the claim you pay yourself. A higher excess lowers the premium.

For a student or young worker in a studio flat, a comprehensive policy often costs around €80 to €200 a year (an order of magnitude, varying widely by city and floor area). Compare at least three quotes, and reread the list of exclusions.

Health: Sécurité sociale and the mutuelle

In France, the Assurance maladie (state health insurance) reimburses part of your healthcare (for example, for a consultation with a GP who follows the official fee scale, a large majority of the standard fee). The rest, the ticket modérateur (patient co-payment), as well as fees above the official rate, glasses or dental care, can be covered by a complémentaire santé (top-up health insurance), often called a mutuelle.

  • Private-sector employee: your employer must offer you a group mutuelle and pay at least half of it. It's often a very good deal.
  • Student: you can often stay on your parents' mutuelle up to a certain age, or take out a student policy.
  • Low incomes: the Complémentaire santé solidaire (a state-backed top-up cover) can be free or cost a few euros a month depending on your resources. Check your eligibility on ameli.fr.

The classic trap: paying for cover you don't use (premium optical "boosts" when you have excellent eyesight). Conversely, hospital cover is the item never to neglect.

Income protection (prévoyance): the forgotten one

Income protection covers what happens to you, and to your ability to earn a living: time off work, disability, death. It's the least-known cover, and yet the one that protects your main source of income: your salary.

On sick leave, the Sécurité sociale pays daily allowances that only replace part of your salary (around half of the daily gross salary, with a ceiling and a waiting period; the rules change, check on ameli.fr or service-public.fr). The employer often tops it up, and a company income protection scheme can top it up further. A self-employed person (lesson 38) is far less well covered: for them, individual income protection is practically essential.

Fictional example: Karim, 28, earns €2,000 net a month. After a skiing accident, he's off work for 4 months. Let's assume that in total (Sécu + employer) he receives €1,600 a month after the first few days. He loses €400 × 4 = €1,600. Unpleasant, but his emergency fund can absorb it. But if he were self-employed with no income protection and received only €900 a month, the loss would be €1,100 × 4 = €4,400, and the scenario of long-term disability would be dramatic.

Death: if nobody depends on your income, life cover is rarely a priority. As soon as you have a partner, children or a mortgage, the question arises (borrower insurance, seen in lesson 24, already covers the loan).

Reviewing your insurance

Here's the fictional annual budget of Jade, 25, a young employee renting a two-room flat in Lyon:

PolicyAnnual costRisk coveredVerdict
Comprehensive home policy€150Home, belongings, civil liabilityEssential
Company mutuelle (her share)€360Healthcare, hospitalEssential
Car insurance (third party plus)€540Motor civil liability (compulsory), theftCompulsory if you have a car
Phone insurance€120Smartphone damage, theftDebatable
TV extended warranty€60Breakdown after 2 yearsOften pointless
Total€1,230

Jade could replace the phone and TV out of her emergency fund: these two policies cost €180 a year for a moderate risk. Over 5 years that's €900, often more than the cost of a repair. Also watch out for duplicates: your premium bank card or your home policy sometimes already cover certain items, travel or car hire.

Good habits

  • List all your policies once a year, with their cost and what they cover.
  • Shop around: the law generally allows you to cancel most home, car and health policies at any time after one year (check your policy's conditions on service-public.fr).
  • When you make a claim: report it quickly (often within a few working days, 2 days for theft), keep photos and receipts.

Key takeaways

  • Insurance swaps a small certain loss (the premium) for removing a rare but heavy risk.
  • Insure first what you could not pay for yourself; small risks are your emergency fund's job.
  • Civil liability is the key cover: it pays for damage caused to others. It's usually included in a comprehensive home policy.
  • The mutuelle tops up the Assurance maladie; hospital cover is the essential item.
